Lennon stepped back to admire the finished tipi, door facing a direction Quill said was always east, toward the sunrise.

"It's basically a perfectly engineered stadium for one family," Lennon said. "I'm stealing this idea for Roblox."

"PLAY ON," Quill said, which Lennon decided was definitely becoming his new favorite phrase.

chapters.heading: Final Whistle
chapters.text:
The tipi faded, and color rushed back in all at once — present day, bright and buzzing.

"Last stop," Quill said. "Now."

Lennon looked around a wide, sunlit gathering — drums, dancing, kids his age laughing near a food stand, elders talking in a language he didn't recognize but liked the sound of anyway.

"Today, there are **574 federally recognized tribes** in the United States," Quill said. "Each with its own government, its own traditions. And people still speak about **175 Indigenous languages** right now, this year, this afternoon."

"That's more teams than the whole World Cup," Lennon said.

"The **Cherokee Nation** is the largest of all of them," Quill added. "But every single one of those 574 has its own story — and most of them never made it into your school's textbook."

Quill nodded toward a woman addressing the crowd with calm, easy authority. "Leaders like her keep those stories alive. Women like Wilma Mankiller, who became the first woman to lead the Cherokee Nation back in 1985. Or Deb Haaland, who in 2021 became the first Native American ever to run a whole department of the United States government."

Lennon watched the dancing a while longer, matching its rhythm the way he'd match a warm-up drill — not performing, just paying attention.

"I didn't know any of this four hours ago," he admitted.

"Now you do," Quill said. "That's the whole match, Captain. You don't win it by watching from the bench."

The light folded again, gentler this time, and Lennon's knees hit his own bedroom carpet.

His laptop glowed, Roblox stadium right where he'd left it — except now, tucked beside the goal he'd built, sat a tiny earthen mound he definitely hadn't placed there himself.

On his desk, the feather lay still again, gold at the tip, exactly like before.

Almost.

Lennon picked it up, turning it slowly in the lamp light. "Same time tomorrow?"

It didn't answer. But he was pretty sure it would.

story.ending_line: Tomorrow there was a free kick to practice — and a whole continent of real history to tell his teammates about.

true_facts.text: Around **13,000 BC**, the ancestors of Native Americans crossed a land bridge from Siberia into Alaska.
About **11,000 years ago**, the Folsom people hunted bison across the Great Plains in small family groups.
Around **3500 BC**, people built **eleven earthen mounds** at Watson Brake in Louisiana — about **800 years before Egypt's first pyramids**.
Around **1000 CE**, the Mississippian culture built wide earthen mounds and plazas along the Mississippi and Ohio Rivers.
Between **1350 and 1600**, the **Cayuga, Mohawk, Oneida, Onondaga,** and **Seneca** nations formed the **Iroquois Confederacy**, with the **Tuscarora** joining in **1722**.
By the **1400s**, nations including the **Apache, Cherokee, Chickasaw, Navajo,** and **Sioux** were already thriving across the land that is now the United States.
In **1492**, Christopher Columbus landed in the Caribbean and mistakenly called the people he met **"Indians,"** thinking he had reached the East Indies.
A **tipi's** frame starts with three or four poles tied into a tripod, then built up with more poles, sometimes **eighteen or more**.
A tipi's outer cover was traditionally made from several **buffalo hides** sewn together, or later from canvas.
A tipi's floor is actually an **oblong**, egg-like shape, not a true circle, which keeps the fire centered.
The tipi's cone shape on that oval base makes it **aerodynamic**, so wind helps hold it steady in storms.
Today there are **574 federally recognized tribes** in the United States, each with its own government and traditions.
About **175 Indigenous languages** are still spoken across the United States today.
The **Cherokee Nation** is the largest tribe in the United States today.

new_recurring.name: Quill
new_recurring.rule: A golden feather guide who wakes whenever Lennon is building or inventing something new. Quill speaks in soccer metaphors, calls Lennon 'Captain,' and says 'Play on' as a catchphrase before sending him into real history.

bible_suggestions.ending_summary: Lennon returns from his Roblox portal adventure to find a tiny earthen mound mysteriously added beside his in-game stadium, with the golden feather Quill resting quietly on his desk once more.

violations.quote: His screen flickered. Black. Then green. Then black again. "No, no, no — not during the save," Lennon muttered, smacking the side of his laptop like that ever worked. The feather on his desk answered instead.

story.title: Theo Presses Start
story.subtitle: One glitch, one pixel, and fifty years of games — all before bedtime.

chapters.heading: Level 1: The Bouncing Dot (1958)
chapters.text:
Theo was lying on his bedroom floor at 10:47 p.m., laptop open, trying to make a penalty-kick game in **Roblox Studio** actually feel right. Every time he scripted the ball, it floated like a balloon or dropped like a brick. Nothing in between.

"Just arc, please," he muttered, mashing the play button for the ninth time.

The screen flickered — green, then black, then green again — and a single square of light popped up in the corner of the screen like a loading icon that had given up loading. It blinked twice.

"Hiya," said the pixel, in a voice like an old dial-up tone learning to talk. "Name's Byte. You've got a bug. I've got fifty years of them. Want to see where this whole mess started?"

Before Theo could answer, the screen swallowed him whole.

He landed in a humming room full of machines the size of refrigerators. A man in a lab coat was hunched over a round green screen — an **oscilloscope**, a machine built to draw wobbly lines of electricity, not games.

"**William Higinbotham**, 1958," Byte whispered. "**Brookhaven National Laboratory**. He wired this thing up so two people could bounce a dot back and forth over a line, like tennis. He called it **'Tennis for Two.'**"

The dot on the screen dropped dead the second it crossed the net, landing with a sad little *thud*.

"Your arc's too flat," Theo said immediately, elbowing in. "You need more curve on the way down — like a free kick." He reached for the gravity knob Higinbotham was fiddling with and eased it back, the way he nudged settings in Studio.

The dot floated up, hung, and dropped in a smooth bounce.

**WHOOOOSH — thud — bounce.**

A line of lab visitors waiting outside the door actually cheered.

"First video game ever shown to the public," Byte said, "and it just got Theo'd."

Theo grinned. Not bad for a Tuesday night.

chapters.heading: Level 2: The Computer That Played Back (1962)
chapters.text:
The lab dissolved into a room stacked with cabinets of blinking lights, a machine Byte called a **PDP-1** — a giant computer that filled a whole wall, back when computers didn't fit on a desk.

A college student was arguing with two friends over a keyboard. "If I can program a line of dots curving around the sun," he said, "I can program two spaceships shooting at each other."

"**Steve Russell**, **MIT**, **1962**," Byte said. "He and his friends are about to build **'Spacewar!'** — the first game people actually competed in, head to head."

The two ships on screen kept drifting into each other by accident, which nobody found impressive.

Theo watched the controls — two buttons each, thrust and turn. It reminded him of setting up a two-player minigame in Studio, where if both players mash the same button layout, chaos happens.

"Give each ship separate controls," he said. "Right now you've basically got one team fighting itself."

Russell blinked, then swapped the wiring so each player had their own thrust and fire key.

**BZZZT — pew — pew!**

The ships finally dodged each other on purpose. One scored a hit.

"THAT'S what a rivalry looks like," Theo said, and the three programmers whooped like they'd won the World Cup.

"Spacewar! never sold a single copy," Byte said as they left, "but almost every programmer who touched a computer in the sixties played it. Sometimes the biggest hit is the one nobody buys."
chapters.shout_line: THAT'S what a rivalry looks like!

chapters.heading: Level 3: The Brown Box in the Garage (late 1960s–1972)
chapters.text:
Next stop: a cluttered workshop with wires everywhere and a plain television in the corner.

"**Ralph Baer**," Byte said, nodding at an engineer soldering something onto a plywood board. "People call him the father of video games. He's trying to make a game you play on your own TV at home — no lab required."

The box on the table was wrapped in wood-grain tape to look less like a tangle of wires. Baer flipped a switch, and two square dots appeared on the television, chasing each other.

"The **Brown Box**," Baer explained, wiping his hands. "Only problem is nobody can tell what they're supposed to do with it."

Theo thought about the first screen every Roblox game shows a new player — the instructions, the big obvious button. "You need something simple printed right on the TV," he said. "Like 'Player 1, Player 2, Score.' People won't guess."

Baer grabbed a grease pencil and scrawled a scoreboard straight onto a clear plastic overlay stuck to the screen.

**CLICK.** Suddenly the chasing dots looked exactly like two paddles playing catch.

"This became the **Magnavox Odyssey** in **1972**," Byte said, "the very first home video game console. Before this, if you wanted to play a game, you had to leave the house."

Theo looked at his own TV-less bedroom setup and felt a small, ridiculous amount of pride on Baer's behalf.

chapters.heading: Level 4: The Machine That Ate Quarters (1972)
chapters.text:
A buzzing arcade cabinet appeared next, lit up with the word **PONG**, a bouncing square ball between two paddles of light.

"**Nolan Bushnell** and **Ted Dabney** started a company called **Atari** in **1972**," Byte said, "and this was their very first arcade hit."

A kid about Theo's age was already hunched over the machine, spinning the paddle dial like his life depended on it. **Bip. Bip. BOOP.** Every point landed with a satisfying electronic chirp.

"There's a story," Byte added, "that one early machine jammed completely — stuffed so full of quarters from people playing nonstop that it stopped working. Might be a bit of a stretch, but it tells you how fast this thing caught on."

Right on cue, the cabinet in front of them made a loud **CLUNK** and the screen froze.

"Called it," Theo said, grinning, and knelt down to the coin slot like he was debugging a script. He gave the machine's coin box a gentle shake — the arcade equivalent of restarting the server.

A cascade of quarters spilled onto the carpet.

**CLATTER-CLATTER-CLATTER.**

The line of waiting kids cheered like he'd scored a goal, and the machine blinked back to life.

"Nice work, support team," Byte said.

chapters.heading: Level 5: Cartridges and Invaders (1977–1978)
chapters.text:
The arcade melted into a living room with wood paneling and a console the size of a shoebox.

"This is the **Atari 2600**, from **1977**," Byte said. "Before this, a machine only knew one game, built right in. This one takes **cartridges** — little plastic slabs you can swap in and out."

A kid was digging through a shoebox of cartridges like Theo digging through his own list of saved Roblox games, trying to find the right one.

"That's basically a game library," Theo said. "You should sort them — by how fun they are, not alphabetically." He started stacking the cartridges by color, fastest ones on top.

The kid popped one in. The TV filled with rows of blocky aliens marching sideways, dropping lower with every pass.

"**Space Invaders**," Byte said, "made in **1978** by a designer named **Tomohiro Nishikado**. It kicked off a worldwide arcade craze — lines out the door, pockets full of quarters."

The aliens picked up speed, **ZAP ZAP ZAP**, and the kid on the couch yelped and then laughed, blasting the last one just in time.

"They get faster as there's fewer of them," Theo said, impressed. "That's such a good trick. I'm stealing that for my game."

"Everyone's been stealing that trick for fifty years," said Byte. "Welcome to game design."

chapters.heading: Level 6: Too Many Bad Games (1980–1983)
chapters.text:
A yellow circle gobbled dots across the next screen, chased by four little ghosts.

"A game from 1980," Byte said. "Designer Toru Iwatani — the story goes he got the idea looking at a pizza with one slice missing. Might be a little too perfect a story, but it's a good one."

Theo laughed and admitted he'd absolutely design a game based on a snack if the chance came up.

Then the scene changed, and changed for the worse. Suddenly the room was stacked floor to ceiling with cartridge boxes, all slightly different, most of them bad.

"**1983**," Byte said. "Everybody tried to cash in on the craze, rushing out games nobody tested properly. Stores filled up with junk, and people stopped buying. It's called the **video game crash** — the whole North American market shrank almost overnight."

A truck outside was dumping crates of unsold cartridges — including some stamped **E.T.** — into a dusty pit in the New Mexico desert.

"They buried them?" Theo asked.

"Buried and basically forgotten," Byte said, "until diggers found the landfill for real in **2014** and confirmed the whole story."

Theo thought about every half-finished Roblox project he'd abandoned because he rushed it. "That's what happens when you ship something before it's actually good," he said. "I test my stuff like six times before I publish it."

"Smartest kid in this chapter," Byte said.

chapters.heading: Level 7: A Plumber and Some Falling Blocks (1984–1985)
chapters.text:
A small office in Japan, sketches of a mustached man taped to every wall.

"**Shigeru Miyamoto**," Byte said. "He's designing a jumping hero for a new console called the **NES**, launching in **1985** — the system that's about to save the whole industry after the crash."

On the test screen, a stubby plumber leapt at a brick and sailed straight over it, missing completely.

"That jump's too floaty at the top and too fast on the way down," Theo said, watching closely. "Same problem as the tennis dot. You want him to hang in the air a half second longer right at the peak — makes it feel like you're actually aiming."

Miyamoto adjusted the numbers. The plumber jumped again, paused at the top like he was deciding something, then landed square on the brick.

**Ding!** A coin popped out.

"**Super Mario Bros.**," Byte said. "It'll be the game that comes packed in the box with every NES. Mario becomes the most famous character in games, full stop."

Next door, a quieter office in Moscow: a programmer named **Alexey Pajitnov** watched blocks tumble down a screen, stacking and vanishing in neat rows.

"**Tetris**, **1984**," Byte said. "No hero, no plot. Just blocks. People still can't put it down."

Theo tried a round, rotating a falling piece at the last second into a perfect gap.

**CLICK.** The whole row vanished.

"Oh, I get it," he whispered. "I get it completely."

chapters.heading: Level 8: Speed, Discs, and Teammates (1991–1994)
chapters.text:
A blue blur shot across the next screen so fast Theo almost missed it.

"A blue hedgehog character from 1991," Byte said. "Sega built that game fast on purpose, to rival another famous game."

Theo clocked Sonic's loop-the-loop and whistled. "He's basically doing a rainbow flick," he said — his favorite trick shot from soccer, just sideways and at ridiculous speed.

Then a disc, spinning and catching light, slid into a slot.

"**PlayStation**, **1994**," Byte said. "Sony's first console. It uses **CDs** instead of cartridges, which means room for fuller video and real music."

A rumble of explosions came from the next room over — not scary, just loud, a crowd of players laughing and shouting through a tangle of cables.

"**Doom**, **1993**," Byte said. "It's a shooter, but the part that changed everything is this: players connected their computers together in the same room, just to play each other. People called it a **LAN party**."

Theo watched four players high-five after a match, same as his own team after a good scrimmage. "That's the whole point of a team game," he said. "Doesn't matter what it is — soccer, this, Studio with my friends. It's better with people yelling next to you."

"Exactly the discovery this whole industry eventually made too," said Byte.

chapters.heading: Level 9: Blocks, Motion, and the Trip Home
chapters.text:
The last room was brighter, more familiar. A white remote with a wrist strap sat on a shelf.

"**Wii**, **2006**," Byte said. "Nintendo put motion controls inside it, so you swing your whole arm instead of pressing a button. Suddenly grandparents and little sisters were gaming too."

Theo swung an imaginary tennis racket and nearly knocked over a lamp. "Okay, that one's dangerous for my room specifically," he admitted.

Beyond it stretched a blocky green world, endlessly under construction.

"**Minecraft**, **2011**," Byte said. "Made by a Swedish developer named **Markus Persson**, who went by **Notch**. It became the best-selling video game of all time — just because people wanted to build."

Theo recognized the feeling instantly. It was exactly what he did every night in Studio: not just playing a world, making one.

One last door opened onto a quiet museum hall lined with glass cases — controllers, cartridges, a worn copy of Tetris.

"**World Video Game Hall of Fame**," Byte said. "Opened **2015**, at a museum called **The Strong**, in Rochester, New York. Every game you just helped fix is in here somewhere."

Theo looked at the cases — Tennis for Two's oscilloscope, Mario's first sketch, a Pong cabinet with a suspiciously full coin box — and felt, for one ridiculous second, like he belonged among them.

Then the museum folded into green static, and he was back on his bedroom floor, laptop glowing, Byte blinking once in the corner of the screen.

He looked at his penalty-kick script. On a hunch, he adjusted the arc the exact way he'd nudged Higinbotham's knob — a little hang at the top, a curve on the way down.

He pressed play.

The ball curled, hung, and dropped into the corner of the net.

**WHOOOOSH — GOAL.**

"Finally," Theo whispered, and saved the file before his eyes could close on their own.

story.ending_line: Tomorrow, the game would be ready to publish — and there was still a Hall of Fame case out there with his name on it, eventually.

true_facts.text: In **1958**, a scientist named **William Higinbotham** built **'Tennis for Two'** on a round-screened machine called an **oscilloscope**, at **Brookhaven National Laboratory**.
In **1962**, a student named **Steve Russell** and his friends at **MIT** programmed **'Spacewar!'** on a giant computer called the **PDP-1**.
**Ralph Baer**'s home TV prototype grew into the **Magnavox Odyssey**, released in **1972** as the first home video game console.
Also in **1972**, **Nolan Bushnell** and **Ted Dabney** founded **Atari** and released the arcade hit **Pong**.
A popular story says an early **Pong** machine once jammed from being stuffed with too many quarters — maybe a stretch, but it shows how fast the game caught on.
In **1978**, designer **Tomohiro Nishikado** created **Space Invaders**, sparking an arcade craze around the world.
The **video game crash of 1983** shrank the North American market after stores filled up with rushed, low-quality games.
A famous story says unsold cartridges, including **E.T.**, were buried in a New Mexico landfill — and diggers confirmed it for real in **2014**.
**Shigeru Miyamoto** designed **Super Mario Bros.** in **1985**, starring the plumber Mario, gaming's most famous character.
In **1984**, **Alexey Pajitnov** invented the falling-block puzzle game **Tetris** at a computer center in Moscow.
Sony entered consoles in **1994** with the **PlayStation**, using **CDs** for fuller video and sound.
The 1993 game **Doom** popularized multiplayer matches, where players linked computers together at **LAN parties**.
**Minecraft**, released in **2011** by Swedish developer **Markus 'Notch' Persson**, later became the best-selling video game ever.
The **World Video Game Hall of Fame** opened in **2015** at a museum called **The Strong**, in Rochester, New York.

new_recurring.name: Byte
new_recurring.rule: A small blinking pixel-square guide who appears whenever a screen glitches green-then-black. Speaks in short, dry, slightly electronic quips, calls games and inventions by their real names and dates, and always leaves one encouraging one-liner per chapter. Returns at the end of each story, blinking once from the corner of the screen.

bible_suggestions.ending_summary: Theo returned to his own bedroom floor, used the exact trick he'd learned from fixing Tennis for Two to finally get his Roblox penalty-kick arc right, and saved the finished file with Byte blinking quietly in the corner of his screen.

violations.quote: A truck outside was dumping crates of unsold cartridges — including some stamped E.T. — into a dusty pit in the New Mexico desert.

story.title: Theo and the Race to the Moon
story.subtitle: A green light, a tiny astronaut, and the whole space race in one long night

chapters.heading: Chapter 1: The Beep in the Dark
chapters.text:
Theo was supposed to be asleep an hour ago.

Instead he was hunched over his desk, headphones crooked, putting the finishing touches on his newest build: a Roblox level called Orbit Run, where players dodge space junk on the way to a tiny moon. He hit Play to test it.

The screen didn't load. It flickered black, then green, then black again.

A thin sound crackled out of his speakers — not a beep exactly, not static either. Something steady, in between, like a slow little heartbeat.

*beep... beep... beep...*

Theo reached for the volume. That was when the whole screen turned green and something climbed right out of his monitor and landed on the desk, about the size of an action figure, in a scuffed white spacesuit with a cracked helmet visor.

"Finally," she said, dusting off her sleeve. "You left me rendering behind that Play button for an hour."

Theo's voice had gone somewhere and not come back.

"Name's Nova," she said. "Test pilot. You built me, remember? For the astronaut level you never finished." She hopped onto his keyboard and looked up at him. "That beep — that's real. That's the actual sound of the first thing humans ever put into space. Want to hear where it came from?"

Before Theo could answer, the green light swallowed the room.

They landed somewhere cold and dark, wind hissing over flat ground. A silver ball the size of a beach ball sat on a steel frame nearby, with four thin antennas sticking out like whiskers.

"**Sputnik 1**," Nova said. "Launched by the Soviet Union on **October 4, 1957**. First man-made thing ever to **orbit** Earth — orbit just means circling all the way around something, over and over, without falling back down. First-ever **satellite**, too — that's any object that circles another one in space."

"That's it? A metal ball?" Theo said. "It doesn't even have thrusters or arms."

"It didn't need any. It just had to beep." Nova pointed at a radio dish nearby, its needle twitching. "It was only about **58 centimeters wide** — smaller than a beach ball, really — and it sent out one simple signal. People all over the world picked it up on ordinary radios. Your great-great-grandparents could've heard this exact sound."

Theo leaned toward the dish. The signal was buried under a layer of crackle, fading in and out. His fingers itched — this was exactly the kind of thing he fixed in Roblox Studio when a sound effect clipped wrong.

"Can I touch the dial?"

Nova shrugged. "It's history. It's not made of glass."

Theo nudged the tuning knob a half-turn, the way he'd nudge an audio slider. The static thinned. The beep came through clean and steady, filling the cold air.

*beep... beep... beep...*

Nova grinned. "Nice ears, Commander."

"I just turned a knob."

"Half the job is knowing which knob." She hopped back toward the green light. "Come on. It gets bigger from here."

chapters.heading: Chapter 2: A Flying Beeper and a Brand-New Agency
chapters.text:
They landed on a different launchpad, this one swarming with men in white shirts and skinny ties, clipboards everywhere.

"The beep you just heard," Nova said, "scared a whole country into action. One year later, their government said: *we need our own space agency.*"

A rocket on the pad hissed white steam. A tall man in round glasses paced beside it, running a hand through his hair.

"That's **Wernher von Braun**," Nova said. "He'd built rockets before, back in Germany, and now he was leading the team building America's."

"**NASA**," Theo said. "I know that one."

"Officially started on **October 1, 1958**. Before that, this guy was just one engineer among a bunch of different, squabbling programs. The new agency got everyone working from the same playbook — like finally agreeing on which plugin the whole team should use."

Von Braun's rocket, called **Explorer 1**, roared off the pad on **January 31, 1958**. Theo watched it climb, a bright needle against black sky, until it was just a dot.

Back inside a cramped control room, a scientist named James Van Allen hunched over a dial that kept spiking way higher than expected.

"That's weird," Theo said, peering at the readout. It looked a little like a leaderboard that refused to make sense. "It keeps jumping, same spot, every orbit."

The scientist rubbed his eyes. "We don't know what that is yet."

Theo traced the pattern with his finger. Same spike, same place, every single loop. "It's not random," he said. "It's like a belt. A ring around the planet where that number's always higher."

The scientist froze, then grabbed his pencil.

He'd just helped name the **Van Allen radiation belt** — a layer of charged particles trapped by Earth's magnetic field, found because Explorer 1 flew straight through it.

"Not bad," Nova said, "for a kid who just wanted to build a moon level."

Theo tried to look modest. It did not entirely work.

"Okay, but seriously," he said. "How do you even find an invisible belt made of nothing you can see?"

"You build the instrument that can," Nova said. "Then you watch the numbers closely enough to notice when they're trying to tell you something."

chapters.heading: Chapter 3: One Hundred and Eight Minutes
chapters.text:
The next landing dropped them into a crowd of men in heavy coats, breath fogging in cold morning air, all staring up at a rocket taller than anything Theo had ever built in-game.

"Who's flying that?" Theo asked.

"**Yuri Gagarin**," said Nova. "A **cosmonaut** — that's just the Soviet word for astronaut. About to become the first human being ever to leave the ground and keep going."

A hatch sealed shut near the top of the rocket. Somewhere inside sat a young man with an easy grin, strapped into a seat barely bigger than himself.

"**April 12, 1961**," Nova said. "He's about to orbit Earth once, in a capsule called **Vostok 1**. One full trip around the planet, in about **108 minutes**."

Theo did the math fast, the way he sized up a soccer match in his head. "That's basically two whole halves of a game. Back to back. In *space*."

"Faster, though," Nova said. "He'll circle the whole planet in less time than it takes you to walk to school and back twice."

The countdown crackled over a speaker. Somebody in the crowd gripped a clipboard so hard it bent. A static burst drowned the radio feed right as the engines lit.

"We're losing the signal!" a technician shouted.

Theo's stomach dropped — then he spotted it, a loose cable swinging near the base of the antenna dish, same wobble he'd seen a hundred times when his own mic cut out mid-game.

"The cable!" he yelled, pointing. "It's not seated right!"

A technician dove for it, jammed it home. The static cleared. Gagarin's voice crackled through, calm as anything: "*Poyekhali!*" — Let's go.

The rocket climbed on a column of fire, impossibly loud, shaking the ground under Theo's sneakers. He watched until it was a spark, then nothing.

One hundred and eight minutes later, word came back: Gagarin had landed safely, grinning, having circled the entire world while most people were still eating breakfast.

The crowd erupted. Someone threw a hat in the air. Theo, somehow, was cheering too.

"First human in space," Nova said. "And you helped keep the signal clean enough for the whole world to hear him say it."

Theo grinned. "I'm basically an astronaut now."

"You're basically a kid who's good with cables. Let's not get ahead of ourselves."

chapters.heading: Chapter 4: Fifteen Minutes and a Really Big Goal
chapters.text:
They landed on a beach in Florida, sun blazing, a smaller rocket steaming on a different pad.

"America's turn," Nova said. "**Alan Shepard**, going up on **May 5, 1961**. He won't orbit — his flight's short, just up and back down. But he'll be the first American ever in space."

Theo watched the capsule, barely bigger than a phone booth, rattle its way upward and arc back toward the ocean, parachutes blooming white against blue sky. Sailors cheered from a ship below.

"That doesn't sound like much," Theo said.

"It's not about how long," Nova said. "It's about going at all. Now watch what happens next."

The scene shifted to a stage, a podium, a crowd of thousands. A man in a dark suit leaned into the microphone.

"That's President **John F. Kennedy**," Nova said. "**May 25, 1961**. Watch."

"*I believe this nation should commit itself,*" Kennedy said, "*to landing a man on the Moon and returning him safely to Earth, before this decade is out.*"

The crowd went quiet, then roared.

Theo blinked. "Wait — they'd barely gotten fifteen minutes off the ground, and he just picked a deadline?"

"That's the whole point," Nova said. "Set the big goal first. Figure out how later."

Theo understood that one in his bones — it was exactly how he built in Roblox Studio. Decide you want a working elevator system before you know a single line of script that makes it move.

Over the next scene, blueprints unrolled across a huge table: a rocket design three times the height of anything built before.

"The **Saturn V**," Nova said. "Once it's finished, it'll stand **363 feet** tall — taller than the Statue of Liberty."

"That's insane," Theo said, actually meaning it as a compliment. "That's like building a stadium and launching the whole stadium."

"Pretty much," Nova said. "Somebody just had to say the deadline out loud first. Turns out that's the hardest part."

chapters.heading: Chapter 5: Forty-Eight Times Around
chapters.text:
The green light dropped them onto a windswept airfield, where a woman in a flight suit walked toward a waiting capsule with the calm of someone heading to a bus stop.

"**Valentina Tereshkova**," Nova said. "Used to work in a textile factory, sewing. Loved parachute jumping on weekends. Volunteered for this the second they asked."

"They let a factory worker fly to space?" Theo asked.

"They trained her first," Nova said. "But yeah. She wasn't a test pilot like the others. She just wanted it enough."

On **June 16, 1963**, Tereshkova's capsule, **Vostok 6**, thundered off the pad. Theo watched the fire fall away beneath it, the same roaring climb he'd seen before, and it still made his stomach flip every time.

She would circle the Earth **forty-eight times** before coming home — more orbits, Nova said, than every American astronaut up to that point combined.

Back on the ground, waiting out the mission in a cramped control room full of static-filled speakers, Theo found himself next to an engineer chewing a pencil to splinters.

"Aren't you scared for her?" Theo asked — the question he figured everyone else was too polite to actually say out loud.

The engineer looked at him like it was a fair question. "Every single orbit," she admitted. "But she trained for this longer than you've been alive. And she chose it."

When Tereshkova's voice finally crackled back over the radio, calm and clear after her last pass around the planet, the whole room exhaled at once. Someone laughed too loud. Somebody else just put their head down on the desk.

"First woman in space," Nova said. "First to do it completely alone. She orbited the planet more times on that one trip than most astronauts manage across an entire career."

Theo thought about asking Tereshkova what it felt like up there, alone with the whole Earth turning beneath her — but Nova was already tugging his sleeve toward the green light.

"Next stop's a little more hands-on," she said. "Hope you're not afraid of heights."

chapters.heading: Chapter 6: Ten Minutes Outside the Ship
chapters.text:
They landed inside a cramped capsule in orbit, a small round window showing the whole curve of the Earth outside, blue and white and enormous.

A cosmonaut in a bulky suit was wrestling with an airlock hatch.

"**Alexei Leonov**," Nova said. "**March 18, 1965**. About to become the first human ever to leave his spacecraft completely and float free in open space, tethered only by a cable."

The hatch hissed open. Leonov pushed out into nothing, turning slowly, lit gold by the sun. Theo's whole chest went tight watching him drift at the end of a thin line, Earth spinning below like the biggest soccer ball anyone had ever kicked.

"That cable's it?" Theo asked. "That's the only thing keeping him attached?"

"That's the whole spacewalk," Nova said. "About ten minutes out there."

Theo studied the tether where it connected to the suit — a single clip, no backup. In every multiplayer build he'd ever made, a single point of failure was the first thing he fixed.

"That needs a backup clip," Theo muttered. "Just in case."

"Engineers said the exact same thing afterward," Nova said. "They always do, once something's actually been tried for the first time."

Leonov made it back inside, breathless and laughing, his suit stiffened oddly from the vacuum outside. The hatch sealed. Everyone in the cramped capsule cheered.

The green light shifted the scene — quieter this time, a launchpad under ordinary daylight, a capsule sitting still on top of its rocket, not going anywhere.

"This one's harder to watch," Nova said, voice dropping. "**January 27, 1967**. A test on the ground, not even a real launch. A fire broke out inside the capsule during the drill. Three astronauts — **Gus Grissom, Ed White,** and **Roger Chaffee** — died before anyone could get the hatch open in time."

Theo went quiet.

"It's okay to feel bad about that," Nova said. "Everyone did. But here's the part that matters: afterward, engineers redesigned the hatch so it could open in seconds instead of minutes. They swapped out flammable materials inside the capsule. Every mission after that flew safer because of what they learned."

Theo thought about every clumsy mistake he'd ever made in Roblox Studio — a broken spawn point, a trap door that wouldn't open — and how he always rebuilt it stronger afterward.

"They turned it into a fix," he said quietly.

"The best teams always do," Nova said. "Come on. There's somewhere better I want you to see next."

chapters.heading: Chapter 7: The Whole Earth in One Photo
chapters.text:
The green light dropped them somewhere Theo hadn't expected — inside a capsule orbiting not Earth, but the Moon, gray and cratered and close enough to touch through the window.

"**Apollo 8**," Nova said. "**December 1968**. First humans ever to leave Earth's orbit completely and circle the Moon instead."

An astronaut floated near the window, camera in hand, muttering to himself about the view.

"That's **William Anders**," Nova said. "Watch what he's about to do."

Anders twisted around mid-sentence, startled, camera already rising. Outside the window, a blue-and-white marble rose slowly over the gray Moon's horizon — small, bright, impossibly alone against black space.

"*Oh my God, look at that picture over there!*" Anders said. "*There's the Earth coming up. Wow, is that pretty.*"

CLICK.

"**Earthrise**," Nova said quietly. "That photo right there. First time anyone ever saw our whole planet hanging in space like that, all at once, with nothing cut off at the edges."

Theo stared at it longer than he meant to. He'd built a thousand skyboxes in Roblox Studio, painted a thousand fake planets into the backgrounds of his levels. None of them had ever looked like that.

"It's so small," he said.

"That's everyone you've ever met," Nova said, "fitting inside one photograph. Every soccer field you've ever played on. Every bedroom you've ever built a game in."

Theo didn't have anything clever to say back to that. For once, he just let the view sit there instead of rushing past it.

"They weren't even trying to take that picture, you know," Nova added. "They were there to study the Moon. The Earth just happened to rise, and somebody grabbed a camera fast enough."

"Good thing he did," Theo said.

"Best accident in the whole space race," Nova agreed. "Ready for the big one?"

Theo already knew what she meant. He nodded, throat a little tight, and the green light rose up around them both.

chapters.heading: Chapter 8: The Giant Leap
chapters.text:
They landed inside a cramped lunar module, alarms chirping, two astronauts hunched over controls thick with switches.

"**Apollo 11**," Nova said. "**July 20, 1969**. This is it, Commander. The big one."

Theo glanced at a small screen bolted to the panel, numbers ticking down fast. "Is that... fuel?"

"Less than you'd think," Nova said. "They're descending toward the surface and running low, looking for a flat spot to land before the tank runs dry."

"That's like the worst possible version of a timed level," Theo said, watching the numbers tick toward empty.

"**Neil Armstrong**," Nova said, "took the controls by hand right at the end, steering past a boulder field toward smoother ground. **Buzz Aldrin** called out the numbers beside him. Their crewmate, **Michael Collins**, orbited alone overhead the whole time, flying the **command module** — that's the part of the ship that stays in orbit and carries everyone home — called **Columbia**."

The fuel number ticked lower. Lower. Theo found himself gripping the edge of the panel, the way he gripped his controller during a penalty shootout.

Then — contact. A small light blinked green.

"*Houston, Tranquility Base here,*" Armstrong's voice crackled. "*The Eagle has landed.*"

Cheering erupted somewhere far below on Earth, loud even through the static.

Hours later, a hatch opened onto gray dust and black sky. Armstrong climbed down a ladder, boot hovering above the surface.

"*That's one small step for man,*" he said, voice crackling through a hundred thousand miles of empty space, "*one giant leap for mankind.*"

His boot touched down. Dust puffed up in slow motion, with no air to carry it far.

Theo realized he'd been holding his breath the whole time.

Aldrin climbed down next, planting his own boots in the gray dust, and the two of them bounced across the surface in slow, floating hops, gathering rocks, planting a flag held stiff with a wire since there was no wind to make it wave.

"Twelve astronauts walked up here in total," Nova said, "across six separate landings, between **1969** and **1972**. Armstrong and Aldrin just happened to go first."

Theo watched them bounce across the gray dust, grinning so hard his face hurt.

"Best level ever," he said.

"Nobody's topped it yet," Nova agreed.

chapters.heading: Chapter 9: The Fix and the Handshake
chapters.text:
The next landing jolted hard, alarms blaring, the whole capsule shuddering around them.

"**Apollo 13**," Nova said, voice tight. "**1970**. An oxygen tank just exploded on the way to the Moon. They're not landing there anymore. Just trying to get home."

Three astronauts floated in a cabin gone suddenly cold, breath fogging in front of their faces. On the floor sat a pile of mismatched parts: a square filter, a round hole it needed to fit into, tape, cardboard, a sock.

"Carbon dioxide's building up," Nova said. "Their air filter's the wrong shape for this part of the ship. Mission Control's trying to build a fix using only what's already on board."

Theo looked at the pile of junk and felt something click — the exact feeling he got staring at a half-built level that refused to work with the pieces he had.

"You don't need a matching part," he said slowly. "You need an adapter. Something in between."

On the radio, an engineer back on Earth was saying almost the same thing, piecing together cardboard and tape and a plastic bag into a clumsy, ugly little box that bridged the square filter to the round hole.

It looked terrible. It also worked.

Days later, the capsule splashed down safely in the ocean, parachutes blooming overhead, three exhausted astronauts pulled out alive and grinning.

"They never got to walk on the Moon that trip," Nova said. "But nobody died, and everybody learned exactly what kind of toolkit to pack next time."

"A good save beats a good plan," Theo said.

"Write that one down," Nova said. "Last stop."

The green light settled them onto a view of two spacecraft easing slowly toward each other against the black of space, one Soviet, one American, floating nose to nose.

"**July 17, 1975**," Nova said. "**Apollo-Soyuz**. The last big moment of the whole space race — and it's not a race anymore. Watch."

A hatch between the two ships swung open. An American astronaut reached through first. A Soviet cosmonaut gripped his hand on the other side, and the two spacecraft **docked** — that just means linked together — right there in the same sliver of space that had once belonged to two countries racing each other to get there first.

"That's it?" Theo asked. "After all that — a handshake?"

"Turns out that's usually how the best rivalries end," Nova said. "Everybody already proved what they came to prove. Might as well dock together and shake hands."

The green light rose up around them both, warm this time instead of cold, and Theo blinked and found himself back at his own desk, headphones crooked, Orbit Run still glowing quietly on the screen.

Nova was gone. In her place, right in the middle of his half-finished level, sat one new piece Theo hadn't built: two tiny blocky spacecraft, docked nose to nose, with two tiny figures shaking hands between them.

Theo stared at it for a long moment, then reached for his keyboard and started building the next level — bigger this time, with room for every single launch he'd just watched happen.

story.ending_line: Saturday couldn't come soon enough — he had a whole space race left to build.

true_facts.text: The Soviet Union launched **Sputnik 1** on **October 4, 1957** — the first man-made object ever to orbit Earth.
Sputnik 1 was only about **58 centimeters wide**, and it sent out a simple radio **beep** that people picked up on ordinary radios.
NASA officially started operating on **October 1, 1958**.
**Wernher von Braun** led the NASA team that later built the **Saturn V** rocket.
On **April 12, 1961**, **Yuri Gagarin** became the first human in space, orbiting Earth once in **Vostok 1** in about **108 minutes**.
On **May 25, 1961**, President **Kennedy** challenged the country to land on the Moon before the decade was out.
The **Saturn V** rocket stood **363 feet** tall — taller than the Statue of Liberty.
On **June 16, 1963**, **Valentina Tereshkova** became the first woman in space, circling Earth **48 times**.
On **March 18, 1965**, **Alexei Leonov** made the first spacewalk, floating outside his ship on a tether for about ten minutes.
On **January 27, 1967**, a fire during a ground test killed three Apollo 1 astronauts, which led to safer hatches and materials on every later mission.
In **December 1968**, Apollo 8 astronauts circled the Moon, and **William Anders** took the famous **Earthrise** photo.
On **July 20, 1969**, **Neil Armstrong** became the first person to walk on the Moon, calling it a giant leap for mankind.
In **1970**, an exploded oxygen tank nearly stranded the Apollo 13 crew, but an improvised fix got them home safely.
On **July 17, 1975**, American and Soviet spacecraft **docked** in orbit, ending the space race with a handshake instead of a finish line.

new_recurring.name: Nova
new_recurring.rule: A foot-tall blocky test-pilot avatar who climbs out of Theo's screen through a glowing green Play button whenever a build he's working on connects to something real; she calls him 'Commander,' explains history in build-and-game metaphors, and always leaves one small keepsake object inside his current project before she vanishes.

bible_suggestions.ending_summary: Theo returns to his half-finished Roblox level to find Nova gone and a new, unbuilt piece sitting in the scene: two tiny docked spacecraft with two tiny figures shaking hands, which he immediately starts building around.

violations.quote: On **January 27, 1967**, a fire during a ground test killed three Apollo 1 astronauts

story.title: Phoenix and Cruz and the Dinosaur Stomp
story.subtitle: A bedtime trip back 230 million years

chapters.heading: Chapter 1: The Glowing Brick
chapters.text:
Phoenix lined up tiny LEGO dinosaurs on the rug. Cruz made shark noises at a tiny T. rex. "CHOMP CHOMP," Cruz said, bonking two dinosaurs together.

Then one brick started to glow. It was green, then gold. **BZZZT!**

A tiny robot popped up from behind the pillow. It was Sprocket, their little glowing friend.

"Well hello, you two," said Sprocket, spinning happily. "Want to meet a real dinosaur?"

Phoenix bounced on his knees. "A REAL one?"

Sprocket's light swirled into a door, round and shimmery like a bubble.

"Step through," said Sprocket. "No shrinking tonight. Just walking."

Cruz grabbed Phoenix's hand. They jumped through together.

**WHOOOOSH!**

The rug was gone. Warm wind blew. Strange plants stood tall around them.

chapters.heading: Chapter 2: The Terrible Lizard Word
chapters.text:
They landed on soft, muddy ground. Little lizard-like creatures scurried past their feet.

"Welcome," said Sprocket, "to **230 million years ago**. That's a super long time back. This is when the very first dinosaurs showed up."

Phoenix tilted his head. "Wait, what even IS a dinosaur?"

"Good question," said Sprocket. "A scientist named **Richard Owen** made up that word in **1842**. **Dinosaur** means **terrible lizard**."

Cruz giggled. "Terrible like a burp?"

"Terrible like amazing," laughed Sprocket.

A small feathered creature hopped by, chirping.

"That looks like a bird," said Phoenix.

"Smart boy," said Sprocket. "Birds ARE dinosaurs. The little feathery ones never really left."

Cruz clapped his hands. "Dinosaurs are still here?"

"Right outside your window," said Sprocket, winking.

chapters.heading: Chapter 3: The Three-Horned Face
chapters.text:
They walked on and heard a deep, rumbly snort. A giant creature with three horns stepped out of the ferns.

"That's a **Triceratops**," said Sprocket. "Its name means **three-horned face**."

Phoenix counted on his fingers. "One, two, three horns!"

"Like goalposts," he said, pretending to kick an invisible ball between them.

The Triceratops lowered its big bony frill, like a giant shield.

Cruz tiptoed closer, then stopped. "Is it mad?"

"Not even a little," said Sprocket. "It only eats plants."

Cruz grinned and waved. "Hi, horn friend!"

The Triceratops huffed softly, almost like a wave back.

Phoenix drummed a beat on his knees. "Three horns, three horns, boom boom boom!"

Everyone laughed. Even Sprocket's light bounced to the beat.

chapters.heading: Chapter 4: The Turkey-Sized Surprise
chapters.text:
Something rustled in the bushes. Cruz jumped back. "Spidey sense! Something's coming!"

A small, feathery creature darted out on quick little legs.

"That's a **Velociraptor**," said Sprocket.

Phoenix frowned. "But raptors are supposed to be HUGE in movies!"

"Nope," said Sprocket. "Real ones were only about the size of a turkey."

Cruz burst out laughing. "A TURKEY?"

The little raptor scuttled sideways, quick and low.

"IT'S CRAB-WALKING!" Cruz shouted, copying its wiggly walk.

Phoenix crab-walked too, and they both giggled on the ground.

"It even has feathers," said Sprocket. "Lots of dinosaurs did."

The raptor fluffed its feathers and scurried off into the leaves, not scary at all.

chapters.heading: Chapter 5: The Long, Long Neck
chapters.text:
A shadow stretched across the ground. Up, up, up went a giant neck.

"Whoa," whispered Phoenix. "That neck doesn't stop!"

"That's **Brachiosaurus**," said Sprocket. "It uses its long neck to reach leaves way up high."

The huge dinosaur chewed slowly, leaves falling like green confetti.

Cruz pointed. "CHOMP CHOMP! It's eating a whole tree!"

"Close," said Sprocket. "Some of these plant-eaters munched hundreds of pounds of leaves every single day."

Phoenix tried to copy the stretchy neck, standing on tiptoes.

"I can't reach," he laughed, flopping back down.

Cruz tried too, then plopped onto the grass giggling.

The giant dinosaur just kept chewing, calm as could be.

chapters.heading: Chapter 6: Sue's Enormous Teeth
chapters.text:
The ground began to go **thump... thump... THUMP**.

Cruz grabbed Phoenix's arm. "Is that... a shark?"

"Nope," said Sprocket. "Say hello to **Tyrannosaurus rex**."

A giant dinosaur stomped into view, as long as a school bus.

Phoenix's eyes went huge. "That's as big as twelve of me!"

"Close," said Sprocket. "T. rex grew up to **12 meters long**."

The dinosaur opened its mouth. Its teeth were as long as bananas.

"Those teeth," said Sprocket, "could grow **20 centimeters** long."

"CRUNCH CRUNCH!" shouted Cruz, snapping his own tiny teeth like a shark.

The T. rex just sniffed the air and lumbered off, not hunting them at all.

Phoenix let out a big breath. "Phew. Glad it wasn't hungry for us."

chapters.heading: Chapter 7: The Long Goodbye
chapters.text:
The sky flickered, like someone dimmed a lamp.

"A long, long time after this," said Sprocket gently, "a giant space rock called an **asteroid** fell from the sky."

Phoenix held Cruz's hand. "Did it hurt the dinosaurs?"

"It did," said Sprocket softly. "Most dinosaurs couldn't live anymore after that. It happened about **66 million years ago**."

Cruz looked sad for a second. "That's not fun."

"But remember the little feathery ones?" said Sprocket. "They survived. Birds today are still dinosaurs."

Phoenix smiled. "So dinosaurs never really left."

"Exactly," said Sprocket. "And their bones turned into **fossils** — old bones that slowly turned to stone, buried in the ground."

Cruz tapped the dirt. "Fossils are hiding down there?"

"Lots of them," said Sprocket, "waiting to be found."

chapters.heading: Chapter 8: Home with Sue
chapters.text:
The bubbly door shimmered open again. **WHOOOOSH!**

They stepped through, and the rug was back under their feet.

On the shelf sat a little dinosaur skeleton toy, standing proud.

"That looks like **Sue**," said Sprocket. "The biggest T. rex skeleton ever found, discovered in **1990**. She lives in a museum in Chicago now."

Phoenix grinned and set the toy skeleton gently beside his soccer ball.

Cruz yawned a huge, shark-sized yawn. "Best. Adventure. Ever."

"PANCAKE POWER," he added sleepily, for no reason at all, which made Phoenix giggle.

Sprocket's light dimmed to a soft little wink.

"Time for two tired dinosaur hunters to rest," said Sprocket.

Phoenix pulled the blanket over both of them.

story.ending_line: Goodnight, Phoenix. Goodnight, Cruz. Print well.

true_facts.text: The word **dinosaur** means **terrible lizard**, made up by **Richard Owen** in **1842**.
The first dinosaurs showed up about **230 million years ago**.
**Triceratops** has **three horns**, and its name means **three-horned face**.
A real **Velociraptor** was only about the size of a **turkey**.
Lots of dinosaurs, like Velociraptor, had **feathers**.
**Brachiosaurus** used its long neck to munch huge amounts of leaves every day.
**T. rex** could grow up to **12 meters long**, as long as a school bus.
T. rex teeth could grow up to **20 centimeters** long.
A giant **asteroid** falling from the sky caused most dinosaurs to disappear about **66 million years ago**.
Old dinosaur bones slowly turned to stone and became **fossils**.
**Sue**, one of the most complete T. rex skeletons, was found in **1990** and now lives in a Chicago museum.

bible_suggestions.ending_summary: A tiny toy dinosaur skeleton named after Sue now sits on the shelf beside Phoenix's soccer ball, and both boys fell asleep giggling about feathery raptors.

violations.quote: Goodnight, Phoenix. Goodnight, Cruz. Print well.

story.title: Theo and the Sputnik Signal
story.subtitle: A Roblox builder debugs the whole space race, one checkpoint at a time.

chapters.heading: Chapter 1: The Glitch in Mission: Orbit (1957)
chapters.text:
It was 11:04 p.m., and Theo was still in Roblox Studio, building a game called *Mission: Orbit*. His satellite model floated above a blocky Earth, wobbling because the script wouldn't behave.

He typed a fix. Nothing. He typed another. Nothing.

Then the monitor flickered green, and a sound came out of the speakers that wasn't in his game at all.

**BZZZT... beep... beep... beep.**

A pixel-shaped figure popped out of the screen and landed on his desk, scattering a cup of pencils. It looked like a tiny blocky astronaut, if astronauts were made of static.

"Ping," it said, and did a small bow. "That beep you just heard? That's me. Or rather, that's what I'm made of — the actual radio signal a satellite sent out in **1957**."

Theo stared. "You're a sound effect."

"I'm *the* sound effect," Ping said. "On **October 4, 1957**, the Soviet Union launched something called **Sputnik 1** — the first man-made object to ever circle the Earth. It was about the size of a beach ball, and it just sent out a steady beep that regular radios on the ground could actually pick up."

"Wait." Theo leaned in. "People just... heard it? On normal radios?"

"Across the whole planet," said Ping. "Everyone suddenly knew something was flying over their heads that nobody had put there before. It scared some people and thrilled everybody else. That's usually how the good stuff starts."

Theo glanced at his wobbling satellite model, then back at Ping. "My satellite's scaled way too big. I made it like a school bus."

"Fix that," Ping said, "and I'll show you the real one."

Theo shrank the model down to beach-ball size and hit compile. The screen didn't just update — it opened, like a loading screen stretching wide, pulling in cold starlight and the smell of rocket fuel.

"One rule," Ping said, floating backward into the light. "You don't just watch history load. You help it run."

**CLICK.**

Theo stepped through.

chapters.heading: Chapter 2: A Dog, an Agency, and a Belt of Radiation (1957–1958)
chapters.text:
Theo landed on a windswept launch pad under a sky full of unfamiliar stars. Beside him, a small shape bounded over the frost — a little dog, nose twitching, tail going like a metronome.

"Meet **Laika**," said Ping. "On **November 3, 1957**, she rode inside **Sputnik 2** and became the first living creature to orbit Earth. She was brave, and she was famous the second her flight began — newspapers everywhere printed her picture."

Theo crouched down. Laika licked his hand like this was any ordinary Tuesday. "She doesn't look nervous at all."

"Dogs rarely do," Ping said. "Unlike certain humans who panic when their code won't compile."

"That was *one time*."

The scene dissolved into a different room — fluorescent lights, chalkboards, men in narrow ties arguing over blueprints. A banner on the wall read **NASA**.

"Sputnik scared the United States into action," Ping explained. "On **October 1, 1958**, the country started a brand-new space agency called **NASA** — short for an organization built to handle everything above the clouds. Four months earlier, on **January 31, 1958**, their first satellite, **Explorer 1**, had already gone up and found something nobody expected: a hidden ring of radiation circling the Earth, now called the **Van Allen radiation belt** — an invisible zone of charged particles trapped by Earth's magnetic field.

"So there's an invisible force field around the planet," Theo said slowly, "and nobody knew until a satellite bumped into it?"

"Exactly. Space doesn't come with a map. You find things by going."

Theo thought about his own game, where players kept finding bugs he hadn't planned for — holes in the floor, doors that led nowhere. "That's basically my Tuesdays."

"Then you'll fit right in here," Ping said. "Builders who expect surprises do better than builders who don't."

A model of Explorer 1 spun lazily nearby, trailing a faint blue shimmer where it crossed an invisible line. Theo reached out and nudged the shimmer with one finger, watching it ripple like water. Somewhere, a chalk-dust engineer cheered at a number on a readout.

"Keep moving," Ping said. "Someone's about to become the first human being to leave the planet entirely."

chapters.heading: Chapter 3: 108 Minutes (1961)
chapters.text:
The next checkpoint smelled like scorched metal and nerves. A silver capsule sat on a gantry, steam hissing from its base.

"On **April 12, 1961**," Ping said, "a Soviet pilot named **Yuri Gagarin** climbed into that capsule, called **Vostok 1**, and became the first human ever to fly in space. He circled the entire Earth once — a full **108 minutes** — and came back smiling the whole way."

Theo watched the hatch close. His stomach did the thing it did before a penalty kick — that mix of *this is enormous* and *I want to see it happen anyway*.

"A hundred and eight minutes to go around the whole planet," he muttered. "My lunch period is longer than that."

"Your lunch period doesn't involve leaving the atmosphere," Ping said. "Although I've seen what you do to a school cafeteria. Comparable chaos."

The rocket lit. Theo felt the ground genuinely shake — not a sound effect, not a script, an actual tremor under his sneakers — and for one second it was loud enough that he flinched.

"Is it going to be okay?" he asked, eyes on the fire.

"He lands safely," Ping said immediately. "Smiling, same as he went up. I promise you that part now so you can actually enjoy the launch."

Theo exhaled and watched the rocket shrink to a spark, then to nothing. Around the pad, engineers in thick coats hugged each other and threw papers in the air like confetti.

"He really just... went around the whole world," Theo said. "Once."

"One careful orbit," said Ping. "After that, everyone else just had to figure out how to go farther."

Theo grinned, already thinking about how he'd script an orbit camera back home — one smooth loop, slow at the top, fast at the bottom, the way a soccer ball curves when it's hit just right.

"Farther," he repeated. "I like farther."

"Good," said Ping, "because farther is exactly where we're headed."

chapters.heading: Chapter 4: The Dare (1961)
chapters.text:
They landed next on a sunlit launch deck where a much smaller capsule sat waiting, barely bigger than a phone booth.

"**Freedom 7**," Ping said. "On **May 5, 1961**, an American named **Alan Shepard** flew inside it and became the first American in space. His flight didn't go all the way around the Earth like Gagarin's — it arced up and came straight back down — but it still counted, and it still mattered."

"So he was second," Theo said, "but first for his team."

"Think of it like a league table," Ping said. "Gagarin scored first. That didn't mean the season was over."

The scene shifted to a podium outside, where a man in a dark suit stood in front of a cheering crowd. Theo recognized the voice before Ping even said the name.

"**President Kennedy**," Ping said. "On **May 25, 1961**, just three weeks after Shepard's flight, he stood up in front of his whole country and made a dare. He said America would land a person on the Moon — and bring them home safely — before the decade ended."

Theo's jaw actually dropped. "He just... announced it? Before anyone knew how to do it?"

"Nobody had the plan yet," Ping said. "They had the goal. Sometimes that's the part that has to come first."

Theo thought of the ambitious game he kept starting in Studio and never finishing — the one with the whole solar system, scripted physics, a full day-night cycle, way too big for one kid to build alone. He'd always told himself he'd wait until he knew exactly how.

"Maybe you don't wait for the plan," he said slowly. "Maybe you just say the goal out loud, and the plan shows up because it has to."

"Now you're thinking like a rocket engineer," Ping said. "Terrifying. I love it."

Theo laughed, and somewhere behind them, the crowd on the podium roared loud enough to rattle the air.

chapters.heading: Chapter 5: Orbit and Open Sky (1963–1965)
chapters.text:
The air changed again, crisp and high and very quiet. A capsule window showed the whole curved Earth.

"On **June 16, 1963**," Ping said, "a Soviet woman named **Valentina Tereshkova** became the first woman in space. She used to work in a textile factory, and then she orbited the Earth — not once, but **forty-eight times** — aboard a capsule called **Vostok 6**."

Theo pressed a hand to the window glass. "Forty-eight times around the whole planet. That's not a flight, that's a season pass."

"She trained for it like an athlete," Ping said. "Same discipline you put into practicing penalty kicks in the backyard until it's dark."

"That's oddly specific."

"I notice things."

The capsule view dissolved into open space — real open space, a hatch cracked wide, stars on every side, no walls at all.

"On **March 18, 1965**," Ping continued, "a cosmonaut named **Alexei Leonov** opened that hatch and floated completely outside his spacecraft. That's called a **spacewalk** — stepping out of your capsule into open space, tethered by a cord so you don't drift away. He was out there about **ten minutes**, just him, a cord, and the entire universe."

Theo stared at the gap in the hatch. For one breathless second it looked like Leonov had nothing holding him there at all — just stars, and silence, and a man floating free.

Then Theo spotted the cord, thin and taut, glinting in the sunlight. He let his shoulders drop.

"He's tied on," Theo said, relieved. "Okay. Okay, that's — that's actually the coolest thing I've ever seen."

"Ten minutes doesn't sound like long," Ping said, "until you remember nobody had ever done it before. Every second was new."

Theo thought about the floating mechanic he'd been trying to script for weeks, the one where a player's avatar drifted weightlessly between platforms. He'd never gotten the physics quite right.

"I know what I'm fixing when I get home," he said.

"Add a tether," Ping said. "Trust me on this one."

chapters.heading: Chapter 6: What Went Wrong, and What Came After (1967–1968)
chapters.text:
The next checkpoint was quieter than the others. A launch pad stood empty under gray sky, no crowd, no countdown.

"I need to tell you something that isn't a happy one," Ping said, voice lower than before. "On **January 27, 1967**, three American astronauts — **Gus Grissom**, **Ed White**, and **Roger Chaffee** — were doing a safety test inside an **Apollo 1** capsule on the ground, not even flying yet, when a fire broke out inside the cabin. All three died."

Theo went still. "On the ground? Before it even launched?"

"Before it even launched," Ping confirmed. "It was a hard lesson, and NASA didn't look away from it. They redesigned the hatch so it could open in seconds instead of minutes. They changed the materials inside the cabin. They tested everything again, slower and more carefully than before."

Theo swallowed. "So because of what happened, later astronauts were safer."

"Every single one," Ping said. "That's the part worth remembering — not just that it was sad, but that people fixed what was broken instead of giving up."

Theo thought of every time his Roblox game had crashed right before he showed it to someone, and how he'd always gone back in and found the actual bug instead of deleting the whole project. It felt like a small, strange echo of something much bigger.

The sky above them lightened, and the scene shifted to the inside of a spacecraft, round windows full of grey, cratered ground.

"**December 1968**," Ping said, brighter now. "**Apollo 8**. Three astronauts became the first humans to ever orbit the Moon. One of them, **William Anders**, looked out his window and saw something nobody had framed quite that way before."

A photograph floated into view — a blue-and-white Earth, small and whole, rising over a grey Moon horizon.

"They called it **Earthrise**," Ping said.

Theo stared at it for a long moment, the little blue marble hanging in all that black. "That's our whole planet," he said quietly. "It just fits in one photo."

"Everyone you've ever known," said Ping, "is in that picture. Pretty good follow-up to a bad week, don't you think?"

chapters.heading: Chapter 7: One Giant Leap (1969)
chapters.text:
The ground rumbled so hard Theo had to steady himself against a rail. In front of him stood a rocket taller than anything he'd ever rendered in Studio — taller, Ping told him, than the **Statue of Liberty**, standing a full **363 feet** high. Its name was painted in block letters down the side: **Saturn V**.

"An American engineer named **Wernher von Braun** led the team that built this," Ping said. "On the Soviet side, their chief designer was a man named **Sergei Korolev** — except almost nobody knew his name at the time. The Soviets kept his identity a secret until after he died in **1966**. He was basically a legendary coder nobody was allowed to credit."

"That's rough," Theo said. "Imagine shipping the whole game and nobody knows you made it."

"Imagine it," Ping agreed. "Now watch this part."

The rocket lit, and this time the roar was so total that Theo felt it in his teeth. It climbed, and climbed, and became a star, and then the scene cut straight to a grey, dusty surface and a ladder reaching down from a strange four-legged lander.

"**July 20, 1969**," Ping said. "**Neil Armstrong** climbed down that ladder and became the first person to ever walk on the Moon. He called it **a giant leap for mankind**. His crewmate **Buzz Aldrin** joined him down on the surface a few minutes later, while a third astronaut, **Michael Collins**, orbited alone overhead in the command module, called **Columbia** — the part of the ship that stayed in space the whole time."

Theo watched a boot print press into grey dust that had never once been touched. "Collins didn't even get to walk on it?"

"Someone has to fly the ship home," Ping said. "Not every important job gets the photo."

Theo thought about that — about goalkeepers, about the kid who scripts the game nobody sees working behind the scenes. "I get that," he said. "That's still a huge job."

"Between **1969** and **1972**, twelve astronauts walked on the Moon across six separate missions," Ping said. "Every single one of them stood where Armstrong stood first."

Theo reached out — hesitated — then pressed his own sneaker print right beside the boot print in the dust, just once, and grinned the whole way back up.

chapters.heading: Chapter 8: The Handshake (1970–1975)
chapters.text:
The floor lurched without warning, lights flashing red, a hiss of escaping air somewhere behind a panel.

"**1970**," Ping said quickly. "**Apollo 13**, on the way to the Moon. An oxygen tank exploded and crippled the spacecraft hundreds of thousands of miles from home."

Theo's heart jumped. "Did they—"

"They made it back," Ping said, fast, firm. "Engineers on the ground spent days improvising a fix using nothing but spare parts already on board — tape, cardboard, a manual, pure stubbornness. The crew followed every instruction and splashed down safely. Nobody was lost."

Theo let his shoulders drop, breathing out slow. "They basically debugged it live. From a hundred thousand miles away."

"The ultimate remote support ticket," Ping agreed. "No patch notes. No restarting the server."

The red lights faded. The next scene was calm, almost gentle — two spacecraft easing toward each other against a black sky, one marked with American letters, one with Soviet ones.

"**July 17, 1975**," Ping said. "After nearly two decades of racing each other, an American spacecraft and a Soviet spacecraft docked together in orbit. The two crews opened a hatch between them and shook hands in space. That's really how the whole race ended — not with a winner, but with a handshake."

Theo watched the hatch open, watched hands meet across the gap where two different countries' hardware had just locked together, click by click, like two halves of the same build finally compiling without an error.

"That's a good ending," Theo said.

"It's my favorite one," said Ping. "Speaking of endings — yours is due back on a bedroom floor."

The stars folded inward like a closing menu, and Theo's sneakers hit familiar carpet. His monitor glowed steady green, no longer flickering, Studio still open exactly where he'd left it.

On the desk sat something new: a tiny model satellite, beach-ball sized just like the real one, blinking a slow, steady beep.

"Keep that," Ping said, already fading back into static. "And fix your satellite's scale in the game. You know the real number now."

"Ping," Theo said. "Will you come back?"

"When your screen goes green," Ping said, "I'm already there."

**BZZZT.**

Then quiet, and the small satellite kept blinking on his desk, patient as a loading screen.

story.ending_line: Tomorrow, he had a satellite to rebuild — this time, at the right scale.

true_facts.text: On **October 4, 1957**, the Soviet Union launched **Sputnik 1**, the first man-made object to orbit Earth — about the size of a beach ball, sending out a steady radio beep.
That beep could be picked up on ordinary radios all over the world.
On **November 3, 1957**, the Soviets launched **Sputnik 2** carrying a dog named **Laika**, the first living creature to orbit Earth.
Shocked by Sputnik, the United States started a new space agency, **NASA**, on **October 1, 1958**.
The first U.S. satellite, **Explorer 1**, launched on **January 31, 1958**, and discovered an invisible ring of radiation now called the **Van Allen belt**.
On **April 12, 1961**, **Yuri Gagarin** became the first human in space, orbiting Earth once in **108 minutes** aboard **Vostok 1**.
On **May 25, 1961**, **President Kennedy** challenged the United States to land a person on the Moon and bring them home safely before the decade ended.
On **June 16, 1963**, **Valentina Tereshkova** became the first woman in space, orbiting Earth **48 times** aboard **Vostok 6**.
On **March 18, 1965**, **Alexei Leonov** made the first spacewalk, floating outside his capsule for about **ten minutes**.
On **January 27, 1967**, astronauts **Gus Grissom, Ed White,** and **Roger Chaffee** died during a ground test of **Apollo 1**, and NASA redesigned the spacecraft to be safer afterward.
In **December 1968**, the **Apollo 8** crew became the first humans to orbit the Moon, and astronaut **William Anders** took the famous **Earthrise** photo.
On **July 20, 1969**, **Neil Armstrong** became the first person to walk on the Moon, calling it **a giant leap for mankind**.
In **1970**, an oxygen tank explosion crippled **Apollo 13**, but engineers improvised a fix and the crew returned safely.
The Space Race ended on **July 17, 1975**, when an American and a Soviet spacecraft docked in orbit and their crews shook hands.

bible_suggestions.ending_summary: Theo returns to his bedroom to find a small beach-ball-sized model satellite blinking steadily on his desk, and he resolves to fix his Roblox satellite's scale now that he knows the real size.
