chapters.heading: Chapter 3: The Tooth as Big as a Hand
chapters.text:
A huge, triangle-shaped tooth sat on the sandy floor, bigger than Jack's whole hand.

"Whoa," said Jack, picking it up carefully.

"That came from **Megalodon**,” said the pouch, “a giant shark that lived millions of years ago."

"Is it coming?" Ellie asked, grabbing Jack's sleeve.

"No," said the pouch gently. "Megalodon is **extinct** — that means none are left anywhere, not one. All we have are old teeth like this, called **fossils**, which are parts of ancient animals turned hard like stone."

Ellie let go of Jack's sleeve. "So it's just... a really big souvenir."

"Exactly," said the pouch. "Teeth don't rot away like the rest of a shark does, so fossil teeth are almost all scientists have to study megalodon."

Jack held the tooth up next to Ellie's hand. It was way bigger.

"Megalodon could've eaten my mermaid dolls for a snack," Ellie said, delighted now instead of worried.

"Good thing it's not around anymore," said Jack, setting the tooth down like treasure.

chapters.heading: Chapter 4: Spots Like Mermaid Scales
chapters.text:
A shadow blocked out the sun. Then another. Then the whole sky-colored ceiling of water went dark.

Ellie spun around and gasped. A shark bigger than a school bus glided past, covered in pale spots.

"That's the **whale shark**," said the pouch. "The biggest fish in the whole world, over **40 feet long**."

"Does it eat people?!" Jack blurted, grabbing Ellie's hand just in case.

"It mostly eats **plankton** — tiny floating bits of food, smaller than your pinky nail," said the pouch. "It just opens its giant mouth and strains the water like soup."

Ellie relaxed and started counting spots on its side. "Ten, eleven, twelve..."

"Every whale shark's spots are different," said the pouch, "like a mermaid's own special pattern."

"They can live over **100 years**," it added.

"A hundred!" said Ellie. "That's older than Grandpa!"

"Way older," said Jack, and they swam alongside the gentle giant until it curved off into the blue.

chapters.heading: Chapter 5: The Tooth Factory
chapters.text:
A sleek gray shark cruised closer, rows of pointy teeth showing when its mouth opened.

"Great white," breathed Jack, who had read every page of his shark book twice.

"Right," said the pouch. "It can grow almost **20 feet long**, with teeth shaped like little triangles, all edged like a saw."

"Doesn't it lose its teeth sometimes?" Ellie asked, wiggling her own loose front tooth with her tongue.

"All the time," said the pouch. "Sharks lose thousands of teeth over their whole life. New ones just keep moving forward in line to replace them, like a never-ending conveyor belt."

"So they never run out?" Jack asked.

"Never," said the pouch.

Ellie grinned, her loose tooth wiggling again. "Lucky. I only get a dollar when mine falls out."

"Sharks get a whole new tooth for free," said Jack. "No tooth fairy required."

The great white swam a slow, unhurried circle around them, then turned and vanished into the blue, in no rush at all.

chapters.heading: Chapter 6: Sandpaper and Secret Sparks
chapters.text:
Jack reached out and brushed his hand along a passing shark's side. "It feels like sandpaper!"

"That's its skin," said the pouch. "Covered in tiny bumps shaped like little teeth, so rough it could scrape your hand if you rubbed hard. They help sharks slip through water fast and smooth."

Ellie had an idea, the way she usually did right before trouble. "Hide my mermaid doll somewhere, Jack. Let's test if a shark can find it without looking."

Jack tucked the tiny doll behind a rock, out of sight.

"Sharks have special dots on their snouts," said the pouch, "that feel tiny electric sparks every living thing makes, even hiding ones."

A small shark drifted straight toward the rock, nosed around it, and found the doll in seconds flat.

"No fair," said Ellie, laughing. "It cheated with invisible spy powers!"

"It's not cheating," said Jack. "It's just really, really good hide-and-seek."

chapters.heading: Chapter 7: The Shark That Walks
chapters.text:
Something strange flopped across the coral below them, using its fins like tiny paddle feet.

"IT WALKS!" Ellie shouted, pointing.

"That's the **epaulette shark**," said the pouch. "It can walk right across reefs and puddly tide pools, even with barely any air in the water, for hours."

Ellie immediately tried to copy it, wiggling her arms like paddles, giggling bubbles everywhere.

Nearby, something even stranger glided past — a shark with a head shaped like a hammer, flat and wide.

"Hammerhead," said Jack, delighted. "Why's its head like that?"

"Its eyes sit way out on each side," said the pouch, "so it sees almost all the way around itself at once."

"Like eyes in the back of its head," said Jack, "like Mom."

"Exactly like Mom," Ellie agreed, and for once the siblings agreed on something completely.

chapters.heading: Chapter 8: The Real Mermaid's Purse
chapters.text:
A streak of silver shot past them so fast it left bubbles spinning.

"**Shortfin mako**," said the pouch. "Fastest shark in the ocean. Quick little bursts of speed to catch fast fish like tuna."

"Race you to that rock," Jack said to the mako, who was already gone.

Ellie spotted something drifting nearby — a dark, leathery pouch with curly strings on its corners. It looked exactly like the one from her bedroom floor.

"Wait," she said slowly. "Is my mermaid's purse... a real thing?"

"It sure is," said the pouch, sounding pleased. "Some sharks lay eggs inside cases just like this one. People really do call them mermaid's purses."

Inside, curled up tiny, was a baby shark shape, waiting to hatch.

"So mermaids and sharks share a purse," Ellie said, grinning at Jack. "Told you they were basically the same."

"Basically not the same," Jack said, "but I'll allow it tonight."

chapters.heading: Chapter 9: Swim Well, Swim Home
chapters.text:
The water glowed gold, like the whole ocean was yawning.

"Last stop," said the pouch. "Sharks sit at the very top of the ocean, keeping everything else balanced, the way a good referee keeps a game fair."

"Do they ever bite people, though?" Jack asked, the question he'd been saving.

"Almost never," said the pouch. "It's actually sharks who need protecting from us, way more than the other way around."

"A scientist named **Eugenie Clark** figured out sharks are curious, even smart," the pouch added. "People called her the **Shark Lady**. She even trained some to do tricks."

"I knew it," said Jack. "They're basically ocean dogs."

The glow swelled around them, warm as a nightlight. The carpet reappeared under Jack's knees. The mermaid's purse sat closed again between them, quiet and still, one curled string now shaped almost like a tiny smile.

Ellie yawned a mermaid-sized yawn. Jack yawned a shark-sized one back.

story.ending_line: Goodnight, Jack. Goodnight, Ellie. Swim well, and dream deep.

true_facts.text: Sharks have **cartilage** instead of bones, bendy like the squishy part of your ear.
There are more than **500 kinds of sharks** swimming in oceans today.
Sharks showed up in the ocean more than **400 million years ago**, before dinosaurs or trees.
**Megalodon** was a giant shark from long ago that is **extinct** now — none are left.
Old shark teeth called **fossils** are almost all we have left to learn about megalodon.
The **whale shark** is the biggest fish in the world, over **40 feet long**, and mostly eats **plankton**.
Whale sharks can live over **100 years**.
The **great white shark** can grow almost **20 feet long** with saw-edged teeth.
Sharks lose thousands of teeth over their life, and new ones keep moving forward to replace them.
Shark skin feels like sandpaper, covered in tiny tooth-shaped bumps.
Sharks feel tiny electric sparks from hiding animals using special dots on their snouts.
The **epaulette shark** can walk across reefs using its fins, even with barely any air around.
The **hammerhead shark**'s wide head spreads its eyes apart so it can see nearly all the way around.
The **shortfin mako** is the fastest shark, using quick bursts of speed to catch prey.

new_recurring.name: The Mermaid's Purse
new_recurring.rule: A glowing leathery pouch with curly corner strings, found among the children's own toys, that hums, opens on its own, and pulls them into a real ocean or nature adventure; it speaks in a warm, swirly voice and always returns them home gently when the night's lesson is done.

bible_suggestions.ending_summary: The children return to Ellie's bedroom carpet, the glowing mermaid's purse now closed and still between them with one string curled into a tiny smile, as both kids yawn themselves toward sleep.

violations.quote: Jack reached out and brushed his hand along a passing shark's side.

story.title: Hana and the Compass That Remembered
story.subtitle: A voyage through steel, ice, and the lessons the sea still teaches.

chapters.heading: Chapter 1: The Keel in Belfast (1909)
chapters.text:
Hana was supposed to be asleep. Instead she was flat on her bedroom floor with her grandfather's old atlas open to the North Atlantic, tracing shipping lines with her finger like rivers.

A page slipped loose from the back cover — a folded chart she'd never noticed, with a small brass compass stitched into a leather loop. The glass was foggy. She breathed on it without thinking.

The needle spun past north, past south, and stopped on a date instead of a direction: **1909**. The compass case clicked open like a tiny door, and a voice came out of it, dry and unhurried.

"You're standing on a keel," it said. "Mind your feet."

Hana looked down. She was not on her bedroom floor anymore. She was in a roaring shipyard in **Belfast, Ireland**, where **Harland & Wolff** built ships, and under her sneakers lay a long steel spine stretched across the yard like the backbone of something enormous.

"I'm Fathom," said the compass, which had become a small brass figure riding on her palm, shaped vaguely like a sailor who had never once been in a hurry. "On **31 March 1909**, this yard laid the **keel** — that's the very first beam, the backbone a whole ship gets built around. They're building her to be the biggest thing afloat. They're calling her **Titanic**."

Hana crouched and ran her hand along the cold steel. On her atlas at home, she'd traced a hundred keel-shaped lines without knowing what they meant. Now she matched the curve in front of her to the curve on her folded chart, and grinned.

"This matches the hull outline on my map," she said. "You drew her to the same lines."

"Good eye," said Fathom. "Most people just see a ship. You see her shape."

Sparks rained down from a riveting crew overhead, and somewhere a foreman shouted for more rivets, more hands, more time. Hana decided she liked this already — a whole city of people building something too big to fit in anyone's head at once.

"How big does she get?" Hana asked.

Fathom's dial spun once, patient. "Patience. You'll want your atlas for that part."

chapters.heading: Chapter 2: The Launch (1911)
chapters.text:
Two years disappeared like a page turning. Hana found herself on a wooden platform above a slipway slick with soap and tallow, crowds pressed along the harbor wall.

"**31 May 1911**," said Fathom. "Launch day. She goes in empty — no engines, no funnels yet, just a hull waiting to learn how to float."

Hana stared down the length of the hull. It went on. And on. She reached for her folded chart out of habit, measuring the shoreline with her thumb the way she always measured distances on a map at home.

"How long is she really?" Hana asked.

"**882 feet**," said Fathom. "Bow to stern. The biggest ship in the world, the day she's finished. She's got two sisters being built alongside her too — **Olympic**, already afloat, and **Britannic**, still waiting her turn."

Hana did the thumb-trick again, converting feet into city blocks in her head, and whistled low. "That's longer than my whole street."

"Longer than most people's imaginations," Fathom agreed. "Which is part of the problem, later. But let's not get ahead of the chart."

A horn blew. Chains released. The hull groaned, shivered, and slid — slow at first, then faster — down the greased slipway toward the water.

Hana held her breath without meaning to. The hull hit the harbor with a **WHOOOOSH** of spray that misted the whole crowd, and everyone roared.

"She floats!" Hana shouted, and found she'd grabbed Fathom's little brass arm in excitement.

"She floats," Fathom agreed. "Floating is the easy part, Hana. Remember that."

Hana looked at him sideways, already suspicious of how calmly he'd said it. But the harbor was full of cheering, and the ship was finally wet, and for one afternoon that felt like enough of an answer.

chapters.heading: Chapter 3: Four Funnels, Three Real (1912)
chapters.text:
The next jolt of the compass dropped them onto a crowded dock in **Southampton, England**, where a band played and gulls wheeled overhead.

"**10 April 1912**," said Fathom. "First voyage. New York, here we come — eventually."

Hana tipped her head back to look up at the ship properly for the first time, finished now, painted and gleaming, with four enormous funnels standing in a row like chimneys for giants.

She counted smoke trails. One, two, three — and nothing from the fourth.

"That one's not working," she said, pointing.

Fathom's dial gave what might have been a shrug. "Sharp eyes again. Only **three of the four funnels** actually carry smoke. The fourth one's mostly there to look impressive — makes her seem even more powerful than she already is."

Hana laughed out loud. "So it's a fake chimney?"

"A very expensive, very convincing fake chimney," said Fathom. "People believed all sorts of things about this ship before she'd even left the dock. Some called her nearly impossible to sink, because her hull was split into **sixteen watertight compartments** — separate flooded sections, like sealed rooms, so water in one part wouldn't spread to the whole ship."

Hana traced the hull's waterline with her finger on her folded chart, imagining the sealed rooms stacked below deck like a long row of lockers.

"Nearly unsinkable," she repeated slowly. "That sounds like the kind of thing people say right before something goes wrong."

Fathom's needle stilled completely, just for a second.

"You," he said, "are going to do very well tonight."

chapters.heading: Chapter 4: CQD and SOS (14 April 1912)
chapters.text:
The air turned cold so fast Hana's breath fogged. Stars hung sharp and close over black water, and the ship hummed along at speed, quiet and confident.

"**11:40 p.m.**," said Fathom, no longer sounding quite so dry. "This is the night, Hana."

Somewhere ahead in the dark, unseen until it was almost too late, an iceberg slid past the hull. Hana felt it more than heard it — a long scraping shudder through the deck under her feet.

"That's it?" she asked. "That's all it takes?"

"That's all it takes," Fathom said quietly. "It opened some of those watertight compartments along one side. More than the ship was built to lose at once."

Down a narrow stairwell, two men worked a crackling machine, tapping out messages into the night air using a brand-new invention called **wireless** — sending words without any wires at all.

"That's **Jack Phillips** and **Harold Bride**," said Fathom. "Sending for help."

Hana leaned close to watch the dots and dashes. "What are they sending?"

"**CQD** first — the old distress call. Then something newer."

The tapping changed rhythm: three short, three long, three short.

"**SOS**," Hana breathed. "I know that one. Everybody knows that one."

"They were some of the first to send it from a sinking ship," said Fathom. "Your job is to remember the position they're sending. Numbers only matter if someone's listening on the other end."

Hana leaned over the operator's shoulder, matching the string of numbers to the lines on her folded chart, whispering them to herself until they stuck.

"Got it," she said. "I won't lose it."

"Good," said Fathom. "Hold onto it tight. Somebody out there needs those exact numbers."

chapters.heading: Chapter 5: Not Enough Boats
chapters.text:
Up on deck, lanterns swung in the cold and the ship had begun, almost gently, to tilt.

"There weren't enough lifeboats," Fathom said, before Hana could ask. "Space for about **1,178 people**. Far short of everyone aboard."

Hana's stomach dropped the way it did at the top of a staircase in the dark. "That's — that's not even half."

"No," said Fathom. "It wasn't. People made brave choices that night anyway. **Captain Edward John Smith**, one of the most experienced captains on the seas, stayed aboard to the end, helping others off first."

A woman in a fur coat was already rowing one of the lifeboats herself, shouting orders to nervous passengers with total confidence. "That's **Molly Brown**," said Fathom. "People started calling her 'unsinkable' afterward. She wasn't about to sit still and wait."

A little dog yapped from inside someone's coat as they climbed into a boat — one of a couple of small Pomeranians who made it off that night, tucked in beside their owners.

Somewhere above them, faintly, music still drifted — a band playing on, led by a man named **Wallace Hartley**. Survivors later said they heard it right up until near the end, though nobody's completely sure which songs they played. It might be part legend. But the idea of it — music, on purpose, to keep people calm — made Hana's throat go tight anyway.

Not everyone found a seat in a boat that night. Many did not make it. Hana didn't need Fathom to soften that; she could feel the weight of it in the quiet between the ship's groaning timbers.

"What do I do?" she asked. "I can't row a boat."

"You already did something," said Fathom. "You kept those numbers. Keep them a little longer."

chapters.heading: Chapter 6: Carpathia's Race
chapters.text:
Hana blinked, and the deck was gone. She stood instead on the bridge of a different ship entirely, one racing flat-out through ice-scattered black water.

"This is the **Carpathia**," said Fathom. "She heard the call. Now she's running."

Hana pulled out her folded chart, found the coordinates she'd memorized, and traced the distance between the two ships with her finger.

"That's close," she said. "If she keeps this speed, she could actually make it in time."

"She pushed harder than she was built to," said Fathom. "Through ice fields, in the dark, with no guarantee she wouldn't hit one herself."

Dawn came up gray and flat. Lookouts on Carpathia's rail scanned the water through binoculars, searching for tiny shapes against the waves.

"There," Hana said, pointing before anyone else did, because she'd kept tracking the position the whole way. A scatter of lifeboats bobbed ahead, small and cold and absolutely still afloat.

The crew began pulling survivors up rope ladders, wrapping them in blankets, pouring hot drinks into shaking hands. Hana counted boats coming alongside, one after another, each one a small miracle of people who had made it through the night.

"You helped get them found faster," Fathom said. "That position you held onto — it mattered."

Hana looked out at blankets and steaming cups and people hugging each other on a stranger's deck, and felt something unclench in her chest for the first time since the iceberg.

"Good," she said simply. "That's good."

chapters.heading: Chapter 7: The Rules That Changed
chapters.text:
The compass hummed, and suddenly they stood in a quiet meeting room full of maps of the North Atlantic, not so different from Hana's own atlas at home.

"After the disaster," said Fathom, "people in charge of the seas asked one obvious question. Why weren't there enough lifeboats for everyone?"

Hana crossed her arms. "That seems like something you'd want to figure out before you built the ship, not after."

"Agreed," said Fathom. "So they fixed it. New rules — part of something called the **SOLAS** treaty, which just means 'safety of life at sea' — said every ship from then on had to carry enough lifeboats for every single person aboard."

Hana nodded slowly, tracing the shipping lanes on the wall map with one finger. "What about icebergs? Somebody has to watch for those."

"They started that too," said Fathom. "The **International Ice Patrol**. Ships whose whole job is tracking ice in these waters, warning everyone else before another ship ever gets close."

Hana looked at the map, at all those careful new lines drawn across the ocean like someone had finally taken the sea seriously.

"It shouldn't have taken a disaster to make the rules obvious," she said.

"No," Fathom agreed. "But sometimes that's exactly how the best rules get made. Somebody has to lose something first, so nobody else has to."

Hana folded that thought up carefully, the way she folded her chart, and tucked it somewhere she wouldn't forget it.

chapters.heading: Chapter 8: Found Again (1985)
chapters.text:
The last jolt of the compass dropped Hana onto the deck of a research ship, sonar screens glowing green in the dark.

"**1 September 1985**," said Fathom. "A long wait. Seventy-three years, actually, before anyone found her again."

A man in headphones leaned toward a screen, and Hana recognized the careful, patient look of someone studying a map. "That's **Robert Ballard**," Fathom said. "He finally located the wreck, split in two pieces, about **12,500 feet** down — that's over two miles of water sitting on top of her."

Hana pulled out her folded chart one last time, matching numbers to the screen. "**370 miles off Newfoundland**," she murmured. "That's exactly where I marked it, back on the night of the iceberg."

"You remembered," said Fathom, and for once there was nothing dry in his voice at all. "The whole way through."

On the screen, grainy shapes resolved slowly out of the dark — a railing, a funnel base, dinner plates still sitting exactly where they'd settled, shoes lined up on the seafloor like someone might come back for them. Pieces of her, waiting in museums around the world for people like Hana to come and look.

"She's not lost anymore," Hana said. "She's just... somewhere else now."

The compass dial spun one last time, warm against her palm, and the research ship dissolved into her bedroom floor, atlas open under the lamp.

Hana sat up. The folded chart was still in her hand, and resting on top of it, where there had been nothing before, sat a small brass compass with a tiny ship etched into the lid.

She traced the route she'd followed all night — Belfast to the ice, the ice to Carpathia, Carpathia all the way home — and smiled at how much of it she could still find, just by looking at a map.

story.ending_line: Tomorrow, she had a hundred more routes on that atlas left to trace.

true_facts.text: **Titanic**'s **keel** — the backbone the whole ship was built around — was laid down at the **Harland & Wolff** shipyard in **Belfast, Ireland**, on **31 March 1909**.
She was launched into the water on **31 May 1911**, as the second of three sister ships alongside **Olympic** and **Britannic**.
At about **882 feet long**, Titanic was the biggest ship in the world when she set sail.
Titanic left **Southampton, England** on **10 April 1912**, heading for New York City.
Of her four funnels, only **three actually carried smoke** — the fourth was mostly there to look impressive.
Her hull was divided into **sixteen watertight compartments**, which made people call her nearly impossible to sink.
At around **11:40 p.m. on 14 April 1912**, Titanic struck an iceberg in the icy North Atlantic.
Wireless operators **Jack Phillips** and **Harold Bride** sent distress calls that night, using both the old **CQD** signal and the newer **SOS**.
The ship carried lifeboats for only about **1,178 people**, far fewer than everyone aboard.
**Captain Edward John Smith** stayed aboard to help others, and passenger **Molly Brown** helped row her own lifeboat.
The steamship **Carpathia** raced through the night and rescued the survivors from their lifeboats by morning.
After the disaster, new safety rules required every ship to carry enough lifeboats for everyone aboard, and the **International Ice Patrol** was formed to watch for icebergs.
The wreck was finally found on **1 September 1985** by explorer **Robert Ballard**, about **12,500 feet** deep, roughly **370 miles off Newfoundland**.

new_recurring.name: The Fathom Compass
new_recurring.rule: A small brass compass that appears tucked in a map or chart; breathing on its foggy glass spins the needle to a date instead of a direction and opens a doorway into real history. It speaks in a calm, dry voice, calls the child by name, and always leaves behind a tiny keepsake tied to that night's journey.

bible_suggestions.ending_summary: Hana returns to her bedroom floor to find the Fathom Compass resting on her folded Atlantic chart, having traced Titanic's whole route from Belfast to her rediscovery in 1985.

violations.quote: Somewhere ahead in the dark, unseen until it was almost too late, an iceberg slid past the hull. Hana felt it more than heard it — a long scraping shudder through the deck under her feet.
Not everyone found a seat in a boat that night. Many did not make it.

story.title: Phoenix and Cruz and the Tap-Tap-Tap of Ireland
story.subtitle: A rainbow, a drum, and the tales leprechauns live in

chapters.heading: Chapter 1: The Tap-Tap-Tap Drum
chapters.text:
Phoenix tapped a beat on his Lego tower. Tap. Tap-tap. TAP.

Lego pieces covered the floor like a tiny city. A half-built Lego castle stood in the corner, towers leaning just a little.

Cruz swam his shark toy across the carpet. "CHOMP CHOMP," he said.

Moonlight came through the window. The clock said way past bedtime, again.

It had been three sleeps since a glowing stone bone sat on their carpet.

Then a tiny light blinked by the closet. BZZZT!

Sprocket the robot zoomed out, round and shiny. His belly glowed soft blue, then green. "Hello again!" he beeped. "I found something new."

He held up a tiny round drum. "This is a **bodhrán**," he said. "It's a real drum from Ireland. That's a country far across the ocean."

Phoenix grinned. "A drum? I know drums!" He bounced on his toes, tapping a beat with his sneakers too.

Cruz banged his shark toy on the floor. "CHOMP CHOMP, tap tap!"

"Tap a beat," said Sprocket. "See what happens."

Phoenix tapped. Tap-tap. TAP-tap-tap.

The carpet glowed green. A rainbow path unrolled right out their bedroom door, swirling and bright.

"WHOOOOSH!" yelled Cruz, jumping up so fast he nearly tripped on a Lego brick.

"Ireland's calling," said Sprocket. "Follow the rainbow. Normal size. Feet on the ground. Let's go!"

They stepped onto the glowing path, hand in hand.

chapters.heading: Chapter 2: The Green, Green Hills
chapters.text:
The rainbow path landed them on a hill. It was so green it looked painted.

"Whoa," said Phoenix. "It's like a Minecraft grass block. But everywhere, and real!"

Stone walls ran across the fields, like giant Lego borders stacked by hand.

Birds sang overhead, and far away a church bell rang, soft and low.

Cruz counted sheep on the hillside. "One, two, three sheep!" he giggled, pointing at each fluffy dot.

Somewhere close, they heard a sound. Tap. Tap-tap. Tap.

"That's a sound from old stories," said Sprocket. "Tap-tap-tap. Like a tiny hammer, fixing a tiny shoe."

They followed the sound down a little path. An old woman sat under a tree, mending a little boot with a small wooden hammer.

"Are you a leprechaun?" Cruz asked, eyes wide.

She laughed, warm and loud. "No, little one. I'm a storyteller. Leprechauns live in our tales. Not under this tree."

"In old Irish stories," she said, "leprechauns are small, old-looking men. They work as shoemakers. Making shoes is their only honest job, the old stories say."

Phoenix nodded hard. "Like a tiny cobbler!"

"Exactly," she said. "People say you hear one before you ever see him. Tap, tap, tap, goes his hammer, somewhere just out of sight."

Cruz tapped his sneakers together. "Tap tap! Am I a leprechaun now?"

Everyone laughed, even the sheep seemed to listen.

chapters.heading: Chapter 3: Three Wishes and a Rainbow
chapters.text:
"Sit," said the storyteller, patting the grass, "and I'll tell you a tale."

The grass felt cool and a little damp, like it had just rained.

"In old stories," she said, "if you catch a leprechaun, he must grant you three wishes. Or show you his pot of gold. That's how you let him go."

Cruz held up three fingers, counting carefully. "Three! One, two, three wishes!"

"And where's the gold hidden?" asked Phoenix, leaning in close.

"Legend says," she smiled, "at the end of a rainbow." She pointed up. A rainbow curled bright over the hill.

"That's just a story, though," she added. "Nobody has ever really found gold there. But it's a fun tale to tell, isn't it?"

Phoenix looked at their own glowing path. "Our rainbow doesn't have gold. It has us!"

"Even better," beeped Sprocket, lights blinking happily.

Cruz wiggled his three fingers at the sky. "Wish one: more sharks. Wish two: more Minecraft. Wish three..." He thought hard, tongue sticking out. "Pancakes!"

"PANCAKE POWER!" shouted Phoenix.

They both fell over laughing in the soft green grass.

chapters.heading: Chapter 4: The Trickiest Trick in Ireland
chapters.text:
"Here's the tricky part," said the storyteller. "Old stories say leprechauns are the trickiest tricksters around. They'd rather fool you than hand over their gold."

The old woman's eyes twinkled, like she already knew the ending.

"What if you catch one?" asked Phoenix. "Does he just stay caught?"

"Not for long," she laughed. "Old tales say if you look away, even for a blink — poof. He's gone!"

Cruz gasped. "Gone? Forever?"

"It's only a story, Cruz," said Sprocket gently. "Nobody's really chasing anybody. It's just a fun old tale. Like a magic trick that always works, every single time."

Cruz relaxed. He grinned wide. "Like Spiderman swinging away!"

"Exactly like that," said the storyteller, chuckling.

Phoenix squinted one eye hard. He tried not to blink at all. His eye watered. He blinked. "Darn it! Nothing there anyway. But still — darn it!"

Everyone giggled, even Sprocket's lights flickered like laughing.

"That," said the storyteller, "is exactly how the story goes. Every single time, in every telling."

chapters.heading: Chapter 5: Music at the Old Castle
chapters.text:
The storyteller walked them to a tall stone castle. Its stones were stacked like giant gray Lego bricks, piled higher than any tower Phoenix had ever built.

"Whoa," whispered Phoenix. "Who built THAT?"

"People, long ago," said Sprocket. "Stone by stone, with their own two hands. Ireland has many old castles like this one."

Music drifted out from inside. A fiddle. A drum. Feet stomping in a quick, happy beat.

Phoenix's whole body started bouncing. "That's a BEAT! That's basically hip hop, with a fiddle!"

Dancers kicked their legs up fast. Arms stiff at their sides. Feet flying so quick they blurred.

Their feet never seemed to touch the ground for long, like stones skipping on water.

"Can we dance?" Cruz asked, already wiggling his hips.

"Dance away," laughed the storyteller.

Phoenix drummed the beat on his knees. Cruz hopped and wiggled his own wild dance. Half shark, half Spiderman, all silly.

"SHARK DANCE!" Cruz yelled, flapping his arms like fins.

The fiddler laughed so hard, she nearly dropped her bow.

Even Sprocket's little lights blinked in time with the music, round and round.

chapters.heading: Chapter 6: Lucky's Cereal Box and the Movie King
chapters.text:
Down in a little village, Sprocket pointed at a cereal box in a shop window.

"That's **Lucky**," he said. "A cartoon leprechaun. That cereal has been around since 1964."

Cruz pressed his nose right to the glass. "He's so silly!"

"There was a movie too," said the storyteller. "In **1959**. A leprechaun king named Brian, who in the old tales was said to grant wishes and play tricks."

"A whole MOVIE king?" said Phoenix. "Leprechauns are basically superheroes now."

"Cartoon superheroes," said Sprocket. "Real leprechauns only ever lived in stories, like hers. But people loved those stories so much. They put leprechauns on cereal boxes. And in movies, too."

"In a town called **Carlingford**," added the storyteller, "folks even made a pretend leprechaun hunting trail. Just for giggles. Nobody really catches one. It's only a game, like hide-and-seek with no seeking at all."

The street smelled like warm bread and new rain.

Cruz nodded wisely. "Like how sharks are real. But Sharknado is just silly."

Phoenix burst out laughing. "Exactly like that, Cruz!"

The shopkeeper gave them each a shamrock sticker. Shaped like a tiny green clover.

"For luck," she winked, waving them off.

chapters.heading: Chapter 7: Green Parade Day
chapters.text:
Outside, a parade was starting. Drums. Fiddles. Green flags waving everywhere you looked.

Green ribbons fluttered from every lamppost along the street.

"It's **St. Patrick's Day**!" said the storyteller. "Every **March 17th**, Ireland celebrates. Parades, just like this one, all across the country."

Phoenix spotted a marcher with a giant four-leaf clover banner. "What's that?"

"A **four-leaf clover**," said Sprocket. "People say it's lucky to find one. It's a different lucky charm than a leprechaun. But they often show up together in pictures."

Cruz counted the leaves carefully. "One, two, three, four! Lucky!"

A drummer winked at Phoenix. He tossed him a spare drumstick. Phoenix caught it and drummed along with the parade beat, grinning the whole way down the street.

Cruz marched behind him, doing his best shark-fin arms, right in time with the music.

"CRUNCH CRUNCH!" Cruz shouted. Just because it felt like a parade kind of sound.

Nobody minded one bit. Everybody just danced along.

chapters.heading: Chapter 8: Back to the Carpet
chapters.text:
The rainbow path still glowed at the edge of the parade, waiting.

"Time to go home," said Sprocket softly. "Say goodbye to Ireland."

"Bye, hills! Bye, castle! Bye, parade!" Phoenix waved at everything at once.

Cruz hugged the storyteller's knee. "Bye, story lady. Tell more leprechaun stories to other kids, okay?"

"Always," she smiled, waving back.

They stepped onto the rainbow. WHOOOOSH! Green light swirled all around them. Then — carpet. Their own bedroom carpet, soft under their feet again.

Phoenix still held the drumstick from the parade. It glowed the tiniest bit of green. Then it settled, just an ordinary wooden drumstick.

Cruz found the shamrock sticker, still stuck on his pajama sleeve. "Lucky," he whispered, yawning big.

Sprocket's lights dimmed to a sleepy blink. "You did great today," he beeped. "Tap-tap-tap, just like a tiny cobbler. PRINT WELL."

The green glow lingered a moment longer than usual, like it didn't want to leave either. Then it blinked out, leaving just a soft green shimmer on the carpet, fading slowly, like the end of a rainbow.

story.ending_line: Goodnight, Phoenix. Goodnight, Cruz. Print well.

true_facts.text: Leprechauns come from old Irish stories, where they are small, old-looking men who work as shoemakers.
Making and mending shoes is said to be their only honest job in the old tales.
People say you can hear a leprechaun's **tap, tap, tap** hammer before you ever see him.
Old stories say if you catch a leprechaun, he must grant **three wishes** or show you his gold.
Legend says leprechauns hide their gold at the end of a **rainbow** — though nobody has ever really found it there.
Stories say leprechauns would rather trick you than ever hand over their gold.
Old tales say a leprechaun vanishes in a blink the moment you look away.
A cartoon leprechaun named **Lucky** has called his cereal 'magically delicious' since **1964**.
A **1959** movie told of a leprechaun king named **Brian** who loved wishes and tricks.
In the town of **Carlingford**, people made a pretend leprechaun hunting trail, just for fun.
Ireland celebrates **St. Patrick's Day** every **March 17th** with parades.
A lucky **four-leaf clover** is a different charm from a leprechaun, though they often appear together.

new_recurring.name: The Lucky Bodhrán
new_recurring.rule: A tiny glowing Irish drum Sprocket brings along; when a child taps a beat on it, a rainbow path unrolls from the bedroom to a real place, and fades again once they step back home.

bible_suggestions.ending_summary: Phoenix and Cruz landed back on their bedroom carpet with a glowing parade drumstick and a shamrock sticker, as Sprocket dimmed out whispering 'Print well.'

violations.quote: Sprocket's lights dimmed to a sleepy blink. "You did great today," he beeped. "Tap-tap-tap, just like a tiny cobbler. PRINT WELL."
Goodnight, Phoenix. Goodnight, Cruz. Print well.

story.title: Jack and Ellie Dive with the Shark Lady
story.subtitle: A nighttime swim through four hundred million years of sharks.

chapters.heading: Chapter 1: The Glowing Tooth
chapters.text:
Jack lay on his bedroom floor, flipping through his shark book for the hundredth time. Around his neck hung a real shark tooth, a souvenir from his very first snorkeling trip.

Ellie flopped down beside him, humming her mermaid song. "Sharks are okay," she said. "But mermaids are better."

"Sharks were here LONG before mermaids," Jack said. "Before everything."

That is when the tooth around his neck began to glow bright green. It HUMMED like a seashell held up to your ear, only louder.

"Jack," Ellie whispered, "it's doing a thing."

The glow spread across the carpet like water, and the carpet turned into cool, dark sea. A woman swam up wearing old-fashioned diving goggles, smiling like she had been waiting for them.

"I'm Eugenie," she said. "Folks call me the Shark Lady, because I have spent my whole life studying sharks."

"Are you real?" Ellie asked.

"Real as this tooth," said the Shark Lady, tapping Jack's necklace. "Sharks don't have bones like you do. Their skeletons are made of **cartilage** — bendy stuff, like the squishy part of your ear. That's why old shark skeletons almost never last."

"So how do we know about old sharks at all?" Jack asked.

"Follow me," she said, "and I'll show you sharks from **more than 400 million years ago** — swimming here before there were even dinosaurs, or trees."

Jack grabbed Ellie's hand. Together they kicked off the carpet and into the glowing water.

chapters.heading: Chapter 2: Before the Dinosaurs
chapters.text:
The water here was murky and green, and strange shadowy shapes drifted past.

"Those are some of the very first sharks," the Shark Lady said. "This ocean is **400 million years** old. No dinosaurs yet. Not even trees on land."

Ellie squinted at the shadows. "They don't look very scary."

"Most weren't big," said the Shark Lady. "But they were tough enough to still have relatives swimming today."

Jack noticed something glinting on the sandy bottom — little pointed shapes, scattered like lost buttons.

"Teeth!" he said, scooping one up. "Lots of them!"

"Good eye," said the Shark Lady. "Since shark skeletons are bendy and don't last, almost everything we know about ancient sharks comes from teeth left behind in the sand and rock. Teeth are hard. They stick around."

Ellie picked up a tiny curved one and held it like a treasure. "This is better than any seashell."

"Keep looking," the Shark Lady said, grinning. "There's a much bigger tooth waiting up ahead — and it belonged to the biggest shark that ever lived."

Jack's eyes went wide. He grabbed Ellie's hand again, and they swam toward the deeper, darker water, teeth clinking in Ellie's cupped palms like coins.

chapters.heading: Chapter 3: The Giant Tooth
chapters.text:
A huge shadow slid across the sea floor, bigger than their whole house.

Ellie froze. "Is it going to eat us?"

"No need to worry," the Shark Lady said gently. "That's just a memory. This giant shark, called **megalodon**, isn't around anymore — it's **extinct**, which just means every single one of them is gone now. This happened millions of years ago."

Jack spotted something huge and triangle-shaped poking out of the sand. He tugged it free. It was a tooth as long as his whole hand.

"WHOA," Jack breathed. "That's bigger than my foot!"

"That's a real megalodon tooth," said the Shark Lady. "Almost everything we know about this giant shark comes from teeth just like that one, since its bendy skeleton didn't last."

Ellie peeked out from behind Jack's shoulder, brave again now that the shadow was only a memory. "So it can't get us?"

"Not even a little bit," the Shark Lady promised.

"That might be a bit of an exaggeration, how huge people say it was," she added, "but one look at this tooth tells you it was REALLY big."

"THAT TOOTH IS AS BIG AS MY HAND!" Ellie shouted, holding it up next to her own fingers.
chapters.shout_line: THAT TOOTH IS AS BIG AS MY HAND!

chapters.heading: Chapter 4: The Gentle Giant
chapters.text:
The water brightened, and something enormous glided out of the blue — longer than a school bus, with a mouth wide enough to swallow a beach ball.

Ellie grabbed Jack's arm. Then she noticed the giant shark wasn't opening its mouth to bite anything. It just drifted, calm and slow, like a gentle whale.

"That's a whale shark," the Shark Lady said. "The biggest fish in the whole world, over **40 feet long**. But don't worry — it only eats tiny floating bits of food called plankton, by gulping water through that huge mouth and filtering the tiny bits out."

"It's like a giant, gentle vacuum," Jack said.

Ellie reached out her hand but didn't touch — the Shark Lady had already told them to only ever watch, never touch. "It's so soft-looking," she whispered instead.

"Some whale sharks live to be **100 years old or even more**," said the Shark Lady. "Longer than almost any other fish."

"A hundred!" Jack said. "That's older than my great-grandpa."

The whale shark swam a slow loop around them, close but careful, its tail swishing gently like a wave goodbye.

"IT'S GENTLE!" Ellie shouted, waving both arms at the giant fish as it drifted off into the blue.

chapters.heading: Chapter 5: Rows and Rows of Teeth
chapters.text:
A sleek gray shadow cut through the water, faster and sharper than the whale shark had been.

"Great white shark," the Shark Lady said. "They can grow up to about **20 feet long**."

Jack pressed close to look, careful to keep his distance. "Its teeth look like little triangles with bumpy edges."

"Sharp eyes," said the Shark Lady. "Those bumpy edges are called serrated — like a steak knife — perfect for catching seals and fish."

"Doesn't it run out of teeth?" Ellie asked, remembering the loose ones scattered in the sand earlier.

"Never," said the Shark Lady. "Sharks grow new teeth their whole lives. Thousands of them. New ones keep moving forward to replace any that fall out or wear down."

"So that's why we found so many on the ground back there," Jack said, snapping his fingers.

"Exactly," said the Shark Lady. "You two are turning into proper shark detectives."

The great white swam a slow circle, gave one last flick of its tail, and vanished into the deep blue, leaving only a trail of bubbles behind.

Ellie counted on her fingers. "So it's basically got a never-ending smile."

Jack laughed so hard he swallowed a mouthful of pretend seawater.

chapters.heading: Chapter 6: The Hammer-Headed Swimmer
chapters.text:
Something strange swam toward them — a shark with a head shaped like a flat hammer, an eye poking out on each end.

"That's a hammerhead," the Shark Lady said. "Its wide head spreads its eyes far apart, so it can see almost all the way around itself."

"Like having eyes on both sides of a ruler," Jack said, holding his hands out wide.

Ellie tilted her head, copying the shark's shape. "Why does it need to see so much?"

"It helps find food hiding in the sand," said the Shark Lady. "And sharks have another trick, too. Little jelly-filled dots on their snouts feel tiny tingles — electricity — made by other animals' bodies. Even a fish holding perfectly still can't hide from that."

"So it's like it can feel heartbeats?" Jack asked.

"Close enough," said the Shark Lady.

The hammerhead swung its strange head side to side, scanning the sandy bottom, then swam off in a smooth S-shape.

"IT SEES EVERYWHERE!" Ellie shouted, spinning in a circle to copy it, until she got dizzy and grabbed Jack's shoulder to steady herself. He caught her, laughing.

chapters.heading: Chapter 7: Walking on the Reef
chapters.text:
The water grew shallow, warm, and bright with coral shaped like brains and fans.

Jack spotted a small, speckled shark creeping along the coral using its fins like little paddles. "Is it... walking?"

"That's an epaulette shark," said the Shark Lady. "It really can walk across the reef with its fins, even in and out of tide pools. It can even survive for hours with hardly any oxygen — the air we need to breathe."

"No way," Jack said, crouching to watch it waddle along.

Nearby, another shark lay completely still on the sandy floor.

"Is that one asleep?" Ellie whispered, worried it might be hurt.

"Resting," said the Shark Lady. "That's a nurse shark. It can pump water over its gills while lying still, so it doesn't need to keep swimming to breathe, like most sharks do."

Ellie relaxed, relieved. "So it's just having a lazy day."

"Exactly," laughed the Shark Lady.

Jack tried waddling along the sand on his hands and knees, copying the little walking shark, until Ellie laughed so hard bubbles shot out of her mouth.

chapters.heading: Chapter 8: Mermaid's Purses
chapters.text:
Ellie spotted something odd caught in the seaweed — a small, dark, leathery pouch with curly strings at each corner.

"What IS that?" she asked, nose nearly touching it.

"That," said the Shark Lady, "is a mermaid's purse."

Ellie gasped. "A REAL mermaid's purse?"

"Sort of," the Shark Lady laughed. "It's actually a shark egg case. Some sharks lay their babies inside pouches like this one, instead of having live babies the way many other sharks do."

"IT'S A MERMAID'S PURSE!" Ellie shouted, cradling it gently in both hands.

Jack rubbed his palm along a nearby shark's side as it swam past, careful and slow. "Its skin feels like sandpaper!"

"That's because of thousands of tiny tooth-shaped bumps covering its skin," said the Shark Lady. "They help it swim smoothly through the water."

"Sharks really do have teeth everywhere," Jack said, shaking his head.

"Sharks sit at the very top of the ocean's food chain," the Shark Lady added. "That means they help keep every other animal's numbers healthy and balanced — like referees of the sea."

"Are they dangerous to us, though?" Jack asked.

"Barely ever," she said. "Shark bites on people are extremely rare. It's people who need to be gentler with sharks, not the other way around."

Ellie tucked the little purse carefully back into the seaweed, right where she'd found it.

chapters.heading: Chapter 9: Home Again
chapters.text:
The water began to glow green again, swirling like it had at the very start.

"Time to go home," the Shark Lady said. "But before you do — did you know there are more than **500 different kinds** of sharks swimming in our oceans right now?"

"Five hundred!" Jack said. "We only met about seven!"

"Plenty more adventures left, then," she said, winking.

"How do YOU know so much about sharks?" Ellie asked her.

"I spent my whole life studying them," said the Shark Lady. "I even proved that sharks are curious, clever animals that can learn tricks, just like a puppy can."

"That's so cool," Jack said.

The green glow swallowed them up, and when it faded, Jack and Ellie were back on the bedroom carpet, exactly where they'd started.

Jack's necklace had stopped glowing. But resting beside it on the carpet was one small, curved tooth, and tucked right next to that, a tiny leathery mermaid's purse.

Ellie picked up the little purse and held it against her cheek. "Mermaids and sharks," she said. "Maybe they both win."

"Deal," said Jack, yawning.

They climbed into their beds, tooth and purse tucked safely on the nightstand between them.

story.ending_line: Goodnight, Jack. Goodnight, Ellie. Swim well.

true_facts.text: A shark's skeleton is made of bendy **cartilage**, not hard bone — like the squishy part of your ear.
There are more than **500 different kinds** of sharks swimming in the oceans today.
Sharks were swimming in the oceans **more than 400 million years ago**, before dinosaurs or even trees.
The whale shark is the biggest fish in the world, over **40 feet long**, but it only eats tiny floating bits of food.
The great white shark can grow up to about **20 feet long** and has rows of bumpy-edged teeth.
Megalodon was a giant shark from millions of years ago that isn't around anymore, known mostly from its **huge fossil teeth**.
Because bendy shark skeletons don't last, almost everything we know about ancient sharks comes from their teeth.
Sharks grow thousands of teeth over their lives, with new ones always moving forward to replace old ones.
Shark skin is covered in thousands of tiny tooth-shaped bumps that make it feel like sandpaper.
Sharks can feel tiny tingles of electricity from other animals' bodies through jelly-filled dots on their snouts.
The epaulette shark can actually walk across the reef using its fins, and can survive a long time with very little air.
The hammerhead shark's wide head spreads its eyes apart so it can see almost all the way around itself.
Some sharks lay their eggs inside leathery pouches nicknamed **mermaid's purses**.
Sharks sit at the top of the ocean's food chain, helping keep all the other animals balanced and healthy.

new_recurring.name: Eugenie the Shark Lady
new_recurring.rule: A kind, curious guide based on real shark scientist Eugenie Clark. Appears whenever Jack and Ellie dive into an ocean adventure, calm and encouraging, always teaching gently and never letting the children touch wild animals.

bible_suggestions.ending_summary: Jack and Ellie wake back on their bedroom carpet to find a small curved shark tooth and a tiny leathery mermaid's purse resting beside Jack's glowing necklace, now dark and quiet.

violations.quote: Jack rubbed his palm along a nearby shark's side as it swam past, careful and slow.

story.title: Nora and the Glowing Tile of Pompeii
story.subtitle: A hushed, hopscotching journey through a buried Roman town.

chapters.heading: Chapter 1: The Tile That Hummed
chapters.text:
Nora sat cross-legged on her bedroom floor. Tiny colored tiles were spread around her like candy. She was making a mosaic coaster, piece by piece. It was way past bedtime, but she just needed one more tile.

She picked up a small gold square. It felt warm in her hand. Then it began to hum, soft and low, like a sleepy bee.

"Ooh," Nora whispered. "That's new."

The tile glowed brighter. Light spilled out, swirling into a window right there on her carpet. A tiny voice crackled from the glow.

"Hello, tile-sorter," it said. "I am Tessera. I am made of a hundred old tiles, and I know a hundred old places."

Nora grinned. "Can you show me one?"

"I can do better," said Tessera. "Step through. I'll pull you home the second you want to come back."

Nora took a breath and stepped into the light. "A window!" she gasped. The carpet disappeared. Sunshine and noise rushed in instead.

She was standing on a busy stone street. Carts rattled by. People called out, selling bread, olives, and fish.

"Welcome to Pompeii," said Tessera, floating beside her like a glowing kite. "A real town, in what is now Italy, near a city called Naples."

"It's loud," Nora laughed. "How many people even live here?"

"Somewhere between eleven thousand and fifteen thousand," said Tessera. "Shops, bathhouses, a theater — a whole busy town."

Nora noticed water trickling nearby, running through a stone fountain on the corner. "Where does the water come from?"

"Pipes," said Tessera, "running under the streets, bringing water to fountains all over town. Pretty clever, for so long ago."

Nora dipped her fingers in the cool water. "Where does the name Pompeii come from, anyway? It's a funny word."

"Nobody's completely sure," said Tessera, "but it might come from an old word meaning five — maybe five little villages that joined into one big town."

"Five friends making one town," said Nora. "That's kind of nice."

chapters.heading: Chapter 2: Stepping Stones and Rattling Carts
chapters.text:
A cart rolled past, wheels splashing through a puddle. Nora jumped back just in time.

"Careful!" said Tessera. "Pompeii streets get messy."

Nora looked down. Big flat stones poked up out of the street, spaced apart like stones in a creek.

"These must be for crossing without getting muddy," she said, "like turtle-back stones in a stream."

She hopped from stone to stone, testing her idea. Her sneakers stayed perfectly dry.

A cart rattled right through the gaps between the stones, its wheels rolling smoothly through the spaces she had left empty.

"You're exactly right," said Tessera. "The street was built so people could cross without stepping in mud, and carts could still roll straight through the gaps."

"It's basically hopscotch," said Nora, hopping back across. "Ancient hopscotch."

"That is exactly what it is," said Tessera, sounding delighted.

A bell clanged somewhere nearby. Nora looked up a wide street, toward a huge, round building rising over the rooftops.

"What's that giant round thing?" she asked.

"Follow the sound," said Tessera. "Let's find out."

chapters.heading: Chapter 3: The Big Round Building
chapters.text:
Nora jogged toward the roar of a cheering crowd. The round building got bigger and bigger as she got closer.

"This is the amphitheater," said Tessera. "A giant oval stadium for watching shows, built around seventy years before the eruption. It's one of the oldest ones ever found."

Nora tipped her head back, staring up at the stone rings of seats. "It's like a stone stadium," she said. "Bet from above it looks like one big mosaic circle."

"You and your mosaics," said Tessera, laughing. "But you're right. Rings and rings, all fitting together."

They climbed partway up the stone steps. Below, crowds filled the seats, clapping and cheering for the show.

"People came from the whole town to watch here," said Tessera. "Games, contests, big performances — it was the place to be."

Nora counted the rows with her finger, tracing circles in the air. "Seven rings," she said. "Eight. It just keeps going."

"That's the fun of a really good circle," said Tessera. "It never seems to end."

Nora laughed. "Just like my mosaic coaster. I keep adding one more tile."

"Speaking of tiles," said Tessera, glow flickering, "there's something you should see on the walls nearby. Come on."

chapters.heading: Chapter 4: Words on the Wall
chapters.text:
They walked along a sunny street. Painted words covered the walls, bright red and black.

"What's all this writing?" asked Nora, tracing a letter with her finger.

"Ancient advertising," said Tessera. "People painted messages right on their houses — shop signs, election slogans, even jokes. Like a wall full of posters."

"So someone's wall was basically a bulletin board," said Nora. "That's kind of brilliant."

"The Romans thought so too," said Tessera.

Then Nora spotted something odd. A thin curl of smoke rose from a mountain far past the rooftops.

"Tessera, look," she said, pointing. "Is that smoke?"

Tessera's glow flickered. "The mountain," it said quietly. "Vesuvius. It's a volcano — a mountain that can spit fire, smoke, and rock. It's starting to wake up."

"Is everyone going to be okay?" Nora asked.

"Everyone here is safe right now," said Tessera gently. "But it's time for us to watch from somewhere safer. Hold on."

The glowing thread around Nora's wrist tugged. In an instant, the street folded away, and they stood high above the whole bay, watching from a calm, misty distance.

"There," said Tessera. "Now we can watch safely, just like a writer named Pliny the Younger did, long ago. He stood across the bay like this, and wrote down everything he saw, in two careful letters."

"Like a reporter," said Nora.

"Exactly like a reporter," said Tessera. "Thanks to him, we know this happened on one single day — August 24, in the year 79."

Below, ash began to fall, soft and gray, like dirty snow.

chapters.heading: Chapter 5: Buried in a Blink
chapters.text:
Nora watched the gray snow fall and fall, covering roofs, streets, and stepping stones.

"It happened fast," said Tessera. "Ash and rock piled up high — in some places, as tall as a two-story house."

"That's so much," Nora said softly.

"It covered everything so quickly," said Tessera, "that it froze the whole town in place. Bread stayed right in its oven. Paintings stayed bright on walls. Even writing on walls stayed exactly as it was."

"Like pausing a movie," said Nora.

"A very long pause," said Tessera. "Almost one thousand seven hundred years long."

Nora was quiet a moment, watching the gray curtain settle over the rooftops below. "Did everyone get away safe?" she asked.

"Many people left the town in time," said Tessera. "It's part of why we know so much about how they lived — because the town stayed so carefully kept, like a secret, until people found it again."

Nora nodded slowly. "Okay," she said. "Let's go see what they found."

The light around them shimmered, and the gray scene melted away.

chapters.heading: Chapter 6: The Sister Town by the Sea
chapters.text:
The light settled into a smaller, breezier town, right along the water.

"This is Herculaneum," said Tessera. "A smaller town nearby, buried by the very same eruption."

"Looks different," said Nora, pointing at dark, solid rock covering everything instead of gray ash.

"Different kind of material here," said Tessera. "It kept things even better in some spots — wooden furniture, even old rolled-up paper called scrolls, stayed in one piece."

"Scrolls? Like ancient books?" Nora asked.

"Exactly like ancient books," said Tessera. "Rolled-up paper, with writing inside. Imagine finding one of those after all this time."

"Can we get a closer look?" Nora asked, stepping toward a doorway. Its wooden frame still stood, dark and shiny like stone.

"It's kind of amazing," she whispered. "Like the sea town kept its own secrets."

"Every buried town keeps a few," said Tessera. "Come on. Let's jump ahead — way, way ahead — to when people finally found them again."

chapters.heading: Chapter 7: Digging Up a Lost Town
chapters.text:
The light swirled, and the world changed again. Now there were tools, ropes, and workers with dusty hands.

"The year is 1748," said Tessera. "Workers digging here found old walls, buried right where the town had been hiding."

"After all that time?" Nora said. "That's so long!"

"Almost seventeen hundred years," said Tessera. "People had nearly forgotten Pompeii was even here."

People who dig up old things to learn about the past are called archaeologists, and a few of them worked nearby, brushing dust from a half-uncovered wall.

Nora crouched close. Something round sat half-buried in the ash.

"Wait — is that bread?" Nora said, pointing.

One of the workers lifted it gently. "Well spotted," she said. "A whole loaf, still marked with the baker's knife lines, like it just came out of the oven."

"It's been down there the whole time," Nora whispered, "just waiting."

Further along, Nora noticed a smudge of red peeking from under crumbling plaster. "There's color under there," she said.

A worker brushed it clean. Red and gold bloomed across the wall.

"A fresco," said Tessera. "A painting made right on wet plaster, so the color sinks in and lasts. There's a whole house nearby with walls full of mysterious painted scenes. Nobody is fully sure what the pictures mean, but they're beautiful."

"I want to make a fresco someday," said Nora.

"You basically already do," said Tessera. "Every mosaic is its own kind of picture that lasts."

chapters.heading: Chapter 8: The Mountain That's Still Watching
chapters.text:
The dusty dig faded, and a new scene bloomed: tall fences, clear paths, and crowds of visitors with cameras.

"This is Pompeii today," said Tessera. "People come from everywhere to walk these streets. Millions of visitors, every single year."

Nora looked around at the ancient walls, still standing in sunshine. "It's like a museum you can walk right through."

"It's protected now," said Tessera, "by a worldwide group that looks after extra-special places. They call it a World Heritage Site."

Far off, over the rooftops, the mountain stood quietly, its top still sometimes smoking.

"Is it still... a volcano?" Nora asked, remembering the gray snow.

"It is," said Tessera. "Vesuvius is still active, and scientists keep a close watch on it, every single day, just to be safe."

Nora nodded, satisfied. "Good," she said. "Somebody should keep an eye on it."

"Somebody always does," said Tessera.

The light began to dim, curling gently back toward its tile shape.

"Time to go home," said Tessera. "You've still got a coaster to finish."

The carpet rushed back beneath her. Nora blinked, back in her own room, the little gold tile warm and quiet in her palm.

She looked down at her half-finished mosaic coaster. Then, carefully, she pressed one more tile into place — a tiny gold square, right in the center, like a little glowing window of its own.

"Goodnight, Pompeii," she whispered. "Thanks for the five little villages."

story.ending_line: Goodnight, Nora. Sleep tight, and keep your tiles bright.

true_facts.text: **Pompeii** was a real town in what is now **Italy**, near the city of **Naples**.
Somewhere between **eleven thousand and fifteen thousand** people once lived in busy Pompeii.
The town had pipes running under its streets, bringing water to **fountains** all over town.
Streets had **raised stepping stones**, so people could cross without mud, while carts rolled through the gaps between them.
The town's **amphitheater** was built around **seventy years before the eruption**, one of the oldest ones ever found.
A young writer named **Pliny the Younger** watched the eruption from across the bay and wrote two careful letters about it.
**Mount Vesuvius** erupted on **August 24, in the year 79**.
The eruption buried the town under ash and rock as tall as **a two-story house** in some places.
The ash fell so fast it froze the town in place — **bread stayed in its oven**, and paintings and writing stayed exactly as they were.
Nearby **Herculaneum** was buried by the same eruption, but kept even wooden furniture and rolled-up paper called **scrolls**.
Pompeii was **rediscovered in 1748**, when workers digging there found old buried walls.
Colorful wall paintings called **frescoes** were found, including a house full of mysterious painted scenes.
**Mount Vesuvius** is still an active volcano, and scientists keep a close watch on it today.
Pompeii is protected as a **World Heritage Site**, visited by **millions of people** every year.

new_recurring.name: Tessera
new_recurring.rule: A single glowing gold mosaic tile from Nora's own craft kit. When it hums and glows, it opens a swirling light-window into a real moment from history. Nora can step through, and a glowing thread always lets Tessera pull her home instantly if needed. Tessera speaks warmly, loves mosaics and patterns as much as Nora does, and never shows her anything invented — only things that really happened.

bible_suggestions.ending_summary: Nora returned to her bedroom carpet and pressed one more gold tile into the center of her half-finished mosaic coaster, a tiny glowing keepsake of her trip to Pompeii.

violations.quote: ash and rock piled up high — in some places, as tall as a two-story house
The eruption buried the town under ash and rock as tall as a two-story house in some places.

story.title: Maya and the Race to the Moon
story.subtitle: A splashy trip through the real Space Race.

chapters.heading: Chapter 1: The Beep in the Fish Tank
chapters.text:
Maya lay on her bedroom floor, drawing a tiny boat with crayons. It had been one whole week since Barnacle waved his flipper at the bridge that hummed.

Her night-light flickered. Then her fish tank started to glow bright green.

BEEP. BEEP. BEEP.

The sound came from the water, not from any speaker. Maya sat up fast. "That's not my fish," she whispered.

A whiskered nose popped up through the glowing water. "All aboard, Maya!" said Barnacle the harbour seal, grinning his big gummy grin.

"Barnacle! Where did that beep come from?"

"From space," said Barnacle. "A real beep, from a real round ball, way back in 1957."

Maya leaned closer. The water swirled like a little round window, showing darkness with tiny white dots.

"On **October 4, 1957**, the Soviet Union launched a round machine called **Sputnik 1**," Barnacle said. "It was the first man-made thing to ever circle the whole Earth."

"How big was it?" Maya asked, already sketching a circle in her notebook.

"About as wide as a beach ball," said Barnacle. "Just **58 centimeters**. But it carried a little radio that went *beep, beep, beep*, and people everywhere could hear it on their own radios at home."

Maya tapped the glass. "Like our fish tank is doing right now?"

"Exactly like that," said Barnacle. "Your tank caught the echo, all the way from long ago."

Maya grabbed her crayon and drew little lines shooting out from her round ball, like the beep was singing a song. "I want to see it fly," she said.

The moment she said it, the water rose up in a glowing bubble. **SPLOOSH!** The bedroom melted away, and Maya and Barnacle floated beside a small silver ball, blinking its beep into the dark.

"Ready for the whole trip?" asked Barnacle.

Maya grinned and grabbed his flipper. "All aboard!"

chapters.heading: Chapter 2: Laika's Big Ride
chapters.text:
The bubble floated past the little silver ball, and a second, bigger one drifted into view behind it.

"One month later, a second satellite went up," said Barnacle. "This one had a passenger."

"A person?" Maya asked.

"A dog," said Barnacle. "A brave little dog named **Laika**. On **November 3, 1957**, she became the first living creature to ever circle the Earth."

Maya pressed her nose to the glowing water. Inside, she could just make out a small furry shape curled up snug inside a round little room built just her size, called a capsule.

"Was she scared?" Maya asked.

"She was a good traveler," said Barnacle gently. "And she made the whole world fall in love with her. Kids everywhere drew pictures of her, just like you draw boats."

That gave Maya an idea. She flipped to a fresh page and drew Laika with a little space helmet and a wagging tail. The moment she finished the tail, the drawing seemed to wag right there on the paper.

"Ooh!" Maya laughed. "Did you see that?"

"Space magic," said Barnacle. "Or maybe just very good drawing."

Maya giggled. "Both, probably."

"Laika showed everyone that a living creature could survive going all the way around the Earth," said Barnacle. "She helped open the door for real people to go next."

Maya tucked her drawing carefully into her notebook, right beside Sputnik. "She gets to come with us," she said firmly.

"She always does," said Barnacle, with a wink.

chapters.heading: Chapter 3: America Answers Back
chapters.text:
The bubble drifted forward, and the dark sky filled with blueprints and busy people in white coats.

"Sputnik's beep gave the United States a big surprise," said Barnacle. "So they built a brand new team just for space."

"What kind of team?" Maya asked.

"It's called **NASA**," said Barnacle. "It started working on **October 1, 1958**. Their whole job was figuring out how to fly to space."

Maya spotted a long silver rocket standing on a launchpad below them. "Is that theirs?"

"That's **Explorer 1**," said Barnacle. "It launched on **January 31, 1958** — America's very first satellite."

The rocket roared up with a **WHOOOSH**, and Maya clapped her hands over her ears.

"What did it find up there?" she asked, once the shaking stopped.

"Something nobody expected," said Barnacle. "A big ring of tiny invisible zaps wrapped around the Earth, like a giant belt. It's called the **Van Allen belt**. It can't reach down to us on the ground, but spaceships flying through it have to be careful."

Maya thought about her swim goggles keeping pool water out of her eyes. "So it's like the Earth wears invisible armbands?"

Barnacle laughed so hard he nearly slipped off his rock. "I like that! Yes — invisible armbands, there to bump anything that flies through too fast."

Maya drew a circle around her picture of the Earth, with a wobbly dotted ring. "There," she said. "Now everyone will know to be careful."

"Good thinking," said Barnacle. "That belt helped scientists learn a lot about space, all because one little rocket went looking."

chapters.heading: Chapter 4: One Trip Around
chapters.text:
The bubble swirled faster, and a bright orange capsule zoomed into view, spinning gently around the glowing Earth.

"**April 12, 1961**," said Barnacle. "A pilot named **Yuri Gagarin** became the first human being to ever fly in space."

Maya's eyes went wide. "A whole person? Up there?"

"All the way around the Earth, once, in his ship called **Vostok 1**," said Barnacle. "The whole trip took about **108 minutes** — shorter than one of your school days."

Maya watched Gagarin's capsule zip past, and she waved both arms at the little round window. Inside, it almost looked like he waved back.

"A few weeks later," Barnacle went on, "an American named Alan Shepard flew too, though his trip was shorter and didn't go all the way around."

"Everybody wanted a turn," Maya said.

"Everybody did," agreed Barnacle. "On **May 25, 1961**, the American President stood up and made a big, bold promise. He said America would land a person on the Moon, and bring them safely home, before the end of that same ten years."

Maya looked out at the small grey Moon hanging in the dark. It looked very, very far away.

"That's a big promise," she said.

"The biggest," said Barnacle. "Want to see if they kept it?"

Maya grabbed his flipper. "Yes! Let's go see!"

"Patience," chuckled Barnacle. "We've got a few more stops first. All aboard."

chapters.heading: Chapter 5: The Factory Worker Who Flew
chapters.text:
The bubble floated on, and a new capsule appeared, painted a cheerful white.

"Two years after Gagarin," said Barnacle, "someone else made history."

Inside the round window, Maya spotted a woman with short dark hair, smiling calmly at the stars.

"Who is she?" Maya asked.

"**Valentina Tereshkova**," said Barnacle. "She used to work in a factory, sewing fabric. On **June 16, 1963**, she became the first woman ever to fly in space, orbiting the Earth in her ship, **Vostok 6**."

Maya pressed her hands to the glass, studying every detail. "I want to draw her," she said.

She sketched quickly: a round capsule window, a woman waving, little stars all around. When she added a smile to the drawing, Tereshkova's tiny window-picture seemed to smile right back.

"She circled the whole Earth **forty-eight times**," Barnacle added.

Maya counted on her fingers, then gave up halfway through. "That's so many laps! More than the whole pool at swim practice."

"Many, many more," Barnacle agreed. "And every single lap, she was showing the world that space wasn't just for one kind of person. It was for anyone brave enough to go."

Maya tucked her new drawing next to the others. "She goes in my book too."

"Your book is getting pretty full," Barnacle said, peering over her shoulder.

"Good," said Maya. "There's room for more."

chapters.heading: Chapter 6: Floating Free
chapters.text:
The bubble bumped gently, like it hit a little wave, and Maya looked out to see something strange: a man floating completely outside his spaceship, tied on by only a long cord.

"Whoa," Maya breathed. "Is he falling?"

"He's floating on purpose," said Barnacle. "His name is **Alexei Leonov**. On **March 18, 1965**, he opened the hatch of his ship, **Voskhod 2**, and stepped right out into open space."

"With nothing holding him but that string?"

"Just that string," said Barnacle. "He floated outside for about **ten minutes** — the very first spacewalk anyone had ever done."

Maya thought of floating on her back in the swimming pool, arms out, looking up at the sky. "Is it like floating in the pool?"

"A little," said Barnacle, "except there's no water, no up, no down — just you and the stars, tied safely to your ship."

Maya kicked her legs gently inside the bubble, pretending to float the same way. For one second, the whole bubble spun lazily with her, stars sliding by.

"Careful," laughed Barnacle. "You'll make us both dizzy."

"Sorry," Maya giggled, holding still. "I just wanted to try it myself."

"That's exactly what Leonov wanted too," said Barnacle. "To try it first, so everyone after him would know it could be done."

Maya watched the little floating figure drift back toward his ship and climb safely inside. "He made it back okay," she said, relieved.

"Safe and sound," said Barnacle. "Now — onward, Maya."

chapters.heading: Chapter 7: The Whole World in One Picture
chapters.text:
The bubble rose higher, past the Moon's grey bumps, until suddenly Maya gasped.

There, over the Moon's edge, hung a small blue and white ball, glowing bright against the black sky.

"That's... that's us?" Maya whispered. "That's Earth?"

"That's Earth," said Barnacle softly. "In **December 1968**, three astronauts flew all the way around the Moon aboard **Apollo 8** — the first people ever to do it."

"Did they land?"

"Not that time. They circled it, then came home. But one of them, a man named **William Anders**, looked out his window at just the right moment and took a photograph."

"Of the Earth?" Maya asked.

"Of the Earth, rising over the Moon, like a little blue marble in a big black bathtub," said Barnacle. "People call it the **Earthrise** picture. It's one of the most famous photographs ever taken."

Maya stared at the small blue dot, thinking of every boat, every pool, every puddle she'd ever drawn, all somewhere down on that tiny ball.

"Can I draw it?" she asked.

"Go ahead," said Barnacle.

Maya pulled out her crayons and drew a careful circle, blue and green and white, rising over a grey curved edge. She held it up next to the real view, comparing the two.

"Pretty close," said Barnacle, nodding.

"I want to show everyone how small we look from up here," Maya said.

"That's exactly what that photograph did," said Barnacle. "It showed the whole world, all at once, how small and precious home really is."

chapters.heading: Chapter 8: One Giant Leap
chapters.text:
The bubble drifted down toward the Moon's dusty grey ground, and a huge rocket roared past them on its way up.

"That's the **Saturn V**," said Barnacle. "**363 feet tall** — taller than the Statue of Liberty standing on her toes."

Maya craned her neck, watching it shrink into the sky. "That's the biggest thing I've ever seen."

"It needed to be," said Barnacle. "It carried **Apollo 11**, and on **July 20, 1969**, it put two astronauts right down on the Moon's surface."

The scene shifted, and Maya saw a figure in a puffy white suit step slowly down a ladder onto the dusty ground.

"**Neil Armstrong**," whispered Barnacle. "The first person ever to walk on the Moon. He called it 'one giant leap for mankind.'"

Maya watched, barely breathing, as Armstrong's boot pressed into the grey dust and left a clear, perfect footprint.

"Who else was there?" Maya asked.

"**Buzz Aldrin** joined him on the ground a little later," said Barnacle. "And a third astronaut, **Michael Collins**, stayed up above, flying their ship, **Columbia**, all alone in orbit, waiting to bring them home."

Maya looked up at the lonely little ship circling overhead. "That sounds lonely."

"He had the best view of anyone," said Barnacle. "Watching both the Moon and the Earth at the very same time."

Maya pressed her hand flat against the glowing glass, matching her fingers to Armstrong's tiny footprint far below.

"We made it," she whispered.

"Humans did," said Barnacle, smiling. "And between **1969 and 1972**, **twelve** astronauts walked on the Moon, across **six** separate landing trips."

Maya grinned. "Twelve footprints. I want to draw every single one."

chapters.heading: Chapter 9: The Trip That Turned Around
chapters.text:
The bubble floated onward, past a spaceship suddenly lit up with flashing warning lights.

"This one didn't go quite as planned," said Barnacle, gently.

"What happened?" Maya asked, sitting up straight.

"In **1970**, an oxygen tank on **Apollo 13** broke while the astronauts were flying toward the Moon," said Barnacle. "It made a loud bang and shook their whole ship."

Maya's stomach fluttered. "Were they okay?"

"They were scared for a moment," said Barnacle, "but they were smart, and so were the helpers back on Earth. Together, using only the tools and parts already onboard, they built a fix to keep the air clean and the ship flying."

"Like fixing a leaky boat with whatever's in the toolbox?" Maya asked.

"Exactly like that," said Barnacle. "And it worked. The crew turned their ship around and came all the way home, safe and sound."

Maya let out a breath she hadn't realized she was holding. "I'm glad they made it."

"Me too," said Barnacle. "Sometimes the best part of an adventure isn't getting everything right the first time. It's figuring it out together, even when things go wrong."

Maya nodded slowly, thinking of the times her own boat drawings didn't come out quite right, and how she'd just tried again.

"Like when my boat picture needed three tries," she said.

"Just like that," said Barnacle, nudging her with his nose. "Three tries, and you still ended up with a beautiful boat."

Maya smiled, feeling a little braver already.

chapters.heading: Chapter 10: A Handshake in Space
chapters.text:
The bubble rose one last time, and Maya saw two very different spaceships drifting slowly toward each other, one marked with American letters, one with Soviet ones.

"This is the last stop," said Barnacle. "**July 17, 1975**."

"Are they going to crash?" Maya asked, worried.

"They're going to **dock**," said Barnacle. "That means two spaceships gently joining together, like two puzzle pieces clicking into one."

Maya watched the two ships line up slowly and touch, nose to nose, with the softest little **CLICK**.

A hatch opened between them, and two astronauts — one American, one Soviet — reached out and shook hands, floating together in the middle of the dark.

"After all that racing," Barnacle said, "that handshake was how the whole Space Race finally ended. Not with a winner. With a hello."

Maya watched the two smiling faces, floating together above the glowing Earth. "That's my favorite part," she said. "The hello part."

"Mine too," said Barnacle.

The bubble began to sink gently, the stars fading, the green glow softening back into ordinary fish-tank light. Maya felt the carpet under her knees again.

Her notebook lay open beside her, full of drawings: a round silver ball, a wagging dog, a smiling woman, a floating astronaut, a blue marble Earth, a dusty footprint, two tiny ships holding hands.

Barnacle's nose poked up through the calm water one last time. "You collected the whole race tonight, Maya."

"I did," Maya said, hugging her notebook to her chest. "All of it."
