"**SPLOOSH**," said Barnacle softly, and slipped back beneath the water, leaving only a few gentle ripples behind.

story.title: Maya and the Race to the Moon
story.subtitle: A splashy trip through the real Space Race.

chapters.heading: Chapter 1: The Beep in the Fish Tank
chapters.text:
Maya lay on her bedroom floor, drawing a tiny boat with crayons. It had been one whole week since Barnacle waved his flipper at the bridge that hummed.

Her night-light flickered. Then her fish tank started to glow bright green.

BEEP. BEEP. BEEP.

The sound came from the water, not from any speaker. Maya sat up fast. "That's not my fish," she whispered.

A whiskered nose popped up through the glowing water. "All aboard, Maya!" said Barnacle the harbour seal, grinning his big gummy grin.

"Barnacle! Where did that beep come from?"

"From space," said Barnacle. "A real beep, from a real round ball, way back in 1957."

Maya leaned closer. The water swirled like a little round window, showing darkness with tiny white dots.

"On **October 4, 1957**, the Soviet Union launched a round machine called **Sputnik 1**," Barnacle said. "It was the first man-made thing to ever circle the whole Earth."

"How big was it?" Maya asked, already sketching a circle in her notebook.

"About as wide as a beach ball," said Barnacle. "Just **58 centimeters**. But it carried a little radio that went *beep, beep, beep*, and people everywhere could hear it on their own radios at home."

Maya tapped the glass. "Like our fish tank is doing right now?"

"Exactly like that," said Barnacle. "Your tank caught the echo, all the way from long ago."

Maya grabbed her crayon and drew little lines shooting out from her round ball, like the beep was singing a song. "I want to see it fly," she said.

The moment she said it, the water rose up in a glowing bubble. **SPLOOSH!** The bedroom melted away, and Maya and Barnacle floated beside a small silver ball, blinking its beep into the dark.

"Ready for the whole trip?" asked Barnacle.

Maya grinned and grabbed his flipper. "All aboard!"

chapters.heading: Chapter 2: Laika's Big Ride
chapters.text:
The bubble floated past the little silver ball, and a second, bigger one drifted into view behind it.

"One month later, a second satellite went up," said Barnacle. "This one had a passenger."

"A person?" Maya asked.

"A dog," said Barnacle. "A brave little dog named **Laika**. On **November 3, 1957**, she became the first living creature to ever circle the Earth."

Maya pressed her nose to the glowing water. Inside, she could just make out a small furry shape curled up snug inside a round little room built just her size, called a capsule.

"Was she scared?" Maya asked.

"She was a good traveler," said Barnacle gently. "And she was known and loved all over the world. Kids everywhere drew pictures of her, just like you draw boats."

That gave Maya an idea. She flipped to a fresh page and drew Laika with a little space helmet and a wagging tail. The moment she finished the tail, the drawing seemed to wag right there on the paper.

"Ooh!" Maya laughed. "Did you see that?"

"Space magic," said Barnacle. "Or maybe just very good drawing."

Maya giggled. "Both, probably."

"Laika showed everyone that a living creature could survive going all the way around the Earth," said Barnacle. "She helped open the door for real people to go next."

Maya tucked her drawing carefully into her notebook, right beside Sputnik. "She gets to come with us," she said firmly.

"She always does," said Barnacle, with a wink.

chapters.heading: Chapter 3: America Answers Back
chapters.text:
The bubble drifted forward, and the dark sky filled with blueprints and busy people in white coats.

"Sputnik's beep gave the United States a big surprise," said Barnacle. "So they built a brand new team just for space."

"What kind of team?" Maya asked.

"It's called **NASA**," said Barnacle. "It started working on **October 1, 1958**. Their whole job was figuring out how to fly to space."

Maya spotted a long silver rocket standing on a launchpad below them. "Is that theirs?"

"That's **Explorer 1**," said Barnacle. "It launched on **January 31, 1958** — America's very first satellite."

The rocket roared up with a **WHOOOSH**, and Maya clapped her hands over her ears.

"What did it find up there?" she asked, once the shaking stopped.

"Something nobody expected," said Barnacle. "A big ring of tiny invisible zaps wrapped around the Earth, like a giant belt. It's called the **Van Allen belt**. It can't reach down to us on the ground, but spaceships flying through it have to be careful."

Maya thought about her swim goggles keeping pool water out of her eyes. "So it's like the Earth wears invisible armbands?"

Barnacle laughed so hard he nearly slipped off his rock. "I like that! Yes — invisible armbands, there to bump anything that flies through too fast."

Maya drew a circle around her picture of the Earth, with a wobbly dotted ring. "There," she said. "Now everyone will know to be careful."

"Good thinking," said Barnacle. "That belt helped scientists learn a lot about space, all because one little rocket went looking."

chapters.heading: Chapter 4: One Trip Around
chapters.text:
The bubble swirled faster, and a bright orange capsule zoomed into view, spinning gently around the glowing Earth.

"**April 12, 1961**," said Barnacle. "A pilot named **Yuri Gagarin** became the first human being to ever fly in space."

Maya's eyes went wide. "A whole person? Up there?"

"All the way around the Earth, once, in his ship called **Vostok 1**," said Barnacle. "The whole trip took about **108 minutes** — shorter than one of your school days."

Maya watched Gagarin's capsule zip past, and she waved both arms at the little round window. Inside, it almost looked like he waved back.

"A few weeks later," Barnacle went on, "an American named Alan Shepard flew too, though his trip was shorter and didn't go all the way around."

"Everybody wanted a turn," Maya said.

"Everybody did," agreed Barnacle. "On **May 25, 1961**, the American President stood up and made a big, bold promise. He said America would land a person on the Moon, and bring them safely home, before the end of that same ten years."

Maya looked out at the small grey Moon hanging in the dark. It looked very, very far away.

"That's a big promise," she said.

"The biggest," said Barnacle. "Want to see if they kept it?"

Maya pointed at his flipper. "Yes! Let's go see!"

"Patience," chuckled Barnacle. "We've got a few more stops first. All aboard."

chapters.heading: Chapter 5: The Factory Worker Who Flew
chapters.text:
The bubble floated on, and a new capsule appeared, painted a cheerful white.

"Two years after Gagarin," said Barnacle, "someone else made history."

Inside the round window, Maya spotted a woman with short dark hair, smiling calmly at the stars.

"Who is she?" Maya asked.

"**Valentina Tereshkova**," said Barnacle. "She used to work in a factory, sewing fabric. On **June 16, 1963**, she became the first woman ever to fly in space, orbiting the Earth in her ship, **Vostok 6**."

Maya pressed her hands to the glass, studying every detail. "I want to draw her," she said.

She sketched quickly: a round capsule window, a woman waving, little stars all around. When she added a smile to the drawing, Tereshkova's tiny window-picture seemed to smile right back.

"She circled the whole Earth **forty-eight times**," Barnacle added.

Maya counted on her fingers, then gave up halfway through. "That's so many laps! More than the whole pool at swim practice."

"Many, many more," Barnacle agreed. "And every single lap, she was showing the world that space wasn't just for one kind of person. It was for anyone brave enough to go."

Maya tucked her new drawing next to the others. "She goes in my book too."

"Your book is getting pretty full," Barnacle said, peering over her shoulder.

"Good," said Maya. "There's room for more."

chapters.heading: Chapter 6: Floating Free
chapters.text:
The bubble bumped gently, like it hit a little wave, and Maya looked out to see something strange: a man floating completely outside his spaceship, tied on by only a long cord.

"Whoa," Maya breathed. "Is he falling?"

"He's floating on purpose," said Barnacle. "His name is **Alexei Leonov**. On **March 18, 1965**, he opened the hatch of his ship, **Voskhod 2**, and stepped right out into open space."

"With nothing holding him but that string?"

"Just that string," said Barnacle. "He floated outside for about **ten minutes** — the very first spacewalk anyone had ever done."

Maya thought of floating on her back in the swimming pool, arms out, looking up at the sky. "Is it like floating in the pool?"

"A little," said Barnacle, "except there's no water, no up, no down — just you and the stars, tied safely to your ship."

Maya kicked her legs gently inside the bubble, pretending to float the same way. For one second, the whole bubble spun lazily with her, stars sliding by.

"Careful," laughed Barnacle. "You'll make us both dizzy."

"Sorry," Maya giggled, holding still. "I just wanted to try it myself."

"That's exactly what Leonov wanted too," said Barnacle. "To try it first, so everyone after him would know it could be done."

Maya watched the little floating figure drift back toward his ship and climb safely inside. "He made it back okay," she said, relieved.

"Safe and sound," said Barnacle. "Now — onward, Maya."

chapters.heading: Chapter 7: The Whole World in One Picture
chapters.text:
The bubble rose higher, past the Moon's grey bumps, until suddenly Maya gasped.

There, over the Moon's edge, hung a small blue and white ball, glowing bright against the black sky.

"That's... that's us?" Maya whispered. "That's Earth?"

"That's Earth," said Barnacle softly. "In **December 1968**, three astronauts flew all the way around the Moon aboard **Apollo 8** — the first people ever to do it."

"Did they land?"

"Not that time. They circled it, then came home. But one of them, a man named **William Anders**, looked out his window at just the right moment and took a photograph."

"Of the Earth?" Maya asked.

"Of the Earth, rising over the Moon, like a little blue marble in a big black bathtub," said Barnacle. "People call it the **Earthrise** picture. It's one of the most famous photographs ever taken."

Maya stared at the small blue dot, thinking of every boat, every pool, every puddle she'd ever drawn, all somewhere down on that tiny ball.

"Can I draw it?" she asked.

"Go ahead," said Barnacle.

Maya pulled out her crayons and drew a careful circle, blue and green and white, rising over a grey curved edge. She held it up next to the real view, comparing the two.

"Pretty close," said Barnacle, nodding.

"I want to show everyone how small we look from up here," Maya said.

"That's exactly what that photograph did," said Barnacle. "It showed the whole world, all at once, how small and precious home really is."

chapters.heading: Chapter 8: One Giant Leap
chapters.text:
The bubble drifted down toward the Moon's dusty grey ground, and a huge rocket roared past them on its way up.

"That's the **Saturn V**," said Barnacle. "**363 feet tall** — taller than the Statue of Liberty standing on her toes."

Maya craned her neck, watching it shrink into the sky. "That's the biggest thing I've ever seen."

"It needed to be," said Barnacle. "It carried **Apollo 11**, and on **July 20, 1969**, it put two astronauts right down on the Moon's surface."

The scene shifted, and Maya saw a figure in a puffy white suit step slowly down a ladder onto the dusty ground.

"**Neil Armstrong**," whispered Barnacle. "The first person ever to walk on the Moon. He called it 'one giant leap for mankind.'"

Maya watched, barely breathing, as Armstrong's boot pressed into the grey dust and left a clear, perfect footprint.

"Who else was there?" Maya asked.

"**Buzz Aldrin** joined him on the ground a little later," said Barnacle. "And a third astronaut, **Michael Collins**, stayed up above, flying their ship, **Columbia**, all alone in orbit, waiting to bring them home."

Maya looked up at the lonely little ship circling overhead. "That sounds lonely."

"He had the best view of anyone," said Barnacle. "Watching both the Moon and the Earth at the very same time."

Maya pressed her hand flat against the glowing glass, matching her fingers to Armstrong's tiny footprint far below.

"We made it," she whispered.

"Humans did," said Barnacle, smiling. "And between **1969 and 1972**, **twelve** astronauts walked on the Moon, across **six** separate landing trips."

Maya grinned. "Twelve footprints. I want to draw every single one."

chapters.heading: Chapter 9: The Trip That Turned Around
chapters.text:
The bubble floated onward, past a spaceship suddenly lit up with flashing warning lights.

"This one didn't go quite as planned," said Barnacle, gently.

"What happened?" Maya asked, sitting up straight.

"In **1970**, an oxygen tank on **Apollo 13** broke while the astronauts were flying toward the Moon," said Barnacle. "It made a loud bang and shook their whole ship."

Maya's stomach fluttered. "Were they okay?"

"They were scared for a moment," said Barnacle, "but they were smart, and so were the helpers back on Earth. Together, using only the tools and parts already onboard, they built a fix to keep the air clean and the ship flying."

"Like fixing a leaky boat with whatever's in the toolbox?" Maya asked.

"Exactly like that," said Barnacle. "And it worked. The crew turned their ship around and came all the way home, safe and sound."

Maya let out a breath she hadn't realized she was holding. "I'm glad they made it."

"Me too," said Barnacle. "Sometimes the best part of an adventure isn't getting everything right the first time. It's figuring it out together, even when things go wrong."

Maya nodded slowly, thinking of the times her own boat drawings didn't come out quite right, and how she'd just tried again.

"Like when my boat picture needed three tries," she said.

"Just like that," said Barnacle, nudging her with his nose. "Three tries, and you still ended up with a beautiful boat."

Maya smiled, feeling a little braver already.

story.title: Zara and the Humming Rock
story.subtitle: A rockhound's trip to the fire inside the Earth

chapters.heading: Chapter 1: The Humming Rock
chapters.text:
It was way past bedtime, but Zara was still sorting rocks on her rug.

Smooth ones in one pile. Sparkly ones in another. Bumpy ones in the last.

She picked up her newest rock, found on the beach with Mom. It was grey, light as a cork, and covered in tiny holes.

It felt warm. Then it started to hum, low and buzzy, like a bee trapped inside.

"Rocks don't hum," Zara whispered.

The holes glowed soft orange, like tiny campfires.

POP! A small, friendly face blinked open in the rock. "They do if they used to be lava," it said. "Hi. I'm Pip."

Zara's mouth dropped open. "You're really from a volcano?"

"Sure am," said Pip. "Want to see where rocks like me are born?"

Zara didn't even look at her sparkly pile. "YES, please."

Orange light filled her room. The rug turned to warm, black ground under her sneakers.

They stood near a smoking mountain. It smelled like a thousand matches.

"So what IS a volcano?" Zara asked.

"It's a hole in Earth's crust," said Pip. "Crust just means the hard outside skin of our whole planet, like the peel on an orange. Way underground, it's so hot that rock melts. That melted rock is called **magma**. When it pushes up through the hole and comes out, people call it **lava** instead."

Zara spotted a smooth, shiny, black rock by her shoe.

"Pip! Was THIS lava once?" she asked, scooping it up.

Pip's glow brightened. "Good eye. That cooled down and went hard, just like a melted crayon turns solid again."

Zara grinned and tucked it in her pocket. "I'm basically a volcano detective now."

"Rock-solid plan," said Pip. "Let's go find more clues."

chapters.heading: Chapter 2: The Ring Around the Ocean
chapters.text:
The ground gave a gentle shiver under Zara's sneakers. Not scary. More like a shiver.

"Pip, why do volcanoes bunch up in some spots?" Zara asked. "Why not just anywhere?"

Pip's glow flickered into a glowing map, floating like a light-up puzzle.

"See these lines?" said Pip. "Earth's crust isn't one piece. It's broken into giant puzzle pieces called **plates**. They float around, super slow, on the hot stuff below. Where plates push together, pull apart, or slide past each other, volcanoes like to pop up."

Zara traced a huge curved line with her finger. It looped almost all the way around an ocean.

"Whoa, it's shaped like a horseshoe!" she said.

"Good eye again," said Pip. "That's the Ring of Fire. It loops around the Pacific Ocean, and it holds about three out of every four active volcanoes on the whole planet."

Zara counted glowing dots along the ring. So many were bunched up in one curvy little country.

"This place has a TON of them," she said, pointing.

"That's Indonesia," said Pip. "It has more active volcanoes than any other country on Earth."

Zara puffed out her cheeks. "I'd never run out of volcanoes to visit there."

"You'd need bigger sneakers," said Pip.

Zara giggled, and the glowing map folded itself into a paper airplane, zooming toward the horizon.

"Follow that map!" said Pip, and they ran.

chapters.heading: Chapter 3: The Hotspot That Never Moves
chapters.text:
They landed on black sand that crunched like cereal under Zara's sneakers.

"Where even are we?" she asked, shielding her eyes from an orange glow ahead.

"Hawaii," said Pip. "But here's the mystery. Hawaii isn't on the edge of a plate at all."

Zara tilted her head. "Then how does it have volcanoes?"

"There's a **hotspot** under here," said Pip. "That just means a spot deep down that stays super hot and stuck in one place, even while the plate above slides over it, kind of like a candle under a moving cake."

Zara watched glowing orange lines creep across black rock, slow as spilled syrup.

"Is that lava?" she gasped.

"That's Kilauea," said Pip. "It's one of the most active volcanoes on Earth. It has been erupting on and off for decades."

Zara counted on her fingers. "That's longer than Mom's whole life!"

"Yep," said Pip.

Zara pointed. "Why's the lava moving so slow? It's not even scary. It's kind of... pretty."

"Exactly," said Pip. "This kind of eruption is usually gentle, not a big explosion. That's why people can watch it safely from far away, like us."

Zara sat on a cool patch of rock to watch the glowing river. "I could watch this forever," she said.

"Careful," said Pip. "You'll turn into a rock yourself if you sit still too long."

Zara jumped up laughing.

chapters.heading: Chapter 4: The Shield and the Party Hat
chapters.text:
As they walked, Zara noticed a giant, wide mountain rising behind them. It wasn't pointy at all. It looked like a shield lying flat on the ground.

"Pip, that mountain's shape is funny," Zara said. "It's not like the drawings in my book."

"That's Mauna Loa," said Pip. "It's the biggest active volcano on Earth, if you count how much rock it's made of. It rises over four thousand meters above the sea."

Zara whistled. "That's not funny. That's HUGE."

"Volcanoes come in different shapes," said Pip. "Wide ones with gentle slopes, like this, are called **shield volcanoes**, shaped like a warrior's shield. Tall, steep, pointy ones are called **stratovolcanoes**, like a party hat. Mount Fuji in Japan is one of those."

Zara grabbed a stick and drew both shapes in the black sand: one low and wide, one tall and pointy.

"So it's like volcano families," she said. "The flat cousins and the pointy cousins."

"Never heard it put that way," said Pip, "but I'll allow it."

Zara patted the wide mountain like it was a sleeping dog. "Good shield volcano," she said.

Pip's glow wiggled, which Zara had learned meant he was laughing.

"Come on, rock detective," said Pip. "Next stop's a pointy cousin. This one's story is almost two thousand years old."

chapters.heading: Chapter 5: The Man Who Wrote It Down
chapters.text:
The ground turned to warm stone steps. A pointy mountain stood across a sparkling bay, puffing a thin trail of smoke.

A man in a long robe stood nearby, scribbling fast, glancing up at the mountain again and again.

"Who's that?" Zara whispered.

"That's Pliny the Younger," said Pip. "He's watching this mountain, Vesuvius, from across the water. In the year **79**, it exploded, burying two whole Roman towns, Pompeii and Herculaneum, under thick ash."

Zara's eyes went wide. "Whole towns? With houses and everything?"

"Whole towns," said Pip. "But here's the neat part. Pliny wrote down everything he saw, in letters to a friend. He described it so well that scientists still use his notes today. Big explosive eruptions like that one are now called **Plinian** eruptions, named after him."

Zara watched the man finish a line, then look up and squint.

"He's basically the first-ever volcano reporter," Zara said.

"Nice way to put it," said Pip.

Zara waved at the distant mountain, staying back with Pip, just watching like Pliny did. "Thanks for writing it down," she called, even though she knew he couldn't hear her, two thousand years away.

"Why'd you say that?" asked Pip.

"Because now I get to visit and know what happened," said Zara. "That seems worth a thank-you."

Pip's glow warmed up, soft and golden. "Rock detective with a heart. Let's keep moving."

chapters.heading: Chapter 6: The Bang Heard Around the World
chapters.text:
A deep BOOM rattled Zara's teeth, even though no mountain was in sight.

"Whoa! Where did THAT come from?" she said, hands over her ears.

"That's an echo," said Pip, "of something that happened on an island called Krakatoa, back in **1883**. It exploded so loudly, people heard it about three thousand miles away, on a tiny island called Rodrigues."

Zara tried to picture that. "That's like yelling in my backyard, and someone hearing it clear across the whole country!"

"Pretty much," said Pip.

The scene shifted. Cold wind replaced warm air. Grey waves crashed below, and smoke puffed up from under the water itself.

"Now we're somewhere chilly," Zara said, hugging her arms.

"Iceland," said Pip. "It has tons of volcanoes because here, two of Earth's plates are pulling apart, instead of pushing together."

Right then, a burst of steam and rock shot up from the sea.

"Pip! Is the ocean making a new ROCK?" Zara shouted.

"Better," said Pip. "It's making a whole new island. In **1963**, an underwater volcano here kept erupting until a brand-new island popped out of the sea. They named it Surtsey."

Zara's jaw dropped. "A volcano can just make LAND?"

"From nothing," said Pip, "but hot rock and time."

Zara watched the baby island steam in the cold wind. "I want to name the next one," she said.

"Get in line," said Pip.

chapters.heading: Chapter 7: The Summer That Didn't Come
chapters.text:
The wind turned icy again. Old-fashioned houses stood around them, with fields of brown, droopy crops.

"Is it winter?" Zara asked, confused. "The trees look like summer trees."

"It's supposed to be summer," said Pip. "This is **1816**, the year people called the Year Without a Summer."

"Why?" Zara asked. "Where'd summer go?"

"The year before, in **1815**, a volcano called Tambora, in Indonesia, had the biggest eruption anyone's ever recorded," said Pip. "All that ash floated way up into the sky and spread around the whole world, blocking some of the sun's warmth."

Zara looked at the grey sky. "So one volcano messed up summer for EVERYONE?"

"Pretty much," said Pip. "Crops had trouble growing. People remembered that cold, strange year for a long time."

Zara shivered and tugged her sleeves down over her hands.

"That's wild," she said, "that something in one place can mess with weather everywhere."

"The whole planet's connected," said Pip. "Like one big, rocky, breathing thing."

Zara looked at the frosty summer field once more, then turned to Pip.

"Okay," she said. "Take me somewhere warm again. Please."

Pip chuckled, and the icy field melted into golden light.

chapters.heading: Chapter 8: The Mountain That Lost Its Top
chapters.text:
Warm light faded into daylight, and Zara found herself looking up at a huge, snow-capped mountain.

A man with a backpack and notebook stood nearby, pointing a little device at the mountain's side.

"Who's that?" Zara asked.

"David Johnston," said Pip. "A scientist who studies volcanoes. He's watching this one closely, to help warn people if it gets dangerous."

"Is it going to erupt?" Zara asked, taking half a step back.

"Not right this second," said Pip gently. "We're just visiting a memory of **May 18, 1980**. Watch, but from a safe distance, like David did."

Right then, the whole side of the mountain slid away in a massive landslide, the biggest ever recorded. A moment later, the mountain blew out sideways in a huge cloud.

"WHOA!" Zara yelped, but Pip's glow wrapped around her like a cozy blanket.

"We're safe," said Pip. "We're just watching, from far away, like you'd watch fireworks."

When the dust cleared, Zara gasped. "The top of the mountain is just... gone!"

"The blast blew off about **1,300 feet** of the summit," said Pip. "That's taller than the tallest skyscrapers, gone in moments."

Zara stared at the new, shorter mountain. "That's wild. And kind of sad for the mountain."

"Scientists like David study volcanoes just like this one," said Pip, "so they can warn people early and keep everyone safe."

Zara nodded slowly. "I like that job. Volcano watcher."

"You're already halfway there, rock detective," said Pip.

chapters.heading: Chapter 9: Home, With a New Rock
chapters.text:
"Pip, is every trip going to end with a big mountain?" Zara asked, giggling, as the ground firmed up under a grassy field full of steaming pools.

"Not always," said Pip. "This one's hiding its whole volcano UNDER the ground. It's called a **supervolcano**, just means a giant, extra-powerful volcano. This one's at Yellowstone."

"Is it gonna blow up?" Zara asked, eyebrows raised.

"Nope," said Pip. "Its last huge eruption was about **640,000 years ago**. Scientists watch it closely, and right now, there's no sign it's waking up soon."

Zara relaxed. "Okay, good. How DO scientists watch, anyway?"

"Machines called **seismographs**," said Pip, "feel tiny shakes in the ground, too small for us to notice. Satellites way up in space check if the ground is puffing up like a balloon. Both are early clues a volcano might be getting ready."

Zara nodded. "Like a volcano's heartbeat monitor."

"Exactly like that," said Pip, clearly impressed.

The scene shifted one last time, to red, dusty ground under a pink sky.

"Where are we NOW?" Zara asked, looking at nothing but rust-colored dirt.

"Mars," said Pip. "See that huge bump on the horizon? That's Olympus Mons, the biggest volcano anyone's found in the whole solar system. It's about thirteen and a half miles high, almost three Mount Everests stacked up."

Zara tried to imagine climbing that and gave up immediately. "No thank you."

Pip laughed. "Fair. One more thing before home. All that ash volcanoes make breaks down into amazing dirt. **Fertile** means it's perfect for growing plants. That's why farmers still live near volcanoes, even knowing the risk."

Zara thought about that. "So volcanoes build stuff AND grow stuff. Not just boom stuff."

"Rocks are complicated," said Pip. "Kind of like people."

Orange light swirled around them, and the red dust melted back into Zara's soft bedroom rug.

Zara blinked. Her rock piles sat right where she'd left them.

Pip's glow dimmed to a cozy flicker in her hand. "Good trip?"

"Best one yet," Zara said, yawning hugely.

She pulled the smooth black rock from her pocket, the one that used to be lava, now cooled and hard, and set it proudly on her nightstand like a tiny trophy.

"I'm keeping this one right here," she said.

"Good choice," Pip murmured, his glow fading to a sleepy ember.

Zara climbed into bed, her new rock standing guard beside her, and closed her eyes.

story.ending_line: Goodnight, Zara. Rock on.

true_facts.text: A **volcano** is a hole in Earth's crust where hot stuff from underground can escape.
Melted rock is called **magma** underground, and **lava** once it flows out.
The **Ring of Fire** is a horseshoe-shaped loop that holds about three out of every four of Earth's active volcanoes.
**Indonesia** has more active volcanoes than any other country on Earth.
Hawaii's volcanoes grow over a **hotspot**, a super-hot spot deep down that stays in one place.
**Kilauea** in Hawaii has been erupting on and off for decades.
**Mauna Loa** is the biggest active volcano on Earth, rising over four thousand meters above the sea.
Wide, gentle volcanoes are called **shield volcanoes**; tall, pointy ones are called **stratovolcanoes**.
In the year **79**, Vesuvius erupted and buried the towns of **Pompeii and Herculaneum** under thick ash.
**Pliny the Younger** watched and wrote about the eruption, so big explosive eruptions are now called **Plinian** eruptions.
**Krakatoa's** 1883 eruption was so loud it was heard about **three thousand miles** away.
In **1963**, a brand-new island named **Surtsey** rose from the sea near Iceland.
On **May 18, 1980**, Mount St. Helens had a giant landslide and then erupted.
Volcanic ash breaks down into **fertile** soil, which is why farmers often live near volcanoes.

new_recurring.name: Pip
new_recurring.rule: A small, warm piece of pumice living in Zara's rock collection. He glows orange and hums to start each adventure, speaks gently, keeps Zara safely at a distance from any danger, and always calls her 'rock detective.'

bible_suggestions.ending_summary: Zara returned home with the smooth cooled-lava rock from her very first stop and set it proudly on her nightstand beside the now-sleepy, glowing Pip.

story.title: Noah and the Midnight Patch Notes
story.subtitle: A sleep-science adventure for a kid who should really be asleep by now

chapters.heading: Chapter 1: Queue Pop, 1953
chapters.text:
The ranked queue had been stuck at ninety-nine percent for four straight minutes, which was somehow worse than losing.

Noah lay flat on his back, phone six inches from his face, blanket up to his chin, bedroom dark except for the screen's cold glow. It was 1:47 a.m. His mom thought he'd been asleep since eleven. The queue was a lie he was willing to tell twice a week.

Then the bar hit one hundred percent, and instead of a lobby, the screen flickered black, then green, then showed two words: **NON-REM 1**.

"That's not a game mode," Noah muttered.

The screen answered him. A glitchy little avatar built out of pixelated eyelids blinked into the corner. "Correct. Name's REM. Not the band, though I get that a lot."

"REM like the sleep thing?"

"REM like the sleep thing. Want to know why you're awake right now instead of doing the one thing your whole species evolved to do at 1:47 a.m.?"

Noah tapped the glowing eyelid icon, mostly out of curiosity, and the room dissolved into black-and-white static.

He landed in a dim lab at the **University of Chicago**, **1953**. A boy about his age lay wired up on a cot, fast asleep. A tired grad student leaned in close, staring at the kid's closed eyes.

"They're twitching," Noah said. "Under the lids. Like a frame drop."

"Good eye," said REM. "That's **Eugene Aserinsky**, and he just noticed the exact same thing you did. He and his professor, **Nathaniel Kleitman**, named it rapid eye movement sleep. REM sleep. Kleitman basically spent his whole career figuring sleep out — people call him the father of the whole field."

Noah grinned. "So the band stole it."

"The band," REM said, "is a coincidence I live with daily."

chapters.heading: Chapter 2: The Playlist
chapters.text:
The lab dissolved into something that looked like a music app, sleep stages laid out like tracks on an album.

"A night of sleep isn't one long black screen," REM said. "It's a playlist. About ninety minutes a loop, over and over till your alarm ruins everything."

Noah scrolled the track list with his finger. "So there's like... chill tracks and loud ones?"

"Close enough. The quiet tracks are **non-REM** — your body doing repair work, nothing flashy. Then every ninety minutes or so you hit a loud one. **REM sleep**. Brain's almost as busy as when you're awake. Dreaming, basically."

"So why doesn't everyone just get up and start swinging during the loud part?"

"Because your body mutes itself." REM grinned, pixel teeth and all. "Muscles go slack during REM — total volume at zero — so you can't act out whatever's happening in the dream. Otherwise half the planet would be sleep-fighting imaginary bosses every night."

Noah thought about cutscenes. "So it's like the controls get disabled during the cinematic."

"That," REM said, "is annoyingly accurate."

chapters.heading: Chapter 3: Patch Notes
chapters.text:
The scene shifted to Noah's own room — his own bed, him asleep in it, which was deeply weird to watch from the outside.

"Creepy," Noah said.

"Educational," REM corrected. "Watch the deep non-REM stage. The really quiet track."

A soft golden glow pulsed through sleeping-Noah's chest on-screen.

"That's **growth hormone** getting released," REM said, "the chemical that actually helps your body grow, inch by inch. The biggest dose of it comes out during the deepest non-REM stage. It's a big part of why growing bodies — yours, for instance — need real sleep and not four hours and a prayer."

Noah glanced down at the jeans he'd outgrown twice this year. "So it's basically installing the update while I'm offline."

"If that helps you sleep, sure."

"It does not currently help me sleep," Noah said. "I'm standing inside a memory right now."

"Fair," REM said. "Patience. We've got six more stops."

chapters.heading: Chapter 4: Dark Mode, Factory Installed
chapters.text:
They zoomed in past Noah's skin, past bone, into a brain lit up like a circuit board, down to one tiny cluster of cells glowing blue.

"That speck," REM said, "sits right above where your eye nerves cross. It's called the **suprachiasmatic nucleus** — basically your body's master clock. It's been running your sleep and wake times since before you had a phone to ignore it with."

"How's a clump of cells a clock?"

"It keeps roughly a twenty-four-hour rhythm. Scientists call that a **circadian** rhythm — the word just comes from Latin for 'about a day.' Your body had a built-in day-and-night schedule a long time before any app did."

Noah blinked. "So I've had dark mode this whole time."

"Factory installed," REM said. "You just keep overriding it at 1 a.m."

"Rude, but accurate," Noah admitted.

chapters.heading: Chapter 5: Achievement Unlocked
chapters.text:
The static resolved into a bright stage, gold curtains, a podium — Noah half expected an esports grand final.

"In **2017**," REM said, "three scientists — **Jeffrey Hall**, **Michael Rosbash**, and **Michael Young** — won the **Nobel Prize**, science's biggest trophy, for finding the actual genes that keep your circadian clock ticking."

"They found the clock itself decades earlier, though," Noah said. "Why'd the trophy take so long?"

"Finding the clock is one achievement. Finding the code that runs it is a whole separate quest line. They cracked the genes. The Nobel committee noticed."

Noah nodded slowly. "Respect. That's a long grind for one award."

"Even your cells have patch notes," REM said. "You just can't read the changelog."

chapters.heading: Chapter 6: The Melatonin Mixtape
chapters.text:
Next stop: a cluttered **1958** laboratory, glass bottles everywhere, a scientist squinting through a microscope at something barely visible.

"**Aaron Lerner**," REM said. "His team pulled a brand-new hormone out of a tiny gland in an animal's brain and gave it a name: **melatonin**. It's the chemical that tells your body nighttime has arrived — basically a volume knob that turns alertness down."

"Isn't that the stuff in the gummies my aunt takes before flights?"

"Same molecule. Your own brain makes it for free, usually around the time you should be putting the phone down and are instead opening a fourth app."

Noah slid his phone a few inches further from his face, which felt like progress.

"Baby steps," REM said.

chapters.heading: Chapter 7: Saved Progress
chapters.text:
The scene turned into a loading screen Noah actually recognized — a save icon, spinning.

"Sleep isn't just downtime," REM said. "It's when your brain sorts the whole day into long-term memory. That riff you've been practicing on guitar, that combo you finally landed — sleep is what saves the file."

"So pulling an all-nighter before a test is..."

"Deleting your own save data before it uploads. Yes."

Noah frowned. "What about dreams, though? Like, actual dream content. Is it secretly trying to tell me something?"

"Depends who you ask. Back in **1899**, a scientist named **Sigmund Freud** wrote a whole famous book arguing dreams reveal your secret hidden wishes. Great story. Mostly not how it actually works, according to sleep science today."

"So my dream about failing a boss fight wasn't secretly about my feelings."

"Almost certainly just leftover footage," REM said. "Also — overnight, your brain runs something scientists nicknamed a 'rinse cycle.' It flushes waste out while you sleep, like taking out the trash before the next day loads."

"Gross but useful."

"Most of biology is."

chapters.heading: Chapter 8: Do Not Attempt This Speedrun
chapters.text:
The next scene was a bedroom in San Diego, **1964**. A teenager sat cross-legged on the floor, eyes red, surrounded by notebooks.

"**Randy Gardner**," REM said. "Seventeen years old. Science-fair project. He stayed awake for about **eleven days straight** — one of the longest stretches anyone's ever done on record."

Noah sat up straighter. "Eleven days? No sleep at all?"

"None. And doctors will tell you, flatly, not to try it. Go without sleep that long and your mood tanks, your focus falls apart, your memory gets foggy fast. Randy's story is interesting. It is not a tutorial."

Noah thought about his last three-day gaming weekend, the one where he'd forgotten his own locker combination on day two.

"Noted," he said. "Not a speedrun category I'm entering."

"Wise," said REM. "Very few achievements are worth your whole brain."

chapters.heading: Chapter 9: Respawn
chapters.text:
The last stop was a blur of animals, flashing past like a nature documentary on fast-forward.

"Quick round," REM said. "**Bottlenose dolphins** sleep with half their brain at a time — one eye stays open, watching for danger, while the other half rests. **Bats**, on the other end, sleep up to **twenty hours a day**. Practically professional sleepers."

"So dolphins are speedrunning sleep and bats are just living in it."

"Pretty much. Point is, sleep isn't some weird human habit. Nearly every animal does some version of it. It's ancient. It matters."

The static began folding back toward black.

"One more thing," REM said, as the room re-formed around him — his own ceiling, his own blanket, his own phone glowing in his hand. "You'll spend roughly a third of your whole life asleep. Might as well stop fighting it."

Noah looked at the time. 2:02 a.m. The ranked queue notification still sat there, untouched.

He closed the app instead. On the lock screen, where the loading bar used to be stuck at ninety-nine percent, a small notification blinked once: **Achievement Unlocked — First Full Cycle.**

He didn't screenshot it. He just put the phone face-down on the nightstand and let his eyes close.

story.ending_line: Tomorrow, the queue could wait.

true_facts.text: In 1953, two scientists at the University of Chicago — Eugene Aserinsky and Nathaniel Kleitman — discovered REM sleep by watching a sleeping boy's eyes twitch under his eyelids.
A night of sleep runs in repeating loops about ninety minutes long, cycling between quiet non-REM sleep and active REM sleep.
During REM sleep the brain is almost as busy as when you're awake, but the muscles go slack so you can't act out your dreams.
The deepest non-REM stage releases the biggest burst of growth hormone, one reason growing bodies need real sleep.
A tiny cluster of brain cells called the suprachiasmatic nucleus works as the body's master clock for sleeping and waking.
The word circadian, for the body's roughly 24-hour clock, comes from Latin words meaning 'about a day.'
In 2017, Jeffrey Hall, Michael Rosbash, and Michael Young won the Nobel Prize for finding the genes that keep the circadian clock ticking.
In 1958, Aaron Lerner's team isolated the sleep hormone melatonin from a tiny gland in an animal's brain.
Sleep helps the brain sort the day's experiences into long-term memories, so a good night's sleep helps you remember what you practiced.
A nightly 'rinse cycle' flushes waste out of the sleeping brain while you sleep.
In 1964, seventeen-year-old Randy Gardner of San Diego stayed awake for about eleven days as a science-fair project, one of the longest recorded stretches without sleep.
Doctors say going without sleep that long quickly harms mood, focus, and memory, and nobody should try to beat that record.
Bottlenose dolphins sleep with only half their brain at a time, keeping one eye open to watch for danger.
Some bats sleep up to twenty hours a day, making them some of the sleepiest animals known.

new_recurring.name: REM
new_recurring.rule: A glitchy, pixel-eyed avatar who appears on Noah's phone screen only after midnight, speaks in gaming and music metaphors with dry deadpan humor, and pulls him into real science and history adventures about sleep and the body. Never appears if Noah is already asleep on time.

bible_suggestions.ending_summary: Noah closed his gaming app, saw a glitch-free 'Achievement Unlocked: First Full Cycle' notification on his lock screen instead of the stuck loading bar, and went to sleep without taking a screenshot.

story.title: Milo, Juno, and the Deep Blue Shark Dive
story.subtitle: The magic red brick goes swimming.

chapters.heading: Chapter 1: The Glowing Brick
chapters.text:
Milo and Juno sat on the carpet. Their tall LEGO tower stood beside them. It had held tight all week, ever since that big CLICK.

Tonight, one brick on top began to glow. It was the magic red brick! It blinked red light. Then it hummed. BZZZT.

Juno giggled. "It wants to play!" she said.

Milo picked up a tiny LEGO diver from the bucket. The diver had a tiny snorkel and tiny flippers. The brick glowed brighter. The diver's eyes lit up too.

"Hello, friends," said a tiny voice. "I'm Dot. Want to see real sharks?"

Milo grinned. Juno grinned bigger. "YES!" they both shouted.

The brick went WHOOOOSH. The carpet turned to water. Down, down, down they went, shrinking smaller and smaller, until they were swimming right next to Dot, in a deep blue sea.

chapters.heading: Chapter 2: The Ocean Before Dinosaurs
chapters.text:
Bubbles tickled Juno's nose. Ppbbbt! "Where are the dinosaurs?" she asked.

Dot the diver laughed a tiny laugh. "No dinosaurs down here. Sharks swam in oceans over 400 million years ago. That's way before any dinosaur walked on land!"

Juno's eyes went wide. Milo watched a shark glide by. It bent and curved like a wiggly noodle.

"Its bones are bendy," said Dot. "Sharks don't have hard bones like you. They have cartilage — soft, bendy stuff, like the squishy part of your ear."

Milo squeezed his own ear. "Whoa, bendy!" He snapped two LEGO pieces together loosely, making them wiggle like a shark tail. CLICK click click. "Look, Juno, a wiggly shark!"

Juno wiggled along with it. "Older than dinosaurs," she whispered. "That's SO old."

chapters.heading: Chapter 3: The Giant Tooth
chapters.text:
Something shiny glinted in the sand. CLINK! Juno picked it up. It was a huge, pointy tooth, as long as her whole hand.

"Whoa, who has THAT tooth?" she asked, eyes big.

"That tooth belonged to Megalodon," said Dot. "The biggest shark that ever lived!"

Juno gulped. "Is it... here?" she whispered.

"Oh no," said Dot gently. "Megalodon isn't around anymore. It lived millions of years ago, and now it's extinct — that means all gone, forever."

Juno breathed out. Phew!

Milo turned the tooth over in his hands. "How do we even know about it?"

"Cartilage doesn't turn into fossils easily," said Dot. "But teeth do! Almost everything we know about Megalodon comes from fossil teeth like this one."

Milo tucked the tooth gently back in the sand. "Thanks for the clue, old shark."

Juno patted the sand. "Night night, Megalodon."

chapters.heading: Chapter 4: The Biggest Fish of All
chapters.text:
A huge shadow swept over them. The sun disappeared! Juno ducked.

"Don't worry," laughed Dot. "That's just a whale shark, the biggest fish in the whole world."

It was over 40 feet long, longer than four school buses in a row.

Milo's mouth dropped open. "What does something THAT big eat?"

"Tiny, tiny food," said Dot. "Plankton — teeny floating bits. The whale shark opens its giant mouth and gulps up water, like a strainer, catching only the tiny bits."

Milo imagined his LEGO tower, as tall as the whale shark was long. "That's taller than our whole tower!"

He held up ten fingers, then ten more, counting with Juno. "One, two, three... forty!"

The whale shark swam on, slow and gentle, like a big friendly cloud.

chapters.heading: Chapter 5: Sandpaper Skin
chapters.text:
Milo reached out and gently touched a passing shark's side. "Ooh, it feels like sandpaper!"

"That's its skin," said Dot. "It's covered in tiny bumpy scales, almost like teeny-tiny teeth. They help the shark zoom through water smoothly."

Juno opened her mouth wide. "What about REAL teeth?"

A nurse shark nearby showed off a mouth full of pointy teeth.

"Sharks grow lots of teeth their whole life," said Dot. "When one falls out, a new one moves up to take its place. Some sharks lose thousands of teeth!"

Milo grinned his own gap-tooth grin. "I only grow two sets. Lucky sharks!"

Juno counted her fingers, trying to count to a thousand, and gave up giggling at twenty. "Too many teeth!" she laughed.

chapters.heading: Chapter 6: The Hammer Head and the Walking Shark
chapters.text:
A strange shape wiggled closer. It had a head shaped like a hammer!

Juno pointed. "That shark's head is SO weird!"

"That's a hammerhead shark," said Dot. "Its wide head spreads its eyes far apart, so it can see almost all around itself."

Milo spun in a circle, trying to see all around too, and bonked his elbow. "Ow! I need a hammer head!" Everyone laughed.

Then a small spotted shark walked past them — actually walked, on little fin-feet, across the sandy floor.

"That's an epaulette shark," said Dot. "It can walk across the reef on its fins, and it barely needs air to do it."

Juno tried to walk like the shark, wiggling her arms like fins. "Look, I'm walking like a shark!" she shouted, flopping onto the sand with a SPLOOSH.

chapters.heading: Chapter 7: The Shark Lady
chapters.text:
A beam of light swept by. It was an old photo, floating like a bubble.

"That's Eugenie Clark," said Dot. "People called her the Shark Lady. She spent her whole life studying sharks and proving how smart and curious they really are."

Milo watched a shark nudge a coral gently, curious, like a puppy. "She even taught sharks little tricks!" said Dot.

Juno looked worried. "Do sharks ever bump people?" she asked in a small voice.

Dot smiled kindly. "Almost never. Sharks mostly just swim along, keeping the ocean healthy and balanced. People are much more likely to help sharks than sharks are to bother people."

Juno felt better. She patted the water. "Good job, sharks," she said.

Milo saluted the old photo. "Thanks, Shark Lady."

chapters.heading: Chapter 8: Home Again
chapters.text:
WHOOOOSH! The water swirled into sparkles. Milo and Juno landed back on their carpet, right next to their tall tower.

Dot waved from the top of the brick. "Thanks for swimming with me. Come back and play well, anytime."

The brick gave one last happy glow, then went still.

Milo looked down. A tiny new LEGO piece sat on the carpet — shaped just like a shark tooth! He snapped it onto the very top of their tower. CLICK! It held.

Juno yawned a big dinosaur-sized yawn. "Sharks are older than my dinosaurs," she mumbled sleepily. "SO OLD."

Milo tucked the blanket over her. "Goodnight, Juno," he whispered. "Goodnight, sharks."

story.ending_line: Goodnight, Milo. Goodnight, Juno. Play well.

true_facts.text: Sharks were swimming in the ocean more than **400 million years** before dinosaurs ever walked on land.
Sharks don't have hard bones — they have **cartilage**, bendy stuff like the squishy part of your ear.
**Megalodon** was the biggest shark that ever lived, but it is **extinct** now — all gone, long ago.
Because cartilage barely turns into fossils, almost everything we know about Megalodon comes from its giant **fossil teeth**.
The **whale shark** is the biggest fish in the whole world, growing over **40 feet** long.
Even though it's huge, the whale shark mostly eats tiny floating bits called **plankton**.
Shark skin is covered in tiny bumpy scales that feel like **sandpaper** and help it swim smoothly.
Sharks grow and lose **thousands of teeth** over their whole lives, with new ones always moving in.
The **epaulette shark** can actually **walk** across the reef on its fins and barely needs air to do it.
The **hammerhead shark**'s wide head spreads its eyes far apart, so it can see almost all the way around.
Sharks help keep the whole ocean healthy and balanced.
Sharks almost never bump into people — people help sharks far more than sharks bother people.
A scientist named **Eugenie Clark**, the Shark Lady, studied sharks for her whole life and showed how curious they are.

new_recurring.name: Dot the LEGO Diver
new_recurring.rule: A tiny LEGO diver minifigure who wakes up when the magic red brick glows, guides the children through a topic with gentle facts, and waves goodbye from atop the brick at the end of each adventure.

bible_suggestions.ending_summary: Milo and Juno came home to find a tiny shark-tooth-shaped LEGO piece on the carpet, which Milo clicked onto the very top of their tower, and it held.

chapters.heading: Chapter 1: The Glowing Brick
chapters.text:
Milo lined up his LEGO sharks on the rug.

Juno stomped by, roaring like a dinosaur.

"Dinosaurs are the best!" she said.

"Sharks were here first," said Milo.

Then the red LEGO brick began to glow.

It pulsed red, then blue, then green.

CLICK! The brick popped open.

Cool water spilled out, like a tiny wave.

A shark popped his snout through the gap.

"Hello again!" he said. "I'm Splash."

"Ready for a swim?" Splash asked.

"YES!" shouted Juno. She hugged her dinosaur toy tight, just in case.

"Play well," said the brick, the way it always did.

WHOOOOSH!

The rug turned into blue water, and Milo and Juno swam down, down, down. He giggled as the water tickled his toes.

Splash flipped, and his whole body bent like a bow.

"Feel my fin," he said.

Milo touched it. It was bendy, not hard at all.

"My skeleton isn't bone," said Splash. "It's cartilage — soft, bendy stuff, like the squishy part of your ear."

Milo squeezed his own ear. "Whoa! Bendy like that?"

"Exactly like that!" said Splash.

"There are more than 500 different kinds of sharks swimming right now!" said Splash.

Milo counted on his fingers. "500?! That's SO many!"

chapters.heading: Chapter 2: The Very Old Ocean
chapters.text:
The water grew darker, and older somehow.

No fish with legs. No dinosaurs. No trees.

"Where are we?" asked Juno.

"Long, long ago," said Splash.

"Sharks have swum here for more than 400 million years — before dinosaurs, before trees, before anything with legs!"

Milo's eyes went wide. "Older than EVERYTHING?"

"Older than everything," said Splash, nodding.

Milo pointed at a glowing coral shape, curious and amazed.

Juno waved both arms like fins, pretending to swim through time.

Juno pointed. "Look! A weird shark!"

A strange fish-shape glided by, with spines on its back.

"That's one of the very first sharks," said Splash.

Milo waved. "Hi, old-timer!"

The shark seemed to wave its fin right back.

Juno giggled. "It waved! It waved!"

"OLDER THAN EVERYTHING!" Milo shouted, laughing.

chapters.heading: Chapter 3: The Tooth as Big as a Hand
chapters.text:
A shadow slid over them, huge and long.

Juno gasped. "Is it going to eat us?"

"No, no," said Splash gently. "He's not really here. We're seeing him in a memory."

The giant shape faded like a dream, soft and slow.

"That was Megalodon," said Splash. "The biggest shark ever."

"Where did he go?" asked Milo.

"Sharks like him don't swim in our ocean anymore," said Splash. "But we still have proof he was real."

He held up a huge pointy tooth, as long as a hand.

Milo whispered, "That's a really big tooth, Splash."

"This is a fossil," said Splash. "A fossil is something old, turned to stone, that tells us a story."

Milo held the tooth carefully. "It's so big!"

"Megalodon's bendy skeleton didn't turn to stone," said Splash. "Only his teeth did. That's almost all we know about him — just his teeth."

Splash patted Milo's shoulder with his fin, kind and steady.

Juno patted the tooth gently. "Night night, old shark."

chapters.heading: Chapter 4: The Gentle Giant
chapters.text:
Something enormous glided toward them, speckled like a starry sky.

Juno ducked behind Milo. Then she peeked. "It's HUGE!"

"That's a whale shark," said Splash. "The biggest fish in the whole world."

"Does it eat people?" asked Juno, giggling at her own silly question.

"No way!" said Splash. "It eats plankton — tiny bits of food floating in the water."

Milo watched its giant mouth open wide, and wide, and wide.

"It just... gulps water?" Milo asked.

"And swallows the tiny bits, like a strainer," said Splash.

Milo patted its enormous side. "You're gentle, aren't you?"

The whale shark blinked slowly, as if to say yes.

Juno blew her own bubble back at the whale shark, proud of herself.

"Some whale sharks live for 100 years!" said Splash.

Juno's mouth fell open. "That's older than Grandpa!"

Milo laughed so hard he swallowed a bubble. BLORP!

chapters.heading: Chapter 5: Rows and Rows of Teeth
chapters.text:
A sleek gray shape cut through the water, smooth and fast.

"Great white shark!" said Milo. "I know this one!"

"He can grow 20 feet long," said Splash. "Almost as long as a school bus!"

Milo counted the rows of teeth, pointy and white.

Juno counted along with him. "One, two, three..." until she lost count and giggled.

"Whoa, so many teeth!" Milo said.

"Sharks lose teeth all the time," said Splash. "New ones just slide forward to take their place."

"Like a conveyor belt!" said Milo, thinking of his LEGO factory set.

"Exactly," said Splash. Splash gave him a proud nod.

Juno poked her own front tooth, wiggly already.

"Mine falls out too!" she said proudly.

Milo tapped his own front tooth, happy it wasn't wiggly yet.

"Just like a shark!" said Splash, and they all laughed.

chapters.heading: Chapter 6: The Hammer-Headed Swimmer
chapters.text:
Something swam by with a head shaped like a hammer.

Juno burst out laughing. "That shark has a silly head!"

"That's a hammerhead shark," said Splash. "His wide head spreads his eyes apart."

"Why?" asked Milo.

"So he can see almost all around him," said Splash.

Milo covered one eye, then the other, trying it out.

"I can only see a little bit!" he said.

The hammerhead swung his head side to side, scanning the sandy floor.

"He's looking for his next snack," said Splash.

Juno copied him, swinging her head side to side too.

"I'm a hammerhead!" she shouted. "SWISH SWASH!"

Splash spun in a circle, mimicking the hammerhead's swing.

Juno added, "Hammerheads are my new favorite, after dinosaurs!"

Milo decided right then to add a hammerhead minifigure to his LEGO ocean set at home.

chapters.heading: Chapter 7: The Walking Shark
chapters.text:
A small spotted shark flip-flopped across the rocks below.

"Is it... walking?" asked Milo.

"Yes!" said Splash. "That's an epaulette shark. He walks on his fins, like tiny paddles."

The little shark scooted from one tide pool to another.

"He can even hold his breath for hours," said Splash.

Juno tried wiggling across the sandy floor. "Look, I'm walking like a shark!"

Milo joined her, flopping his arms like fins.

"WIGGLE WIGGLE!" they both shouted, giggling.

Splash wiggled his tail too, trying to keep up with the tiny walker.

Juno clapped her hands, delighted by the little walker.

Splash laughed so hard that bubbles popped out of his gills. PFFT!

chapters.heading: Chapter 8: The Shark Lady
chapters.text:
The light shifted, warm and golden.

A kind woman in scuba gear swam up, smiling.

"This is Eugenie Clark," said Splash. "We called her the Shark Lady."

"She studied sharks for years and years," said Splash. "She proved sharks are curious, and smart enough to learn tricks!"

Milo gasped. "Sharks can learn tricks? Like a puppy?"

"Just like that," said Eugenie, winking.

She touched a shark gliding past. Its skin felt rough, like sandpaper.

"Feel this," she said. Milo ran his hand along it. "Whoa, it's bumpy!"

"Tiny tooth-shaped bumps called denticles," said Eugenie. "They help him swim smoothly."

"Sharks help keep the whole ocean healthy," said Eugenie. "They're very important."

Milo thanked Eugenie with a big smile.

Juno hugged a passing shark-shaped bubble. "Good job, sharks!"

Then the water began to swirl, pulling them up, up, up.

WHOOOOSH!

Milo and Juno landed back on their rug, soft and dry.

The red brick glowed one last time, then went still.

On the carpet sat a tiny LEGO shark tooth, shiny and new.

"Play well," whispered the brick.

Milo picked up the tiny tooth and grinned at Juno.

Juno yawned a dinosaur-sized yawn.

story.ending_line: Goodnight, Milo. Goodnight, Juno. Play well.

story.title: Milo, Juno and the Brick That Found the Sharks
story.subtitle: A splashy, toothy, gentle-giant adventure

chapters.heading: Chapter 1: The Glowing Brick
chapters.text: Milo and Juno sat on the carpet. Their LEGO tower stood tall beside them. It had held all week. Ever since the final brick went CLICK. Milo tapped the top brick. It was the little red one. It started to glow, bright and warm. Juno gasped. "It's doing the thing!" The brick buzzed in Milo's hand. Then: WHOOOOSH! The carpet turned into soft, blue water. Milo blinked. Bubbles floated past his nose. "We're swimming!" he said. A shape swam close. Long and gray, with a gentle smile. "Hello," said the shark. "I'm your guide tonight." Milo grinned so big. He loved sharks almost as much as LEGO. "Sharks are fish," said the guide. "But our bones aren't hard like yours. We have cartilage instead. It's bendy, like the squishy part of your ear." Juno squeezed her own ear. "Squishy!" she said happily. "There are more than five hundred kinds of sharks," said the guide. "Swimming all over the world." Juno counted on her fingers. "One, two... five hundred is SO many!" Everyone laughed, bubbles rising all around.

chapters.heading: Chapter 2: Older Than Dinosaurs
chapters.text: The water grew darker and older-looking. Bubbles rose from somewhere deep below. "Where are we now?" asked Milo. The guide swirled slowly around them. "Long, long ago," she said. "Sharks swam here over four hundred million years ago. That's before the dinosaurs. Before even trees!" Juno's eyes went wide. "Before DINOSAURS?" she shouted. "That's SO old!" Milo thought about his LEGO dinosaur set at home. "So sharks are older than my triceratops?" "Much older," said the guide. A strange, fish-shaped shadow swam past them. Milo pointed. "Was that a shark's great-great-grandparent?" The guide nodded, smiling. "One of the very first ones." Juno floated near an old rock. "Were sharks here before LEGO too?" she asked. Milo laughed. "Everything was before LEGO, Juno." She paddled her arms like fins. "I'm an old-timey shark!" she yelled. Milo laughed so hard he swallowed a tiny bubble. They swam on, past rocks older than any story Milo had ever heard.

chapters.heading: Chapter 3: The Gentle Giant
chapters.text: A huge shadow blocked the sunlight above them. Milo froze. "Is that a monster?" The guide laughed, soft and bubbly. "That's a whale shark. The biggest fish in the whole world. Over forty feet long!" Juno looked up, up, up. "That's bigger than our house!" The whale shark's skin was covered in pale spots, like stars. Milo swam closer, carefully. "What does it eat? Boats? Us?" "Nothing like that," said the guide. "It eats tiny floating food called plankton. Bits smaller than your fingernail. It just opens its giant mouth and gulps water through, like a strainer." The whale shark opened its mouth. SLLLLURP! Milo giggled. "It's basically a giant, gentle vacuum cleaner!" Juno clapped her hands. "Gentle giant! Gentle giant!" she sang. The whale shark swished its tail, slow and happy, and swam off into the blue.

chapters.heading: Chapter 4: Rows and Rows of Teeth
chapters.text: Something sleek and silver cut through the water. Milo's heart jumped. "Great white!" he whispered. The guide nodded. "Up to twenty feet long. Look at those teeth." The great white opened its mouth, just a little. Rows of triangle teeth, lined up like LEGO bricks in a box. Milo gasped. "They're like little saws!" "For catching fish and seals," said the guide. Juno tugged Milo's sleeve. "Is it going to eat US?" she asked, a tiny bit worried. The guide shook her head quickly. "No, no. Great whites don't want to eat kids. It's just swimming by." Far away, a seal swam safely past, never even noticing. Juno relaxed and grinned. "Phew!" Milo had an idea. "When we get home, I'm building a LEGO shark with a hundred tiny teeth!" The great white swished away, teeth and all, looking for its dinner somewhere else.

chapters.heading: Chapter 5: The Giant from Long Ago
chapters.text: The guide led them to a cave wall. It was covered in huge, pointy shapes. "Fossils," she said. "Old, old teeth turned to stone." Milo touched one. It was as long as his whole hand. "Whose teeth are THESE?" "Megalodon," said the guide. "A giant shark that lived millions of years ago. It's extinct now. That means none are left today." Juno patted the fossil tooth gently. "Goodnight, big shark," she whispered, sweetly. Milo looked closer. "Why do we only have teeth, not bones?" "Shark skeletons are cartilage, remember?" said the guide. "It almost never turns into fossil. Only the hard teeth stick around." Milo nodded slowly. "Sharks keep growing new teeth their whole life," the guide added. "Thousands and thousands. New ones pop in to replace old ones." Juno's mouth dropped open. "Thousands?! I only have baby teeth!" Everyone laughed, and swam on.

chapters.heading: Chapter 6: Sandpaper Skin and Wobbly Heads
chapters.text: Milo reached out and touched a passing shark's side. "Whoa, it's rough!" "That's dermal denticles," said the guide. "Tiny tooth-like bumps, all over shark skin. Rough like sandpaper, but it helps them swim fast and smooth." Juno rubbed her own arm. "Mine's not rough." "Nope," laughed the guide. "Just sharks." A strange shark swam by with a wide, flat, hammer-shaped head. Juno pointed. "Why's its head so WEIRD?" "That's a hammerhead," said the guide. "Its wide head spreads its eyes apart. It sees all around, like wraparound goggles." Milo loved that. "Best superpower ever." Then something even stranger happened. A small shark near the sandy bottom used its fins to WALK across a rock. "That's an epaulette shark," said the guide. "It can walk right over the reef on its fins. It can even hold its breath for hours in a puddle!" Juno gasped. "Sharks can WALK and HOLD THEIR BREATH?!" She tried walking like a shark, wobbling and giggling on imaginary fins.
chapters.shout_line: Sharks can WALK and HOLD THEIR BREATH?!

chapters.heading: Chapter 7: Mermaid's Purses and River Sharks
chapters.text: In a patch of swaying seaweed, Milo spotted something strange. A leathery pouch, curled like a noodle. "What IS that?" he asked. "A mermaid's purse," said the guide. "That's just a fun nickname. It's really a shark egg case. A baby shark grows inside until it's ready." Juno peeked inside carefully. "I see a tail!" she whispered, delighted. "Other sharks don't use eggs at all," the guide added. "Their babies are born ready to swim, right away." They swam on, and the water turned brownish and murky. "Where'd the blue go?" Milo asked. "This is a river," said the guide. "Bull sharks can swim here too, not just in the salty sea. They go wherever they want." Juno splashed happily. "Sharks in a RIVER? That's wild!" Nearby, a sleepy shark lay still on the sandy bottom. "That one's resting," said the guide. "Some sharks can pump water over their gills while they nap. They don't even have to swim to breathe." Milo grinned. "Lucky. I have to get out of bed for water."
chapters.shout_line: Sharks in a RIVER? That's wild!

chapters.heading: Chapter 8: The Shark Lady
chapters.text: A kind woman in a diving suit swam up, smiling behind her mask. "Hello! I'm Eugenie," she said. "People called me the Shark Lady." Milo's eyes lit up. "You study SHARKS? For real?" "My whole life," she said. "I learned sharks are curious, and smart. I even trained some to do tricks, like ringing a bell." Juno giggled. "A shark doorbell!" Eugenie smiled. "Sharks matter a lot," she said. "They're apex predators. That means they sit at the top of the ocean's food chain. They help keep everything else balanced and healthy." Milo thought hard. "So the ocean needs them." "Exactly," said Eugenie. A huge whale shark glided by, slow and peaceful. "Some whale sharks live over a hundred years," Eugenie said. Juno counted on her fingers again, way past ten, then just threw her hands up. "That's SO many birthdays!" Everyone laughed, bubbles rising all around.

chapters.heading: Chapter 9: Back to the Carpet
chapters.text: Eugenie waved goodbye, sinking into the blue. "Play well, you two," she called. The water began to spin, slow at first, then fast. WHOOOOSH! Milo and Juno landed softly on the carpet. Their LEGO tower stood right where they'd left it. On the very top brick sat a tiny new piece. A little gray LEGO shark, smiling, with tiny gray teeth. Milo picked it up gently. "The ocean left us a present!" Juno hugged the shark piece against her cheek. "I'm naming him Chomp," she announced. Milo set Chomp on top of the tower. The brick gave one last happy little CLICK. Juno yawned a giant yawn. Milo yawned right back. Outside, the window had gone dark and quiet. They climbed into bed, still thinking about whale sharks big as houses, and teeth as long as hands, and a lady who talked to sharks.

story.ending_line: Goodnight, Milo. Goodnight, Juno. Play well.

true_facts.text: Sharks have **cartilage** instead of hard bones — bendy, like the squishy part of your ear.
There are more than **five hundred** kinds of sharks swimming in the world.
Sharks swam in the ocean over **four hundred million years** ago, before dinosaurs.
The **whale shark** is the biggest fish in the world, over **forty feet** long, and it eats tiny plankton.
A **great white shark** can grow up to **twenty feet** long, with rows of triangle teeth.
**Megalodon** was a giant shark from long ago. It is **extinct** now, which means none are left today.
Because shark skeletons are **cartilage**, mostly their hard teeth turn into **fossils**.
Sharks keep growing new teeth their whole lives, thousands and thousands of them.
Shark skin feels rough like sandpaper because of tiny bumps called **dermal denticles**.
The **epaulette shark** can walk across rocks on its fins and hold its breath for hours.
The **hammerhead shark** has a wide head that spreads its eyes apart for a wraparound view.
**Eugenie Clark**, the **Shark Lady**, studied sharks her whole life and even trained some to do tricks.
Some **whale sharks** live over a **hundred years**, one of the longest fish lifespans around.

new_recurring.name: Eugenie Clark, the Shark Lady
new_recurring.rule: A warm, curious guide who appears in ocean-themed adventures, shares real shark facts kindly, and signs off with 'Play well.'

bible_suggestions.ending_summary: Back home, a tiny new LEGO shark piece named Chomp appeared on top of the tower, and the brick gave one last happy CLICK before the children climbed into bed.
