story.title: Ben and the Pixel Time Machine
story.subtitle: A blocky guide takes Ben on a tour through video game history.

chapters.heading: Chapter 1: The Green Dot in the Lab
chapters.text:
Ben sat on his bedroom floor, drawing a pixel dog on his tablet. Each square was its own color. He loved counting every tiny block until the dog looked just right.

Then the screen flickered. Green. Black. Green again.

"Whoa," Ben said. "Did you just glitch?"

A burst of tiny squares popped out of the screen. They swirled together into a blocky little creature with blinking eyes, like a sprite that had escaped the game.

"BOOP!" it said. "I'm Blip. I live inside old screens. Want to see where games began?"

Before Ben could answer, green light filled the room. WHOOSH. The floor turned into a glowing grid, and his chair became a lab stool.

They landed in a big room full of humming machines. A scientist leaned over a strange box with a round screen.

"That's an **oscilloscope**," Blip said. "It's a machine that draws wiggly lines of light to test electricity."

The scientist, **William Higinbotham**, flipped a switch. A green dot bounced across the round screen, back and forth.

Ben leaned closer. "It's a ball! Is that tennis?"

"Good eye," said Blip. "In **1958**, at a lab called **Brookhaven**, he built this. He called it Tennis for Two. It's one of the very first video games ever made."

Ben swung an imaginary paddle at the dot. People lined up to try it, laughing every time they missed.

"This is way before Minecraft," Ben said.

"Everything starts somewhere," Blip said. "Ready for stop two?"

"BOOP! Let's go," Ben grinned.

chapters.heading: Chapter 2: The Humming Computer Room
chapters.text:
WHOOSH. They landed in a room the size of a garage, filled with one giant machine.

"That's a computer?" Ben asked. "It's huge!"

"This one's called a **PDP-1**," Blip said. "Back then, computers filled whole rooms."

A student typed quickly at a keyboard. Two little triangle ships appeared on the round screen, shooting tiny dots at each other.

"In **1962**, a student named **Steve Russell** and his friends made this," Blip said. "They called it Spacewar! It was one of the first computer games made just for fun."

Ben studied the ships. "They look like pixel art. Like, really early pixel art."

"That's exactly what they are," Blip said.

Ben watched the dots fly past the ships, missing every time. "What if the ships could spin around? Then you could dodge better."

The student typed something new. The ship spun in a slow circle.

"Whoa, it worked!" Ben said.

"Players kept asking for new tricks," Blip said. "That's how games grow. Somebody always asks, what if?"

Ben counted how many shots missed before one finally hit. "Eleven misses. That guy needs practice."

Blip laughed, a sound like a tiny beep. "Next stop is a house with a brand-new kind of television."

chapters.heading: Chapter 3: A Box for the TV
chapters.text:
They landed in a cozy living room. A man sat on the floor surrounded by wires and plastic parts.

"That's **Ralph Baer**," Blip said. "People later called him the father of video games."

Ben watched him connect wires to an old television. "What's he building?"

"A **prototype**," Blip said. "That means a first try, before the real thing gets made. He called it the Brown Box."

Ralph flipped a switch. Two white paddles appeared on the TV screen, with a square dot bouncing between them.

"It's like Tennis for Two," Ben said, "but on a TV, in someone's living room."

"Exactly," Blip said. "In **1972**, his invention became the **Magnavox Odyssey**, the first video game console you could play at home."

Ben pointed at the screen. "What if you stuck colored plastic over it? Like, orange for a basketball court?"

Blip nodded. "People really did stick plastic sheets right over their screens, just like that, to make it look fancier."

The room suddenly shifted into a noisy arcade, machines blinking everywhere. A new game sat in the middle: two paddles, one ball, simple white lines.

"That same year," Blip said, "**Nolan Bushnell** and **Ted Dabney** started a company called Atari. They made an arcade game called **Pong**."

A crowd of kids lined up with coins in their hands.

"Some people say one Pong machine got so stuffed with coins it actually jammed shut," Blip said. "That part might be stretched a little tall, but it shows how fast everyone fell in love with it."

Ben laughed. "A coin traffic jam."

"BOOP! Let's see what came after paddles," Blip said.

chapters.heading: Chapter 4: Swap the Cartridge
chapters.text:
They landed in a den with a big wood-paneled TV. A kid was sliding a flat plastic rectangle into a slot.

"That's a **cartridge**," Blip said. "It's like a little plastic box with a game stored inside. You could swap it out for a different one."

Ben's eyes lit up. "Like changing worlds in Minecraft! You don't need a whole new game machine, you just pick a new game."

"Right," Blip said. "In **1977**, the **Atari 2600** let players do exactly that."

The screen flashed, and rows of blocky aliens marched sideways, slowly dropping lower.

"Whoa, who made this one?" Ben asked.

"A designer named **Tomohiro Nishikado**," Blip said. "In **1978**, he made **Space Invaders** for a company called Taito. It caused a giant craze in arcades everywhere."

Ben counted the aliens. "Five rows. Eleven across. I'd shoot the edges first, so they can't speed up as fast."

He pretended to fire. Two rows of aliens blinked out.

"Good strategy," Blip said. "Players lined up around the block to try that game."

"It's basically pixel art that shoots lasers," Ben said.

"That's one way to put it," Blip laughed. "Next stop, a hungry yellow circle."

chapters.heading: Chapter 5: The Hungry Circle and the Buried Games
chapters.text:
A bright maze appeared, glowing blue. A yellow circle zipped through it, gobbling up little dots.

"This is **Pac-Man**," Blip said. "A designer named **Toru Iwatani** made it in **1980** for a company called Namco."

Ben watched the circle chase four colorful ghosts, then turn and chase them back after eating a bigger dot.

"Why's he shaped like that?" Ben asked.

"People say he got the idea from looking at a pizza with one slice missing," Blip said. "Nobody's totally sure that story's true, but it's a fun one."

Ben laughed. "Pac-Man is a pizza. I'm never looking at pizza the same way again."

The scene shifted. Shelves of game cartridges crowded a store, dusty and unwanted.

"By **1983**, so many rushed, sloppy games got made that shoppers stopped trusting them," Blip said. "Stores had way too many games and not enough buyers. People call it the video game crash."

Ben frowned. "That sounds sad."

"It wasn't the end, though," Blip said. "Watch this."

A truck rolled up to a big dirt pit in the desert and dumped boxes of cartridges inside.

"Some unsold games, including one called E.T., got buried in a landfill in New Mexico," Blip said. "A landfill is just a huge dump where trash gets buried."

"Did anyone ever check if that's true?" Ben asked.

"Good question," Blip said. "In **2014**, diggers actually dug there and found the buried cartridges, just like the story said."

"So it's buried treasure," Ben said, "treasure nobody wanted."

Blip giggled. "Something like that. Don't worry, Ben, games were about to make the biggest comeback ever."

chapters.heading: Chapter 6: The Plumber and the Falling Blocks
chapters.text:
They landed in a toy store. A new gray box sat on a shelf, with a game box beside it.

"In **1985**, Nintendo brought games back to America with this," Blip said. "It's called the **NES**. It came packed with a brand new game."

The TV flicked on. A small mustached man in overalls jumped over a mushroom creature.

"That's **Mario**!" Ben shouted.

"A designer named **Shigeru Miyamoto** made **Super Mario Bros.** that same year," Blip said. "Mario became the most famous game character of all time."

Ben watched Mario leap onto a floating block. "What if he jumped on top instead of running into it?"

On screen, Mario did exactly that, bopping the block from below. A coin popped out.

"You've got good instincts," Blip said.

The scene shifted to a snowy office in another country, where a scientist stared at a screen full of falling shapes.

"This is **Alexey Pajitnov**," Blip said. "In **1984**, in Moscow, he invented a puzzle game called **Tetris**. Blocks fall, and you fit them together."

Ben watched a long piece drop into a gap, clearing a whole row with a satisfying CLACK.

"It's like stacking blocks in Minecraft," Ben said, "except they disappear when you get it right."

"Exactly like that," Blip said.

chapters.heading: Chapter 7: Speedy Hedgehogs and Spinning Discs
chapters.text:
The room spun into a blur of colors. Blip grabbed Ben's sleeve. "Hang on, this part moves fast."

A blue hedgehog blasted across the screen, curling into a spinning ball.

"In **1991**, a company called Sega made **Sonic the Hedgehog**," Blip said. "He was built to be fast, to race against Mario."

"He's basically a speedrunner," Ben said.

Next, a silver disc spun inside a new gray console.

"In **1994**, **Sony** made the **PlayStation**," Blip said. "It used **CDs**, shiny discs, instead of cartridges. That meant games could have longer stories and fuller sound."

The scene flicked again. Two kids sat at computers connected by a tangle of cables, grinning at their screens.

"In **1993**, a game called **Doom** let players team up or compete through a bunch of connected computers," Blip said. "Friends plugging their computers together to play got called a LAN party."

"Like a sleepover, but for games," Ben said.

"Exactly," Blip said.

One more flash, and a family stood in a living room swinging their arms at a TV, holding small white controllers.

"In **2006**, Nintendo's **Wii** let you swing the controller like a tennis racket or a sword," Blip said. "Even people who never played games before started trying it."

Ben swung an imaginary controller. "This is a lot of history for one afternoon."

"We're nearly caught up to you," Blip said, grinning.

chapters.heading: Chapter 8: Back to the Blocks
chapters.text:
The light shifted to soft blue, and Ben recognized the shape of a block-built world stretching in every direction.

"Wait," Ben said. "Is this—"

"**Minecraft**," Blip said. "A developer named **Markus Persson**, who people called **Notch**, released it in **2011**."

Ben looked around at the cube-shaped trees and grassy hills. "This is literally the thing I play every day."

"It became the best-selling video game ever made," Blip said.

Ben grinned, thinking about every tower, every farm, every pixel-art banner he'd ever built. "I guess I'm part of this story too."

"You always were," Blip said.

One last WHOOSH carried them into a bright museum hallway, glass cases glowing with old consoles and posters.

"This is **The Strong museum**, in Rochester, New York," Blip said. "In **2015**, it opened the **World Video Game Hall of Fame**, to remember games that mattered."

Ben peered into a case holding an old Pong machine, a Mario cartridge, a dusty Tetris disk.

"They're like fossils," Ben said, then paused. "Wait, not fossils. Like, old treasures."

"Good save," Blip laughed.

Then the museum lights blurred into green and black, and the floor turned back to carpet.

Ben blinked. He was back in his room, tablet glowing in his lap. His pixel dog drawing was still there, finished, every square exactly where he'd left it.

Sitting beside the tablet was one tiny square pixel, glowing faintly green, shaped like the dot from Tennis for Two.

"Blip?" Ben whispered.

No answer. Just the little glowing pixel, and a quiet room.

Ben tucked it under his pillow and climbed into bed, smiling at the ceiling.

story.ending_line: Goodnight, Ben. Game well.

true_facts.text: In **1958**, a scientist named **William Higinbotham** built one of the first video games, Tennis for Two, at a lab called **Brookhaven**, using a bouncing green dot on a round screen.
In **1962**, a student named **Steve Russell** and his friends made a space-ship game called Spacewar! on a giant room-sized computer.
**Ralph Baer**, later called the father of video games, built a test version of a home game called the Brown Box.
In **1972**, Ralph Baer's invention became the **Magnavox Odyssey**, the first video game console you could play at home.
Also in **1972**, **Nolan Bushnell** and **Ted Dabney** started Atari and made the arcade game **Pong**.
A fun story says one Pong arcade machine got so stuffed with coins it jammed shut, though that part might be a bit of an exaggeration.
The **Atari 2600**, which came out in **1977**, let players swap in plastic game cartridges instead of being stuck with one game.
In **1978**, designer **Tomohiro Nishikado** made **Space Invaders**, which caused a huge arcade craze.
In **1980**, **Toru Iwatani** made **Pac-Man**, maybe inspired by a pizza missing a slice.
By **1983**, too many rushed, sloppy games flooded stores, and the video game business had a big crash.
Some unsold games, including E.T., were buried in a desert landfill, and diggers actually found them there in **2014**.
In **1985**, the **NES** brought video games back to America, packed together with a brand new game.
**Shigeru Miyamoto** designed **Super Mario Bros.** in **1985**, starring Mario, the most famous game character ever.
A developer named **Markus 'Notch' Persson** released **Minecraft** in **2011**, and it became the best-selling video game ever made.

new_recurring.rule: A tiny pixel sprite who lives inside old screens. He appears through flickering green-and-black glitches to guide kids through true history or science adventures, says 'BOOP' when excited, and signs off with the catchphrase 'Game well.'

bible_suggestions.ending_summary: Ben woke back in his bedroom with his finished pixel-dog drawing still glowing on his tablet, and a tiny glowing green pixel from Tennis for Two tucked under his pillow.

story.title: Maya and the Great Space Race
story.subtitle: A bedtime splashdown among the stars

chapters.heading: Chapter 1: The Beeping Bathtub
chapters.text:
Maya lay in the bathtub, drawing a wobbly sailboat on the tile with a bath crayon.

It had been four whole nights since the big bridge hummed its last note, and Barnacle waved a flipper goodbye from the river. Tonight the water was just plain water. Or so she thought.

Then her little plastic rocket-boat went **BEEP. BEEP-BEEP. BEEP.**

Maya sat up fast. "Boats don't beep!"

The water began to swirl, glowing blue-white like a nightlight. Up popped a round, whiskery face. "All aboard, Maya!" said Barnacle the harbour seal, grinning his gap-toothed grin.

"That beeping sound," he said, "is really old. Long ago, on **October 4, 1957**, the Soviet Union — that's a country that doesn't exist anymore, but people there spoke Russian — launched a shiny ball called **Sputnik 1** into space. It was the first man-made thing ever to circle Earth, which just means go round and round it like a toy train on a track."

"How big was it?" Maya asked, dipping her crayon like a paintbrush.

"About the size of a beach ball," said Barnacle. "And it didn't do much. Just floated up there going **BEEP, BEEP, BEEP** on an ordinary radio, so people everywhere could listen in."

Maya grabbed her floating rocket-boat and held it to her ear. It beeped right along with the glowing water.

"That's the actual sound?" she said. "That's so weird. And so cool."

"Everyone thought so too," said Barnacle. "It scared some folks and thrilled everybody else, all at once. Two countries were racing to be first in space, and Sputnik had just won the first lap."

The water rose up around the tub in a shining ring, like a hula hoop made of light.

"Want to see where it went?" Barnacle asked.

Maya didn't even answer. She just grabbed the sides of the tub and held on.

**SPLOOSH!**

The bathroom disappeared. The bath crayon sailboat on the tile was the last thing she saw before the stars rushed in.

chapters.heading: Chapter 2: Laika's Big Loop
chapters.text:
Maya and Barnacle floated gently, surrounded by a soft dark sky full of tiny lights.

A little silver capsule, shaped like a goldfish bowl with wings, drifted past. Through its round window, Maya spotted something fuzzy and brown.

"Is that... a dog?" she gasped.

"Her name was **Laika**," said Barnacle. "On **November 3, 1957**, just a month after Sputnik, she became the first living creature to ever orbit Earth. She was small and brave, and the whole world cheered for her."

Maya pressed her hand against the glowing air, as close to the little dog as she could get. "Good girl," she whispered. "Good, good girl."

"People back home felt just like you do," said Barnacle softly. "They loved her for it."

On the other side of the sky, a second light blinked on, red, white, and blue.

"That one's new," said Maya, pointing. "What's that?"

"Good eye," said Barnacle. "The Americans were shocked that the Soviets kept winning. So on **October 1, 1958**, they started a brand new space team called **NASA**. That's just a short way of saying the group of people in America whose whole job is space."

A little rocket zoomed by with a toy-sized satellite riding on top.

"Their first satellite went up not long after," said Barnacle, "and it found something nobody expected floating around way up high — an invisible ring of space weather circling the whole planet."

Maya blinked. "You can't see weather!"

"Not with your eyes," grinned Barnacle. "But their instruments could. Pretty great for a first try, don't you think?"

Maya giggled and gave a little salute to the fuzzy dog drifting by. "Good job, Laika. Good job, everybody."

chapters.heading: Chapter 3: Gagarin's Giant Loop
chapters.text:
A loud **WHOOOOOSH** rattled the stars, and a silver rocket shot past so close that Maya's hair blew sideways.

"Whoa!" she laughed. "Who's driving that?"

"A pilot named **Yuri Gagarin**," said Barnacle, paddling after it. "On **April 12, 1961**, he climbed aboard a capsule called Vostok 1 and became the very first human being ever to go to space."

Maya watched the little rocket circle all the way around a glowing blue marble that looked an awful lot like Earth.

"How long did that take?" she asked.

"About **108 minutes**," said Barnacle.

Maya counted on her fingers, then gave up. "That's not even two whole movies!"

"Nope," said Barnacle. "One whole trip around the world, faster than you can finish popcorn."

Through the rocket's little round window, Maya could just make out a smiling face. She waved both arms as hard as she could.

"Do you think he can see me?" she asked.

"I think," said Barnacle, "wherever he is now, he'd be glad somebody's still waving."

The rocket gave a friendly wobble, almost like a wave back, before zooming off into the dark. Maya grinned so wide her cheeks hurt.

"Best. Loop. Ever," she said.

chapters.heading: Chapter 4: The President's Dare
chapters.text:
The stars thinned out, and a tall man in a dark suit appeared, standing on a little floating stage with a microphone.

"Why's there a grown-up just standing in space?" Maya whispered.

"That's **President Kennedy**," said Barnacle. "He ran the United States. On **May 25, 1961**, he stood up and made a big, bold promise."

The man's voice rolled out across the dark like thunder, even though he wasn't shouting. "We choose to land a man on the Moon," it echoed, "before this ten-year stretch — what grown-ups call a decade — is over."

Maya's mouth dropped open. "The actual Moon? Like, the one outside my window?"

"That very same Moon," said Barnacle, pointing at a pale round shape glowing in the distance.

"But nobody had ever done that," Maya said. "How did he even know it was possible?"

"He didn't, not for sure," said Barnacle. "That's what made it such a big dare. Sometimes the bravest thing you can do is promise something before you know exactly how."

Maya thought about the time she'd promised to swim a whole pool length without stopping, before she'd ever tried it even once.

"I get that," she said quietly. "I did it anyway. It just took practice."

"Just like this will," said Barnacle, nudging her shoulder with his nose. "Lots and lots of practice. Ready to watch some of it?"

Maya nodded so hard her teeth clicked.

chapters.heading: Chapter 5: Valentina's Turn
chapters.text:
A bright capsule zipped by, spinning gently like a top.

"Girls get to go too, right?" Maya asked suddenly. "It can't just be the boys having all the fun."

Barnacle's whiskers twitched into a smile. "Funny you should ask. On **June 16, 1963**, a woman named **Valentina Tereshkova** climbed aboard that very capsule, Vostok 6, and became the first woman ever to fly in space."

"What did she do before that?" Maya asked, paddling closer to peek through the window.

"She worked in a factory," said Barnacle. "Then she trained hard, and she went and circled the whole Earth, again and again and again."

Maya watched Valentina's capsule loop around the glowing Earth-marble, over and over, trailing a little sparkle each time like a skipping stone on a pond.

"She just kept going," Maya said, grinning. "Round and round and round."

"Just like that," said Barnacle. "Some people said girls couldn't do it. She went and circled the whole planet instead of arguing."

Maya pumped her fist in the air. "That's way better than arguing."

She waved as hard as she could, and for just a second, she was sure she saw a tiny wave wave back through the glass.

chapters.heading: Chapter 6: The Floating Walk
chapters.text:
A hiss of air drifted past, and a figure in a puffy white suit floated right out of a capsule door, tethered by a long cord like a kite string.

Maya's eyes went huge. "He's just... floating? Outside the ship? In space?"

"That's **Alexei Leonov**," said Barnacle. "On **March 18, 1965**, he opened the hatch of his capsule, Voskhod 2, and became the first person ever to step outside into open space. Folks call that a spacewalk."

"Isn't that terrifying?" Maya asked, though she said it with a grin, not a worry.

"Maybe a little," said Barnacle. "But he had his tether, his suit kept him safe and breathing, and he floated right there for about **ten minutes** before climbing back in."

Maya watched Leonov tumble slowly, doing a lazy somersault with nothing below him but stars.

"I want to try that," she said, and tried a somersault of her own right there in the glowing dark. She spun clean around, giggling the whole way.

"Not bad," laughed Barnacle. "Though you'll want a spacesuit next time. It's a bit chilly out here."

"Worth it," said Maya, still spinning. "Totally worth it."

chapters.heading: Chapter 7: The Photograph
chapters.text:
A quiet capsule drifted by, far bigger than the others, with a round window at its front.

"Shh," said Barnacle, for once not cracking a joke. "Watch this part."

Through the window, an astronaut lifted a camera. In **December 1968**, the Apollo 8 crew became the first people ever to circle the Moon, and one of them, **William Anders**, pointed his camera back the other way.

Maya followed his gaze.

There, hanging over the Moon's grey edge, was Earth. Blue and white and small, like a marble somebody had dropped and forgotten to pick up.

"That's... us?" Maya whispered. "That's everything? My whole house and the pool and everybody I know?"

"All of it," said Barnacle. "Right there in one little picture. People call it Earthrise."

Maya pulled her bath crayon from behind her ear, where it had somehow stayed tucked this whole time, and sketched the curve of it in the air, just to feel like she'd drawn it herself.

"It's so small," she said.

"And so is everyone on it," said Barnacle gently. "Which maybe makes it worth taking care of."

Maya tucked the invisible drawing against her chest, like she meant to keep it forever.

chapters.heading: Chapter 8: One Giant Leap
chapters.text:
A huge rocket roared by, taller than anything Maya had ever seen, trailing fire like a comet.

"That one's enormous!" she shouted over the noise.

"That's Saturn V," said Barnacle. "Taller than the Statue of Liberty. It's carrying three astronauts to the Moon."

They followed it all the way down to a dusty grey ground. A ladder unfolded. A boot stepped down.

"On **July 20, 1969**," said Barnacle, "**Neil Armstrong** became the very first person to ever walk on the Moon. He said it was one small step for a man, one giant leap for mankind."

Maya watched him bounce across the dust in big, slow, floaty hops.

"The gravity's different there," she said. "He's basically flying!"

"Good thinking," said Barnacle. "A second astronaut, **Buzz Aldrin**, came down and bounced right along beside him. A third one, **Michael Collins**, stayed up above the whole time, flying the ship that would bring them all home."

"That seems lonely," said Maya. "Staying up there all by himself."

"Maybe," said Barnacle. "But somebody has to mind the boat while the others explore. Sound familiar?"

Maya thought of the times she'd held the rope while her family waded out from their little rowboat. "Yeah," she grinned. "Actually, it does."

She cupped her hands and shouted down at the little bouncing figures, even though she knew they couldn't hear her.

"ONE GIANT LEAP!" she yelled, and Barnacle yelled it right along with her.

chapters.heading: Chapter 9: The Scare and the Save
chapters.text:
The sky darkened, just a little, and the glow around them flickered.

"Uh oh," said Maya, grabbing Barnacle's flipper. "What's wrong?"

"In **1970**," said Barnacle, keeping his voice calm and steady, "a tank of oxygen — that's the air astronauts need to breathe — broke apart on a ship called Apollo 13, on its way to the Moon."

Maya's eyes went wide. "Were they okay?"

"Here's the good part," said Barnacle quickly. "Everyone on the ground worked together, day and night, and came up with a clever fix using things the astronauts already had on board. Every single one of those astronauts made it home safe."

Maya let out a breath she hadn't known she was holding. "That's such a relief."

"It sure was," said Barnacle. "Sometimes the bravest part of a story isn't the scary bit. It's everybody working together to fix it."

A little capsule drifted calmly past, splashing down into a wide, glittering sea below.

"They always land in water?" Maya asked, suddenly brightening. "Like boats?"

"Exactly like boats," said Barnacle, splashing his tail happily. "Big ships would come scoop them right up afterward. Space and water, Maya. Always more connected than people think."

Maya grinned her biggest grin of the whole night.

chapters.heading: Chapter 10: Splashdown Home
chapters.text:
The dark sky began to brighten, turning gold, then pink, then the familiar blue-white glow of the bathroom light.

"One more stop," said Barnacle, "before we head home."

Two spaceships drifted together, slow and careful, until their doors lined up.

"On **July 17, 1975**," said Barnacle, "an American ship and a Soviet ship docked together way up in orbit. The astronauts and cosmonauts opened their hatches and shook hands, right there in space."

"After racing each other the whole time?" Maya asked.

"That's how the whole race ended," said Barnacle. "Not with a winner and a loser. With a handshake."

Maya thought that sounded like exactly the right ending for a race that had started with a beeping ball and a very brave dog.

The glowing ring of light swirled around them again, pulling them gently down, down, down—

**SPLOOSH!**

Maya landed back in the bathtub with a splash, her bath crayon still tucked behind her ear, her little rocket-boat bobbing beside her, quiet now.

On the tile, her wobbly drawing of a sailboat had a tiny new addition next to it: a small, round Earth, blue and white, exactly like the one from the photograph.

"Did I draw that?" Maya whispered.

Barnacle winked one whiskery eye from the swirling water. "All aboard, Maya. Sleep tight."

He slipped beneath the surface with one last happy **SPLOOSH**, and the water went still and ordinary again.

Maya climbed out, wrapped herself in her towel, and carried her little rocket-boat all the way to bed.

story.ending_line: Goodnight, Maya. All aboard for dreamland — SPLOOSH.

On **October 1, 1958**, the Americans started a new space team called **NASA**.
On **April 12, 1961**, **Yuri Gagarin** became the first human ever to go to space, circling Earth once in about **108 minutes**.
On **May 25, 1961**, **President Kennedy** promised the Moon would be reached before the decade — ten years — was over.
On **June 16, 1963**, **Valentina Tereshkova** became the first woman ever to fly in space.
On **March 18, 1965**, **Alexei Leonov** became the first person to float outside his ship in space, for about **ten minutes**.
In **December 1968**, the Apollo 8 crew became the first people to circle the Moon, and one of them photographed the famous **Earthrise**.
On **July 20, 1969**, **Neil Armstrong** became the first person ever to walk on the Moon.
**Buzz Aldrin** walked on the Moon too, while **Michael Collins** stayed above, flying the ship.
In **1970**, a broken oxygen tank put the Apollo 13 crew in danger, but everyone made it home safely.
The giant Saturn V rocket that flew to the Moon was taller than the Statue of Liberty.
On **July 17, 1975**, an American ship and a Soviet ship docked together in space, and the crews shook hands.

story.title: Jack, Ellie, and the Shell That Opened the Sea
story.subtitle: A bedtime dive through shark history, with the Shark Lady herself

chapters.heading: Chapter 1: The Shell That Hummed
chapters.text:
Jack lined up seven plastic shark teeth on the carpet, biggest to smallest. Ellie flopped down next to him, her mermaid-tail blanket flapping like a fin.

"Watch it, guppy," Jack said, grinning.

"Watch it yourself, shark breath," Ellie said, and flicked his elbow with her tail.

On the dresser, the little seashell nightlight glowed its usual soft blue-green. Then it did something new. It went HMMMMM, low and warm, like a seashell held up to an ear. The glow grew until it popped into a round, shimmering bubble.

Inside stood a woman in a wetsuit, holding a clipboard, somehow completely dry. "I'm Eugenie," she said. "Most people call me the Shark Lady. I study sharks for fun. Want to see one up close?"

"Do sharks even have bones?" Jack asked, holding up his biggest plastic tooth.

"Sort of," said Eugenie. "Real shark skeletons are made of **cartilage** — bendy stuff, like the squishy part inside your ear, not hard bone like yours."

Jack's eyes went wide. He grabbed Ellie's hand and stepped toward the bubble.

"Mermaids belong in water," Ellie announced, stepping in right behind him.

The bubble swallowed them both. WHOOOOSH.

chapters.heading: Chapter 2: The Gentle Giant
chapters.text:
They landed with a SPLOOSH in warm, blue water, bubbles streaming past their faces.

Something enormous glided by overhead, blotting out the sunlight like a cloud.

"Is that a whale?" Ellie whispered.

"Nope," said Eugenie, floating beside them. "That's a fish. There are more than **500 kinds** of sharks in the ocean, and that's one of the biggest."

Jack counted its spots like stars. "It's not even eating anything big."

"Right," said Eugenie. "The whale shark grows over **40 feet** long — longer than a school bus — but it mostly eats **plankton**, tiny floating bits of food smaller than rice."

Ellie giggled. "A giant eating crumbs."

The whale shark swam slow circles around them, calm as a cloud.

"How old do you think he is?" Eugenie asked.

Jack studied its patterns. "A hundred?"

"Good guess," said Eugenie. "Some whale sharks live **100 years** or more."

Ellie reached out a hand, then pulled it back on her own. "We just look, right? We don't touch."

"That's exactly right," said Eugenie, nodding. "We watch. We never touch."

They waved instead, and the whale shark swam on, unbothered, into the blue.

chapters.heading: Chapter 3: The Oldest Fish in the Sea
chapters.text:
The water around them shimmered and went dark, like a light switching off. When it brightened again, the ocean looked empty and strange.

"Where are we?" Jack asked.

"Way, way back," said Eugenie. "The very first sharks swam here more than **400 million years** ago — before dinosaurs, before trees, before almost anything."

Ellie spun around slowly. "It's so quiet."

Then a huge shadow slid past below them, bigger than their whole house.

"That," said Eugenie, "was megalodon. The biggest shark that ever lived."

"Is it going to come back?" Ellie asked, gripping Jack's arm.

"No," said Eugenie gently. "Megalodon is **extinct** now. That means it doesn't swim anywhere anymore. It only lived long, long ago."

Jack spotted something half-buried in the sand below — a huge, triangle-shaped tooth as long as his hand.

"Can I grab it?" he asked.

"Go ahead," said Eugenie. "That's how we know about megalodon at all. Almost everything we know comes from **fossil teeth** like that one."

Ellie held it up to the light. "Its owner must have been bigger than a bus."

"Spot on," said Eugenie, smiling.

Jack tucked the huge tooth under his arm like a trophy.

chapters.heading: Chapter 4: A Mouthful of Teeth
chapters.text:
Back in brighter water, Jack rubbed his own jaw. "My tooth took forever to grow back when I lost it."

"Sharks don't wait around," said Eugenie. "A shark can grow and lose **thousands of teeth** in its life. New ones are always lined up, moving forward to replace the old ones."

"Thousands?" Jack said. "Lucky. No tooth fairy could keep up."

A small reef shark cruised past close enough for them to see its skin shimmer.

"Looks bumpy," said Ellie.

"Good eye," said Eugenie. She held up a smooth gray patch of shark skin from her bag for them to feel, careful and still. "It feels rough, like sandpaper. Tiny tooth-shaped bumps called **denticles** cover the whole body. They help the shark slide through water fast and smooth."

Jack ran one finger over it. "It's like tiny teeth all over its skin."

"Exactly," said Eugenie.

Ellie wrinkled her nose. "So if a shark hugged you, it would feel like sandpaper."

"Good thing sharks don't hug," said Jack, and Ellie swatted him with her tail fin, laughing.

chapters.heading: Chapter 5: The Hammer-Headed Hunter
chapters.text:
A strange shape drifted ahead — a shark with a head shaped like a flattened hammer.

Ellie gasped. "Why does its head look like that?"

"That's a hammerhead," said Eugenie. "Its wide head spreads its eyes far apart, so it gets a wraparound view all around itself."

"Like having eyes on the sides of a helmet," Jack said.

"Sort of," said Eugenie.

Jack watched it swing its head side to side over the sand. "What's it doing?"

"Searching," said Eugenie. "Sharks have special dots on their noses that feel tiny sparks of electricity. Every swimming animal makes a little spark, even hiding under the sand."

Ellie's eyes lit up. "So it's not looking. It's feeling for sparks!"

"That's it exactly," said Eugenie, clapping once.

The hammerhead swung its wide head one more time, snapped up something small from the sand, and glided off into the blue, unbothered by its audience.

chapters.heading: Chapter 6: Three Strange Sharks
chapters.text:
They surfaced near a sunny coral reef, shallow enough to see everything.

"Look!" Jack shouted. A small shark was using its fins like little paddles, walking across the coral instead of swimming.

"That's the epaulette shark," said Eugenie. "It can walk across reefs on its fins, and it can go hours with barely any air at all."

"A shark that walks," Ellie said. "That's basically a mermaid with extra steps."

Suddenly something streaked past in a blur, gone before they could blink.

"Whoa! Was that even real?" Jack asked.

"That's the shortfin mako," said Eugenie. "Fastest shark there is. It uses quick bursts of speed to catch fast fish."

Nearby, a wide gray shark lay perfectly still on the sandy bottom.

"Is it asleep?" Ellie whispered.

"Resting," said Eugenie. "That's a nurse shark. It can pump water over its gills — the parts it breathes through — while it just lies there. It doesn't have to keep swimming to breathe."

"Walking, racing, and napping," Jack said. "Sharks do it all."

"I pick the walking one," said Ellie.

"I pick the fast one," said Jack. "Obviously."

chapters.heading: Chapter 7: The Mermaid's Purse
chapters.text:
Something small and leathery drifted past Ellie's nose, shaped like a tiny black pillow with curly strings on each corner.

"What IS that?" she asked, scooping it gently into her palm.

"That," said Eugenie, "is called a mermaid's purse."

Ellie's whole face lit up. "A real one?"

"Some sharks lay their eggs inside pouches like that one," said Eugenie. "Other sharks just have live babies instead."

Ellie held it up to the light, careful not to squeeze. "Is there a baby shark inside this one right now?"

"There could be," said Eugenie, smiling. "Good guess."

A shark glided by in the shallows nearby, then turned and swam toward a muddy river mouth.

"Wait, sharks don't go in rivers," Jack said.

"Some do," said Eugenie. "Bull sharks can swim in salty ocean water and in **freshwater** rivers — water that isn't salty at all."

Jack's jaw dropped. "A shark. In a river. That's wild."

Ellie tucked the little purse carefully back into the water where she'd found it, waving it off like saying goodbye to a friend.

chapters.heading: Chapter 8: Swim Deep, Dream Deep
chapters.text:
The light began to change, turning that same soft blue-green as the nightlight back home.

"Time to go soon," said Eugenie. "But first — sharks matter. They sit at the top of the ocean's food chain, which means they help keep everything else balanced, like a steady hand on a seesaw."

"Are they dangerous?" Ellie asked, a little quiet.

"Barely at all," said Eugenie. "Shark attacks on people are **very rare**. Sharks are in far more danger from people than we are from them."

Jack looked at the plastic teeth he still had clipped to his pocket. "Is that why you study them?"

"Exactly why," said Eugenie. "My whole life, people thought sharks were just scary. I wanted to show the world they're curious, not cruel."

"You're basically a shark whisperer," Jack said.

"I like that," Eugenie laughed. "Ready for home?"

The bubble wrapped around them again. WHOOOOSH.

They landed back on the carpet, blanket tail and plastic teeth right where they'd left them. The seashell nightlight glowed softly on the dresser — and beside it sat one tiny shell, shaped exactly like a shark's tooth, glittering faintly blue.

"Keepsake," Jack whispered, grinning at Ellie.

"Goodnight, mermaid," he said.

"Goodnight, shark breath," she said back, smiling.

story.ending_line: Goodnight, Jack. Goodnight, Ellie. Swim deep, and dream deep.

story.title: Maya and the Race to the Moon
story.subtitle: A splashy trip through the real Space Race.

chapters.heading: Chapter 1: The Beep in the Fish Tank
chapters.text:
Maya lay on her bedroom floor, drawing a tiny boat with crayons. It had been one whole week since Barnacle waved his flipper at the bridge that hummed.

Her night-light flickered. Then her fish tank started to glow bright green.

BEEP. BEEP. BEEP.

The sound came from the water, not from any speaker. Maya sat up fast. "That's not my fish," she whispered.

A whiskered nose popped up through the glowing water. "All aboard, Maya!" said Barnacle the harbour seal, grinning his big gummy grin.

"Barnacle! Where did that beep come from?"

"From space," said Barnacle. "A real beep, from a real round ball, way back in 1957."

Maya leaned closer. The water swirled like a little round window, showing darkness with tiny white dots.

"On **October 4, 1957**, the Soviet Union launched a round machine called **Sputnik 1**," Barnacle said. "It was the first man-made thing to ever circle the whole Earth."

"How big was it?" Maya asked, already sketching a circle in her notebook.

"About as wide as a beach ball," said Barnacle. "Just **58 centimeters**. But it carried a little radio that went *beep, beep, beep*, and people everywhere could hear it on their own radios at home."

Maya tapped the glass. "Like our fish tank is doing right now?"

"Exactly like that," said Barnacle. "Your tank caught the echo, all the way from long ago."

Maya grabbed her crayon and drew little lines shooting out from her round ball, like the beep was singing a song. "I want to see it fly," she said.

The moment she said it, the water rose up in a glowing bubble. **SPLOOSH!** The bedroom melted away, and Maya and Barnacle floated beside a small silver ball, blinking its beep into the dark.

"Ready for the whole trip?" asked Barnacle.

Maya grinned and grabbed his flipper. "All aboard!"

chapters.heading: Chapter 2: Laika's Big Ride
chapters.text:
The bubble floated past the little silver ball, and a second, bigger one drifted into view behind it.

"One month later, a second satellite went up," said Barnacle. "This one had a passenger."

"A person?" Maya asked.

"A dog," said Barnacle. "A brave little dog named **Laika**. On **November 3, 1957**, she became the first living creature to ever circle the Earth."

Maya pressed her nose to the glowing water. Inside, she could just make out a small furry shape curled up snug inside a round little room built just her size, called a capsule.

"Was she scared?" Maya asked.

"She was a good traveler," said Barnacle gently. "And she made the whole world fall in love with her. Kids everywhere drew pictures of her, just like you draw boats."

That gave Maya an idea. She flipped to a fresh page and drew Laika with a little space helmet and a wagging tail. The moment she finished the tail, the drawing seemed to wag right there on the paper.

"Ooh!" Maya laughed. "Did you see that?"

"Space magic," said Barnacle. "Or maybe just very good drawing."

Maya giggled. "Both, probably."

"Laika showed everyone that a living creature could survive going all the way around the Earth," said Barnacle. "She helped open the door for real people to go next."

Maya tucked her drawing carefully into her notebook, right beside Sputnik. "She gets to come with us," she said firmly.

"She always does," said Barnacle, with a wink.

chapters.heading: Chapter 3: America Answers Back
chapters.text:
The bubble drifted forward, and the dark sky filled with blueprints and busy people in white coats.

"Sputnik's beep gave the United States a big surprise," said Barnacle. "So they built a brand new team just for space."

"What kind of team?" Maya asked.

"It's called **NASA**," said Barnacle. "It started working on **October 1, 1958**. Their whole job was figuring out how to fly to space."

Maya spotted a long silver rocket standing on a launchpad below them. "Is that theirs?"

"That's **Explorer 1**," said Barnacle. "It launched on **January 31, 1958** — America's very first satellite."

The rocket roared up with a **WHOOOSH**, and Maya clapped her hands over her ears.

"What did it find up there?" she asked, once the shaking stopped.

"Something nobody expected," said Barnacle. "A big ring of tiny invisible zaps wrapped around the Earth, like a giant belt. It's called the **Van Allen belt**. It can't reach down to us on the ground, but spaceships flying through it have to be careful."

Maya thought about her swim goggles keeping pool water out of her eyes. "So it's like the Earth wears invisible armbands?"

Barnacle laughed so hard he nearly slipped off his rock. "I like that! Yes — invisible armbands, there to bump anything that flies through too fast."

Maya drew a circle around her picture of the Earth, with a wobbly dotted ring. "There," she said. "Now everyone will know to be careful."

"Good thinking," said Barnacle. "That belt helped scientists learn a lot about space, all because one little rocket went looking."

chapters.heading: Chapter 4: One Trip Around
chapters.text:
The bubble swirled faster, and a bright orange capsule zoomed into view, spinning gently around the glowing Earth.

"**April 12, 1961**," said Barnacle. "A pilot named **Yuri Gagarin** became the first human being to ever fly in space."

Maya's eyes went wide. "A whole person? Up there?"

"All the way around the Earth, once, in his ship called **Vostok 1**," said Barnacle. "The whole trip took about **108 minutes** — shorter than one of your school days."

Maya watched Gagarin's capsule zip past, and she waved both arms at the little round window. Inside, it almost looked like he waved back.

"A few weeks later," Barnacle went on, "an American named Alan Shepard flew too, though his trip was shorter and didn't go all the way around."

"Everybody wanted a turn," Maya said.

"Everybody did," agreed Barnacle. "On **May 25, 1961**, the American President stood up and made a big, bold promise. He said America would land a person on the Moon, and bring them safely home, before the end of that same ten years."

Maya looked out at the small grey Moon hanging in the dark. It looked very, very far away.

"That's a big promise," she said.

"The biggest," said Barnacle. "Want to see if they kept it?"

Maya grabbed his flipper. "Yes! Let's go see!"

"Patience," chuckled Barnacle. "We've got a few more stops first. All aboard."

chapters.heading: Chapter 5: The Factory Worker Who Flew
chapters.text:
The bubble floated on, and a new capsule appeared, painted a cheerful white.

"Two years after Gagarin," said Barnacle, "someone else made history."

Inside the round window, Maya spotted a woman with short dark hair, smiling calmly at the stars.

"Who is she?" Maya asked.

"**Valentina Tereshkova**," said Barnacle. "She used to work in a factory, sewing fabric. On **June 16, 1963**, she became the first woman ever to fly in space, orbiting the Earth in her ship, **Vostok 6**."

Maya pressed her hands to the glass, studying every detail. "I want to draw her," she said.

She sketched quickly: a round capsule window, a woman waving, little stars all around. When she added a smile to the drawing, Tereshkova's tiny window-picture seemed to smile right back.

"She circled the whole Earth **forty-eight times**," Barnacle added.

Maya counted on her fingers, then gave up halfway through. "That's so many laps! More than the whole pool at swim practice."

"Many, many more," Barnacle agreed. "And every single lap, she was showing the world that space wasn't just for one kind of person. It was for anyone brave enough to go."

Maya tucked her new drawing next to the others. "She goes in my book too."

"Your book is getting pretty full," Barnacle said, peering over her shoulder.

"Good," said Maya. "There's room for more."

chapters.heading: Chapter 6: Floating Free
chapters.text:
The bubble bumped gently, like it hit a little wave, and Maya looked out to see something strange: a man floating completely outside his spaceship, tied on by only a long cord.

"Whoa," Maya breathed. "Is he falling?"

"He's floating on purpose," said Barnacle. "His name is **Alexei Leonov**. On **March 18, 1965**, he opened the hatch of his ship, **Voskhod 2**, and stepped right out into open space."

"With nothing holding him but that string?"

"Just that string," said Barnacle. "He floated outside for about **ten minutes** — the very first spacewalk anyone had ever done."

Maya thought of floating on her back in the swimming pool, arms out, looking up at the sky. "Is it like floating in the pool?"

"A little," said Barnacle, "except there's no water, no up, no down — just you and the stars, tied safely to your ship."

Maya kicked her legs gently inside the bubble, pretending to float the same way. For one second, the whole bubble spun lazily with her, stars sliding by.

"Careful," laughed Barnacle. "You'll make us both dizzy."

"Sorry," Maya giggled, holding still. "I just wanted to try it myself."

"That's exactly what Leonov wanted too," said Barnacle. "To try it first, so everyone after him would know it could be done."

Maya watched the little floating figure drift back toward his ship and climb safely inside. "He made it back okay," she said, relieved.

"Safe and sound," said Barnacle. "Now — onward, Maya."

chapters.heading: Chapter 7: The Whole World in One Picture
chapters.text:
The bubble rose higher, past the Moon's grey bumps, until suddenly Maya gasped.

There, over the Moon's edge, hung a small blue and white ball, glowing bright against the black sky.

"That's... that's us?" Maya whispered. "That's Earth?"

"That's Earth," said Barnacle softly. "In **December 1968**, three astronauts flew all the way around the Moon aboard **Apollo 8** — the first people ever to do it."

"Did they land?"

"Not that time. They circled it, then came home. But one of them, a man named **William Anders**, looked out his window at just the right moment and took a photograph."

"Of the Earth?" Maya asked.

"Of the Earth, rising over the Moon, like a little blue marble in a big black bathtub," said Barnacle. "People call it the **Earthrise** picture. It's one of the most famous photographs ever taken."

Maya stared at the small blue dot, thinking of every boat, every pool, every puddle she'd ever drawn, all somewhere down on that tiny ball.

"Can I draw it?" she asked.

"Go ahead," said Barnacle.

Maya pulled out her crayons and drew a careful circle, blue and green and white, rising over a grey curved edge. She held it up next to the real view, comparing the two.

"Pretty close," said Barnacle, nodding.

"I want to show everyone how small we look from up here," Maya said.

"That's exactly what that photograph did," said Barnacle. "It showed the whole world, all at once, how small and precious home really is."

chapters.heading: Chapter 8: One Giant Leap
chapters.text:
The bubble drifted down toward the Moon's dusty grey ground, and a huge rocket roared past them on its way up.

"That's the **Saturn V**," said Barnacle. "**363 feet tall** — taller than the Statue of Liberty standing on her toes."

Maya craned her neck, watching it shrink into the sky. "That's the biggest thing I've ever seen."

"It needed to be," said Barnacle. "It carried **Apollo 11**, and on **July 20, 1969**, it put two astronauts right down on the Moon's surface."

The scene shifted, and Maya saw a figure in a puffy white suit step slowly down a ladder onto the dusty ground.

"**Neil Armstrong**," whispered Barnacle. "The first person ever to walk on the Moon. He called it 'one giant leap for mankind.'"

Maya watched, barely breathing, as Armstrong's boot pressed into the grey dust and left a clear, perfect footprint.

"Who else was there?" Maya asked.

"**Buzz Aldrin** joined him on the ground a little later," said Barnacle. "And a third astronaut, **Michael Collins**, stayed up above, flying their ship, **Columbia**, all alone in orbit, waiting to bring them home."

Maya looked up at the lonely little ship circling overhead. "That sounds lonely."

"He had the best view of anyone," said Barnacle. "Watching both the Moon and the Earth at the very same time."

Maya pressed her hand flat against the glowing glass, matching her fingers to Armstrong's tiny footprint far below.

"We made it," she whispered.

"Humans did," said Barnacle, smiling. "And between **1969 and 1972**, **twelve** astronauts walked on the Moon, across **six** separate landing trips."

Maya grinned. "Twelve footprints. I want to draw every single one."

chapters.heading: Chapter 9: The Trip That Turned Around
chapters.text:
The bubble floated onward, past a spaceship suddenly lit up with flashing warning lights.

"This one didn't go quite as planned," said Barnacle, gently.

"What happened?" Maya asked, sitting up straight.

"In **1970**, an oxygen tank on **Apollo 13** broke while the astronauts were flying toward the Moon," said Barnacle. "It made a loud bang and shook their whole ship."

Maya's stomach fluttered. "Were they okay?"

"They were scared for a moment," said Barnacle, "but they were smart, and so were the helpers back on Earth. Together, using only the tools and parts already onboard, they built a fix to keep the air clean and the ship flying."

"Like fixing a leaky boat with whatever's in the toolbox?" Maya asked.

"Exactly like that," said Barnacle. "And it worked. The crew turned their ship around and came all the way home, safe and sound."

Maya let out a breath she hadn't realized she was holding. "I'm glad they made it."

"Me too," said Barnacle. "Sometimes the best part of an adventure isn't getting everything right the first time. It's figuring it out together, even when things go wrong."

Maya nodded slowly, thinking of the times her own boat drawings didn't come out quite right, and how she'd just tried again.

"Like when my boat picture needed three tries," she said.

"Just like that," said Barnacle, nudging her with his nose. "Three tries, and you still ended up with a beautiful boat."

Maya smiled, feeling a little braver already.

chapters.heading: Chapter 10: A Handshake in Space
chapters.text:
The bubble rose one last time, and Maya saw two very different spaceships drifting slowly toward each other, one marked with American letters, one with Soviet ones.

"This is the last stop," said Barnacle. "**July 17, 1975**."

"Are they going to crash?" Maya asked, worried.

"They're going to **dock**," said Barnacle. "That means two spaceships gently joining together, like two puzzle pieces clicking into one."

Maya watched the two ships line up slowly and touch, nose to nose, with the softest little **CLICK**.

A hatch opened between them, and two astronauts — one American, one Soviet — reached out and shook hands, floating together in the middle of the dark.

"After all that racing," Barnacle said, "that handshake was how the whole Space Race finally ended. Not with a winner. With a hello."

Maya watched the two smiling faces, floating together above the glowing Earth. "That's my favorite part," she said. "The hello part."

"Mine too," said Barnacle.

The bubble began to sink gently, the stars fading, the green glow softening back into ordinary fish-tank light. Maya felt the carpet under her knees again.

Her notebook lay open beside her, full of drawings: a round silver ball, a wagging dog, a smiling woman, a floating astronaut, a blue marble Earth, a dusty footprint, two tiny ships holding hands.

Barnacle's nose poked up through the calm water one last time. "You collected the whole race tonight, Maya."

"I did," Maya said, hugging her notebook to her chest. "All of it."

"**SPLOOSH**," said Barnacle softly, and slipped back beneath the water, leaving only a few gentle ripples behind.

story.ending_line: Goodnight, Maya. All aboard for dreamland now — SPLOOSH, and off to sleep.

true_facts.text: The first man-made thing to ever circle the Earth was a round machine called **Sputnik 1**, launched on **October 4, 1957**.
Sputnik 1 was about as wide as a beach ball — **58 centimeters** — and sent out a beeping radio sound anyone could catch on an ordinary radio.
A brave little dog named **Laika** became the first living creature to circle the Earth, riding **Sputnik 2** on **November 3, 1957**.
America built a brand new space team called **NASA**, which started working on **October 1, 1958**.
America's first satellite, **Explorer 1**, launched on **January 31, 1958**, and found a ring of tiny invisible zaps around the Earth called the Van Allen belt.
On **April 12, 1961**, pilot **Yuri Gagarin** became the first person ever to fly in space, circling Earth once in about **108 minutes**.
On **May 25, 1961**, the American President promised that the country would land a person on the Moon and bring them safely home before the decade ended.
On **June 16, 1963**, **Valentina Tereshkova**, who used to work in a factory, became the first woman in space, circling Earth **forty-eight times**.
On **March 18, 1965**, **Alexei Leonov** opened his spaceship's hatch and floated outside for about **ten minutes** — the first spacewalk ever.
In **December 1968**, Apollo 8 astronauts circled the Moon and took the famous **Earthrise** photo of Earth rising over the Moon's edge.
On **July 20, 1969**, **Neil Armstrong** became the first person to walk on the Moon, calling it 'one giant leap for mankind.'
During an Apollo 13 flight in **1970**, a broken oxygen tank shook the ship, but the crew and helpers on the ground fixed the problem and everyone came home safe.
The **Saturn V** rocket that carried astronauts to the Moon stood **363 feet** tall — taller than the Statue of Liberty.
On **July 17, 1975**, an American and a Soviet spaceship gently joined together in space, and their crews shook hands, ending the Space Race with a friendly hello.

new_recurring.name: The Puddle-Porthole
new_recurring.rule: Any glowing patch of water near Maya — fish tank, bath, puddle — can swirl open into a round window onto real history whenever Barnacle calls it; it never rushes her and always opens right after he says 'All aboard, Maya.'

bible_suggestions.ending_summary: Maya's notebook lies open on the carpet, filled with new drawings of Sputnik, Laika, Tereshkova, Earthrise, and the Apollo-Soyuz handshake, as Barnacle slips back beneath the fish-tank water with a soft SPLOOSH.

story.title: Phoenix and Cruz and the Lucky Green Rainbow
story.subtitle: A St. Patrick's Day adventure with Sprocket

chapters.heading: Chapter 1: The Tiny Green Sparkle
chapters.text:
Phoenix stacked red bricks into a tall LEGO tower. Tap, tap, tap. He drummed a little beat on the floor. He bounced like he'd just scored a goal.

Cruz flapped a blue blanket like a shark fin. CHOMP CHOMP! He snapped his pretend jaws near Phoenix's toes.

On the shelf sat a small stone, shaped like a bone. It used to glow bright. Tonight it sat quiet and still.

'I miss our adventures,' said Phoenix, sighing.

Then — BZZZT! A tiny light blinked awake. It was Sprocket, their small round robot friend.

Sprocket's glow was not blue tonight. It was bright green, like a shamrock leaf.

'Hello, friends!' chimed Sprocket. 'Tonight is something different. No swirly door this time.'

He spun around in a circle. WHOOOOSH! A ribbon of rainbow light unrolled across the carpet. It stretched all the way to the bedroom door.

Cruz counted the colors on his fingers. 'Red, orange, yellow...' He ran out of fingers and giggled.

'Follow the rainbow,' said Sprocket. 'It leads to real leprechaun stories, all the way from Ireland, across the sea.'

Phoenix grabbed Cruz's hand tight. Together, they stepped onto the glowing rainbow.

WHOOOOSH!

chapters.heading: Chapter 2: The Tap-Tap-Tap Shoemaker
chapters.text:
Tap. Tap. Tap.

A tiny hammer knocked somewhere close by. Phoenix looked all around. 'Where's that sound coming from?'

Behind a mossy rock sat a tiny old man. He wore a little green coat. He held a tiny shoe.

'That's a leprechaun,' whispered Sprocket. 'Old Irish stories say leprechauns are small, old-looking men who make and fix shoes. That is their one honest job, says the legend. A legend is a story told for a very long time, even if we're not totally sure it's true.'

The leprechaun looked up, surprised. 'Well, hello there! You heard my hammer before you saw me. That's how it always goes in the old tales. Tap, tap, tap — then surprise!'

Cruz giggled. 'Like Spiderman's spidey-sense!'

'Exactly like that,' laughed the leprechaun. 'My name is Finn. I'm fixing a boot for a very fast fairy.'

Phoenix tapped the beat right along with Finn's hammer. Tap-tap, tap-tap-tap!

Finn grinned. 'You've got rhythm, lad. Want to help me finish this shoe?'

Phoenix held the little boot steady. Finn stitched quick and neat. CLICK, went the very last stitch.

'Good work, team!' said Finn, tipping his hat.

chapters.heading: Chapter 3: Rainbow's End
chapters.text:
Finn hopped up onto a toadstool. 'Want to see something shiny?'

He pointed way up at a rainbow arching over green hills.

'Old stories say leprechauns hide pots of gold at the very end of a rainbow,' said Sprocket. 'That's why rainbows and treasure go together in the old tales.'

Cruz bounced on his toes. 'Let's find it! Let's find it!'

They raced along the rainbow's edge. Phoenix drummed his feet like a beat. Cruz did his best shark swim through the tall grass.

At the very end, they found... a little patch of clovers.

'Aww,' said Phoenix. Then he looked closer. 'Wait — four leaves!'

'A four-leaf clover,' said Sprocket. 'In Ireland, these are their own kind of lucky charm. Not quite the same as leprechaun gold, but just as special.'

Finn popped up beside them. 'No pot of gold under this one, I'm afraid. But every rainbow has its own little surprise.'

Cruz picked one gently. He tucked it behind his ear like a tiny green crown.

'SHARK DANCE!' he shouted, wiggling both arms, and everybody laughed.

chapters.heading: Chapter 4: The Trickiest Trick
chapters.text:
Finn suddenly hopped backward. 'Catch me if you can!' he teased, and dashed off through the grass.

'Wait!' laughed Phoenix, chasing after him. Cruz galloped behind, counting his steps. 'One, two, three, four!'

'Old stories say if you catch a leprechaun,' said Sprocket, 'he must grant you three wishes, or show you his hidden gold, before you let him go. That's the legend, anyway. Nobody knows for sure.'

'And another story says leprechauns are the trickiest tricksters of all,' Sprocket added. 'They'll try every clever trick to wriggle free.'

Phoenix dove — and gotcha! He gently caught Finn's little coat sleeve.

'Oh, clever lad!' laughed Finn. 'Fine, fine. One wish, coming right up!'

'I wish,' said Phoenix, 'for Cruz to get a turn catching you too!'

Finn winked, wiggled free quick as a blink, and hopped right into Cruz's waiting hands.

'I GOT HIM! I GOT HIM!' cheered Cruz, bouncing in a happy circle.

Finn laughed so hard his hat nearly fell off. 'Best catch of the whole day, little shark!'
chapters.shout_line: I GOT HIM! I GOT HIM!

chapters.heading: Chapter 5: Blink and He's Gone
chapters.text:
'Want to see my very best trick?' asked Finn, hopping up onto a stump.

'Old stories say if you look away from a leprechaun, even for one blink,' said Sprocket, 'he vanishes before you can look back.'

'No blinking!' said Phoenix, staring hard with wide-open eyes.

Cruz tried too, but his eyes watered. He blinked. BZZZT!

Finn was gone!

Cruz gasped — then giggled instead of worrying, because right behind him, Finn popped up from under a leaf.

'Boo!' said Finn.

Cruz jumped, then laughed so hard he flopped right over in the grass.

'You vanished!' said Cruz.

'Quick as a wink,' said Finn, bowing low. 'That's the game, little one. Don't feel bad — even grown-ups blink sometimes!'

Phoenix tried the staring game too. He lasted three whole seconds before Finn popped up somewhere brand new, waving both tiny hands.

'PANCAKE POWER!' shouted Cruz, for no reason at all, and everyone laughed anyway.

chapters.heading: Chapter 6: The Town of Little Green Doors
chapters.text:
The rainbow led them to a cozy little town by the sea. It had green doors and flower boxes on every window.

'This is Carlingford,' said Sprocket, 'a real town in Ireland, right by the water, where people love telling leprechaun stories.'

Phoenix pointed at a little sign shaped like a tiny footprint. 'What's that one?'

'In Carlingford,' said Sprocket, 'visitors can get a silly paper called a leprechaun hunting license. Then they follow a trail of clues all through the town, just for fun.'

'Can we get one?' asked Phoenix, bouncing on his toes.

Finn handed them each a little paper, stamped with a green shamrock. 'Here you are. Official leprechaun hunters!'

Cruz held his up proudly. 'I'm a shark AND a leprechaun hunter now!'

'This town gets extra busy every March seventeenth,' added Sprocket. 'That's a day called St. Patrick's Day, when people everywhere wear green and celebrate.'

Phoenix drummed a happy little rhythm on a lamppost. Tap tap, ta-tap!

Finn tipped his hat. 'Best day of the whole year, if you ask me.'

chapters.heading: Chapter 7: Lucky and the King
chapters.text:
Sprocket's light flickered like a tiny movie screen. A cartoon leprechaun popped up, waving a spoon.

'That's Lucky the Leprechaun,' said Sprocket. 'He's been smiling on cereal boxes since 1964. He always says his cereal is magically delicious — which just means he thinks it tastes extra wonderful, like a little bit of magic got sprinkled right on top.'

Cruz licked his lips. 'I want magically delicious pancakes!'

'PANCAKE POWER!' Phoenix shouted, and they both cracked up laughing.

The picture changed again. A tall man stood beside a tiny crowned leprechaun.

'That's from an old movie called Darby O'Gill and the Little People,' said Sprocket, 'made in 1959. It had a character called the king of the leprechauns. That movie made leprechauns famous all over the whole world.'

Finn puffed out his chest. 'I knew King Brian! Very fancy fellow. Loved his tricks even more than me.'

Phoenix grinned. 'Everybody loves a good trick tonight.'

Cruz nodded hard. 'CHOMP CHOMP! Trick time!'

chapters.heading: Chapter 8: Back Home, Pockets Full of Luck
chapters.text:
'Time to go home,' said Sprocket gently. His green glow softened.

Finn pressed something small into Phoenix's hand. It was a round gold coin, shiny as sunshine.

'Chocolate,' Finn winked, 'but it sparkles just like the legend. Share it with your brother.'

Cruz tucked his lucky clover safely behind his ear.

The rainbow ribbon unrolled again, right back toward their bedroom door.

WHOOOOSH!

Phoenix and Cruz tumbled onto their own carpet, right where they'd started. The LEGO tower still stood tall. The shark blanket still lay in a heap. Down the hall, the night-light glowed soft and gold.

On the carpet between them sat the little gold coin. It glowed the softest green. Beside it lay one small four-leaf clover.

Sprocket dimmed to a sleepy wink. 'You were excellent leprechaun hunters tonight.'

'Shark hunters too!' said Cruz, yawning a giant yawn.

Phoenix broke the chocolate coin in half. He handed Cruz the bigger piece.

'Best brother ever,' said Cruz, munching happily. CRUNCH CRUNCH.

'Print well, little hunters,' whispered Sprocket. His light blinked out like a tucked-in star.

story.ending_line: Goodnight, Phoenix. Goodnight, Cruz. Print well, and dream in green and gold.

true_facts.text: Leprechauns are little old-looking men from Irish stories who make and fix shoes.
Fixing shoes is said to be a leprechaun's one honest job.
Stories say you can hear a leprechaun's tap-tap-tap hammer before you ever see him.
Old tales say leprechauns hide pots of gold at the end of a rainbow.
Four-leaf clovers are a different lucky charm in Ireland, separate from leprechaun gold.
Legend says if you catch a leprechaun, he must grant wishes or show his gold before you let him go.
Stories say leprechauns are super tricky and will try every clever trick to get away.
Folklore says a leprechaun can vanish the second you look away, quick as a blink.
In a real town called Carlingford, in Ireland, visitors can get a silly leprechaun hunting license and follow a fun trail through town.
Leprechauns are linked to St. Patrick's Day, celebrated every year on March seventeenth.
Lucky the Leprechaun has smiled on cereal boxes since 1964, calling his cereal magically delicious.
An old 1959 movie called Darby O'Gill and the Little People made leprechauns famous, with a character called the king of the leprechauns.

new_recurring.name: The Rainbow Ribbon
new_recurring.rule: A shimmering rainbow ribbon of light that Sprocket spins into being with a WHOOOOSH. The children walk along it, staying their normal size, to reach a real place or story, then it unrolls again to carry them home.

bible_suggestions.ending_summary: Phoenix and Cruz landed back on their bedroom carpet with a soft-glowing chocolate gold coin, which Phoenix shared with Cruz, and one small four-leaf clover, as Sprocket blinked out whispering 'Print well.'
